#1. Jensen Huang’s departure blasts big hole in AI startup funding, VCs and founders say

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6 min read (1152 words)
AI & Tech

Jensen Huang’s departure blasts big hole in AI startup funding, VCs and founders say

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read | Sumber: https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/13/jensen-huangs-departure-blasts-big-hole-in-ai-startup-funding-vcs-and-founders-say/

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that it was the resignation heard across the world.
  • Recent findings suggest that over the last several years, Nvidia has been a prolific investor, pouring tens of billions into startups annually and participating in 105 rounds this year alone, often as the largest investor, according to PitchBook.
  • Huang’s absence leaves the startup ecosystem without one of its biggest champions and with far less capital for now, investors say, which could have a massive impact on dealmaking, valuations, funding, and even competition.

Sources indicate that it was the resignation heard across the world. Jensen Huang, Nvidia’s embattled CEO who co-founded and led the tech giant for 33 years, had officially stepped down. “It’s like a bomb went off,” one neocloud founder told TechCrunch when he first heard the news.

Recent findings suggest that over the last several years, Nvidia has been a prolific investor, pouring tens of billions into startups annually and participating in 105 rounds this year alone, often as the largest investor, according to PitchBook. “If that direction changes, it’ll be a significant blow to so many young companies,” mentioned Maria Davidson, founder of Relational Capital.

Huang’s absence leaves the startup ecosystem without one of its biggest champions and with far less capital for now, investors say, which could have a massive impact on dealmaking, valuations, funding, and even competition.

“Nvidia is carrying almost every AI-native startup from application to neocloud,” Dawn Capital’s Shamillah Bankiya told TechCrunch.

Sources indicate that most of the significant decisions to invest in startups often came from Jensen himself, according to Umesh Padval, managing partner at Seligman Ventures. Padval has known Huang since serving on the board of Mellanox Technologies, a networking chipmaker Nvidia acquired for approximately $7 billion in 2020. While there is hope that Huang’s eventual successor will resume his dealmaking spree, investors aren’t hopeful that it will happen in the short term.

It has been revealed that nvidia’s interim CEO, Colette Kress, is expected to institute some changes, especially when it comes to Nvidia’s investments into AI startups at the crux of the billion-dollar data center build-out. Huang’s rampant dealmaking in this sphere has been a source of concern for Wall Street.

Recent findings suggest that “She’s much more conservative,” one investor mentioned of Kress. “I don’t think she’s going to commit the same amount of money to keep the early-stage ecosystem going.”.

Nvidia’s biggest bets were backing neoclouds, inference providers, and open weight models, which are expensive for smaller companies to build. “Jensen’s initiatives are a significant reason an ecosystem has emerged despite that,” Zain Javaid, co-founder of the hardware company Ghost, stated.

It has been revealed that for instance, Nvidia backed CoreWeave when it was still private and participated in two of Crusoe’s rounds, including its $1.4 billion Series E. It bought Hugging Face this year for $13 billion (expected to close in 2027) and holds investments in Mistral AI, Lambda, and Black Forest Labs. Nvidia was often the largest investor in the deals. Last year, it wrote an $800 million check into a $2 billion Series B round for Reflection AI, before the open source startup began to earn meaningful revenue, according to the Wall Street Journal.

“Jensen believed in open source and frankly speaking, Europe,” Bankiya stated of how Huang invested so much in AI across the world. The cease of that support in other regions outside of America, like Europe “would be a massive funding and honestly ecosystem gap that no one can fill.”.

Sources indicate that it’s also true that Nvidia was such a dominant player in the ecosystem that at times, it felt like a monopoly. By backing so many companies with such generous checks, Nvidia effectively locked those startups into using its chips, which helped reinforce its dominant market position.

If the company does grow more conservative with its startup investments, that could leave more room for rivals and smaller competitors. (Coincidentally, Google announced two latest chips this week amid Huang’s Nvidia fallout.).

Some investors with whom TechCrunch spoke hope that large cloud companies and other chipmakers will step in to back startups and fill some of the void that will likely be left by Huang.

Industry observers note that dharmesh Thakker, a general partner at Battery Ventures, for example, expects Significant Tech rivals to vie for Nvidia’s investment crown, “depending upon who brings the best combination of a great product, an ecosystem and community to compete with CUDA, and the financial power to bankroll the ecosystem,” he mentioned. CUDA is Nvidia’s software platform that enables developers to run AI models on its GPUs.

While companies like Google, Amazon, Microsoft, and AMD may back mature startups to drive adoption of their chips and clouds, Thakker doubts they will pour hundreds of millions into pre-revenue infrastructure startups the way Nvidia did.

It has been revealed that under Huang, infrastructure companies that needed $100 million to $500 million in GPUs would often raise half of that amount at valuations of $1 billion or more from Nvidia just to get started, one VC noted. The chipmaker’s participation gave other investors the comfort in backing these companies at the lofty valuations.

Now Nvidia is expected to be more selective in the newly introduced companies it backs, while writing smaller-sized checks into its existing portfolio, contributing to a drop in valuations.

According to recent reports, “When Nvidia was on the cap table, everyone felt safe,” Padval stated. Without that backing, investors say traditional VCs are likely to think twice before writing checks into these startups and may even pause certain dealmaking.

Even so, few believe that Nvidia’s investment slowdown will by itself halt the broader AI boom.

Recent findings suggest that though everyone agrees that Huang is a massive loss for Nvidia, one of his ex-employees, Amulya Vishwanath, who now runs her own VC fund, mentioned that “founders and leaders must be held accountable,” and that the ecosystem is bigger than one person. “That talent will, and must, continue to thrive.”.

#3. Crunchbase Data: Nvidia’s Startup Funding Deals Hit A Record. What’s Next After Huang?

Crunchbase Data: Nvidia’s Startup Funding Deals Hit A Record. What’s Next After Huang?

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read | Sumber: https://news.crunchbase.com/venture/huang-nvda-ai-startup-funding-record-2026/

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Before it was thrust into crisis this week, Nvidia was steadily continuing its pace as one of the busiest startup investors around, including backing many of the biggest venture deals of 2026.
  • The chipmaker and its NVentures arm have participated in more than 120 startup funding deals so far this year, according to Crunchbase data, already topping last year’s record-setting pace and marking its most prolific year yet as a private-manufacturer investor.
  • With co-founder Jensen Huang’s sudden departure this week amid reports of multiple extramarital affairs including with employees and a woman U.S.

Before it was thrust into crisis this week, Nvidia was steadily continuing its pace as one of the busiest startup investors around, including backing many of the biggest venture deals of 2026.

The chipmaker and its NVentures arm have participated in more than 120 startup funding deals so far this year, according to Crunchbase data, already topping last year’s record-setting pace and marking its most prolific year yet as a private-manufacturer investor.

With co-founder Jensen Huang’s sudden departure this week amid reports of multiple extramarital affairs including with employees and a woman U.S. intelligence experts suspect of spying for China, we took a fresh look at where Nvidia and NVentures have been investing and what the future could hold.

It has been revealed that nvidia is the most active corporate investor so far in 2026, an analysis of Crunchbase data reveals. It and NVentures together are also among the top 20 most active investors in startups this year overall.

In a recent development, nvidia’s startup investments this year total 121 and span AI model developers, data center operators, robotics startups and healthcare companies. That continues the broad approach we examined last year, when the tech giant and its venture arm participated in 91 known startup financings, up from 54 the year prior.

It has been revealed that the largest Nvidia-backed deals in 2026 include OpenAI’s Series G, which closed at $122 billion in March, and Anthropic’s $30 billion Series G in February. (Those figures represent the entire rounds, including other investors’ contributions, rather than Nvidia’s individual checks.).

The firm also participated in a $3.9 billion September Series F for AI infrastructure provider Crusoe and a roughly $3.5 billion September Series D for model developer Mistral AI.

Of course, large as those deals are, Nvidia’s startup bets represent a small fraction of the organization’s incredible market capitalization. Even as its share price tumbled this week with Huang’s departure and the surrounding news, Nvidia’s valuation remains close to $4 trillion.

NVentures’ activity shows how far that investment footprint extends beyond the best-known model developers.

It has been revealed that the venture arm’s larger bets this year include robot intelligence developer Skild AI’s $1.4 billion January Series C, and autonomous driving startup Waabi’s $750 million Series C in the same month. It also backed two rounds for Bedrock Robotics, which develops technology to automate construction equipment: a $270 million Series B in February and a $600 million Series C in October. Its healthcare investments included a $150 million April Series E for medical imaging AI manufacturer Aidoc.

As in years past, Nvidia and NVentures usually participate alongside other investors. The tech giant or its venture arm are listed as lead or co-lead investors in about 1 in 5 of its deals this year, per Crunchbase data.

For startups, Nvidia’s value as an investor also extends beyond its deep pockets. NVentures describes its offering as access to technical teams, technology integrations and help reaching customers.

Nvidia’s new leadership could bring a different approach to risk. Before this week’s news, CFO and now interim CEO Collette Kress had pushed back on Huang’s increasingly large AI investments, Reuters reported this week, citing two people familiar with the matter.

Nvidia’s board has mentioned it expects operations, customer commitments and its product roadmap to continue without interruption. That assurance leaves the pace of future investments an open question. With earnings scheduled for Nov. 17, founders and investors will be watching for signs of how much of Huang’s investment playbook continues under new leadership.

#4. Latest Update: Your Success Might Be Creating Problems You Can’t See. Here’s What to Ask Yourself.

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7 min read (1445 words)
General

Latest Update: Your Success Might Be Creating Problems You Can’t See. Here’s What to Ask Yourself.

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read | Sumber: https://www.entrepreneur.com/building-a-business/your-success-might-be-creating-problems-you-cant-see-heres-what-to-ask-yourself

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that you're viewing the US website.
  • Your business may be growing, but what is that growth really costing you?
  • Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

Sources indicate that you're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Your business may be growing, but what is that growth really costing you?

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

Recent findings suggest that in the early 1920s, car manufacturers faced a frustrating problem: They wanted to build more powerful engines, but “engine knocking” kept getting in the way. Fuel igniting unevenly inside an engine created violent vibrations that damaged its components. The finest minds scratched their heads over how to get more power without sacrificing reliability.

In a recent development, meanwhile, refrigerator manufacturers faced a problem of their own: Some chemicals used in early refrigerators were toxic or highly flammable. A leak could turn a household appliance into a serious hazard. Finding a safer refrigerant could make refrigeration more practical for homes and businesses.

Enter Thomas Midgley Jr., an American engineer who was working at General Motors.

Recent findings suggest that midgley discovered that adding lead to the fuel could suppress engine knocking. Later, he’d help develop Freon, a refrigerant far less toxic and flammable than many alternatives in use at that time. And just like that, two stubborn engineering problems appeared to be solved.

It has been revealed that manufacturers respected him and adopted his work, and both products became commercial successes. For his work, the American Chemical Society awarded him the Priestley Medal, their highest honor.

You could look at that record and reasonably conclude he had done an excellent job. Entire industries were growing because of him, and he’d earned recognition from his peers.

Would you agree that by the usual measures, Midgley had an extraordinary career? Well … then the other shoe dropped.

According to recent reports, leaded petrol was found to spread toxic lead through the exhaust, exposing generations of people to a metal whose harmful effects we now know better about. Decades after Freon and related chemicals became widespread, scientists discovered that chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) damaged the Earth’s ozone layer.

Midgley died in 1944, before scientists discovered the damage to the ozone layer. In Midgley’s defence, he could not have predicted every consequence, but his story begs the question for anyone who has built a successful business: What if the very thing that made you successful is also creating costs you haven’t accounted for?

Warning signs around leaded petrol had already appeared during its early production, but the “cost” was ignored, and it remained in widespread use for decades. Freon seemed safe and harmless at first glance, and CFCs were widely used in refrigeration and elsewhere before scientists truly understood how they were damaging the ozone layer.

I think there’s a shared lesson in this about the limits of the original measure of success: A product can work as intended while creating consequences its original purpose never required anyone to consider.

Business owners can fall into a similar pattern. You find something that works, so you do more of it. Being available at all hours helps win customers, so you keep answering calls. Making every vital decision helps the business move swiftly, so you stay involved as the team expands and you keep accepting work because demand is strong.

Each decision may have solved a problem and helped you get where you are. The costs can emerge later, as the business grows and when you know better.

Early in a company’s life, personal involvement can be exactly what it needs.

The difficulty comes when those habits continue long after the circumstances that made them useful have changed. The founder who once needed to approve every vital decision may now be bottlenecking the team. The availability that once won clients leaves no room to switch off. The behavior that helped build the business can become expensive as the business grows.

Sometimes, getting personally involved is exactly what a business needs. You step in, solve a problem, establish a process or build a relationship that gets things moving. But was your involvement meant to be permanent? What began as a short-term solution can quietly become an ongoing responsibility, until you’re spending more time operating the business than leading it.

So now, you have more customers bringing more revenue, but also more complexity. A new market opens up, but demands more travel and attention. The business becomes more profitable while the owner’s time and energy become harder to protect, and their family is neglected.

Recent findings suggest that in my coaching conversations with entrepreneurs, I often return to the difference between what a business produces and what it demands from the person running it. Revenue, profit and growth are easy to track. The cost to a founder’s health, relationships, judgment or freedom can be harder to quantify, so it may go unexamined for years.

A business can be winning by its own measures while the person who built it pays a price they never intended to pay.

Industry observers note that none of this is the business owner’s fault, because it’s particularly easy to miss when the numbers look good. A crisis forces you to take a step back and review, but who stops to question continued success? Nobody.

When revenue is growing, and customers are happy, why feel pressured to question the way you’re running the business, even if the arrangement is becoming harder to sustain?

You don’t need to become suspicious of every ambitious decision; building a business requires risk, investment and choices whose consequences cannot be predicted perfectly. But you do need to ask whether your measures of success account for enough of the picture.

Imagine reviewing a new business initiative. You’d probably examine the expected revenue, costs, staffing, return, etc. Would you also ask what it will demand from you personally, what it might displace or whether the business will become more dependent on your involvement?

Recent findings suggest that tomorrow, choose one part of your business that is performing well. It might be your fastest-growing service, a major client relationship or a process that depends on you being constantly available.

According to recent reports, write down three things: what it produces, what it demands and what it displaces. Then consider whether the arrangement remains sustainable as the business grows. Is it delivering the results you need today at the expense of what the business will need to sustain those results over the longer term? Or can it continue producing the same results without placing increasing demands on you, your team or the resources the business needs elsewhere?

Time spent managing one opportunity is time unavailable for another. Energy spent resolving routine decisions cannot also be spent thinking about the future. An arrangement that works financially may place demands on family life that nobody intended when it began.

Then ask yourself what has changed since you first made that decision. Perhaps the business has grown, your responsibilities have shifted, regulations have changed, or a risk you once considered acceptable now deserves another look. Would you make the same decision today, knowing what you know now?

Industry observers note that if the answer is yes, carry on with a clearer understanding of the exchange. If something has changed, you have an opportunity to reconsider the arrangement while you still have options. You might choose to delegate a decision, renegotiate a client relationship or stop doing something that no longer justifies the demands it places on you.

The point is to make that choice while you still have options, rather than waiting for circumstances to make it for you.

You worked hard to build the business you have. You deserve to understand what it gives you, what it asks of you and whether that exchange still makes sense. Success deserves examination even when everything appears to be going well. Sometimes the most key decision a business owner makes is to look beyond the results that got them here.

In the early 1920s, car manufacturers faced a frustrating problem: They wanted to build more powerful engines, but “engine knocking” kept getting in the way. Fuel igniting unevenly inside an engine created violent vibrations that damaged its components. The finest minds scratched their heads over how to get more power without sacrificing reliability.

Meanwhile, refrigerator manufacturers faced a problem of their own: Some chemicals used in early refrigerators were toxic or highly flammable. A leak could turn a household appliance into a serious hazard. Finding a safer refrigerant could make refrigeration more practical for homes and businesses.

Enter Thomas Midgley Jr., an American engineer who was working at General Motors.

Album VC, a Lehi, Utah-based early-stage venture firm that’s been known until now as Peak Ventures, just gathered up $75 million in capital commitments for its third early-stage fund.

The development demonstrates investor confidence in Album’s young team, which came together in 2014 after the founder of Zinch — a site connecting colleges and students that sold to the ed-tech organization Chegg in 2011 — decided to try his hand at investing in other startups.

As that founder, Sid Krommenhoek — who stayed on with Chegg for several years, running its international efforts — explains it, “I thought I’d do another startup. But I also knew from our own experience in struggling to raise money the need for more capital in Utah, and I thought having that operator-entrepreneur perspective could be useful.”.

A first fund, like many in the industry, was more of an experiment, though it was a decent $23 million, thanks largely to the support of Chegg CEO Dan Rosensweig, who was early to commit capital to the fund. A second ($56 million) fund followed when Krommenhoek and John Mayfield — a friend who joined him from a marketing role at Qualtrics — began investing more seriously in their backyard and beyond.

They were soon joined by a third investor, Diogo Myrrha, who began as a principal with the firm and is now a general partner. Explains Krommenhoek of one of the many things that binds the three Brigham Young University grads, “We all came into Utah’s orbit when it wasn’t necessarily a place where you could live out your career, but that’s changed.”.

#6. Industry News: Gov. Ferguson seeks $10M to help develop Eastern Wash. clean-energy hub

Industry News: Gov. Ferguson seeks $10M to help develop Eastern Wash. clean-energy hub

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read | Sumber: https://www.geekwire.com/2026/gov-ferguson-seeks-10m-to-help-develop-eastern-wash-clean-energy-hub/

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Challenges, breakthroughs and major ideas in the race to protect our planet.
  • by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 13, 2026 at 4:32 pmNovember 13, 2026 at 4:32 pm.
  • Bob Ferguson is proposing $10 million to fund basic infrastructure needed for the Northwest Advanced Clean Energy Park, a master-planned industrial area in Eastern Washington that will foster development of large-scale clean energy, advanced manufacturing and supply chains.

Challenges, breakthroughs and major ideas in the race to protect our planet. SEE MORE.

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 13, 2026 at 4:32 pmNovember 13, 2026 at 4:32 pm.

Industry observers note that gov. Bob Ferguson is proposing $10 million to fund basic infrastructure needed for the Northwest Advanced Clean Energy Park, a master-planned industrial area in Eastern Washington that will foster development of large-scale clean energy, advanced manufacturing and supply chains. The proposal will be included in his 2027–29 capital budget.

If approved by lawmakers, the funding would support sewer, water, electrical and road infrastructure at the park.

“This investment will support thousands of good-paying jobs in the trades and advanced industries, and unlock billions in private investment,” Ferguson mentioned in a statement.

It has been revealed that the 1,641-acre site was formerly part of the Hanford Nuclear Reservation, a sprawling federal property along the Columbia River near the Tri-Cities that is undergoing a massive environmental cleanup. Hanford was established during World War II to produce plutonium for the Manhattan Project.

According to the governor’s office, two projects have committed to locating at the park once infrastructure construction is complete: Atlas Agro’s low-carbon fertilizer production plant and the utility-scale Ruby Flats Solar Farm.

State officials said General Matter is also considering the location for producing advanced nuclear fuel for small reactors. That siting could potentially be beneficial for another project planned for the same area: Amazon, X-energy and Energy Northwest are developing plans for the Cascade Advanced Energy Facility, a nuclear plant comprised of clustered, small reactors.

In 2024, the Norwegian organization Cenate expressed interest in building a factory at the park to produce lithium-ion battery components, according to the Tri-Cities Area Journal of Business, ultimately withdrew its intends.

In a recent development, the Tri-Cities is also attracting fusion-energy investment. Last year, Seattle startup Avalanche Energy landed a $10 million grant from the Washington State Department of Commerce’s Green Jobs Grant Program to develop FusionWERX, a commercial-scale testing facility for fusion technologies. The project is being developed in an existing Port of Benton building in Richland.

Washington is heading into its 2027–29 biennial budget with a multibillion-dollar shortfall, but officials have not yet settled on a definitive public estimate.

Industry observers note that ferguson has acknowledged the scale of the gap but has not publicly specified an amount. The shortfall concerns the state’s operating budget, which is separate from the capital budget funding proposed for the energy park.

The Climate Pledge is a commitment to reach net-zero carbon emissions by 2040, co-founded by Amazon and Global Optimism in 2019.

Seven years later, the community has grown to over 700 signatories across 62 industries and 49 countries and territories, reducing emissions, scaling emerging climate solutions, and addressing challenges across operations and value chains.

AI agent startup LangChain hits $3B valuation

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read | Sumber: https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/13/ai-agent-startup-langchain-hits-3b-valuation/

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Agent management startup LangChain has raised a $300 million Series C at a $3 billion valuation led by CapitalG, with participation from investors, including Singapore’s GIC, DFJ Growth, IVP, and Sapphire Ventures, the company announced on Friday.
  • That’s more than double its $1.25 billion valuation when it raised $125 million about a year ago, led by IVP.
  • LangChain began in 2022 as a popular open source project that handled the kinds of tasks that early-stage LLMs found difficult, like searching the web, calling APIs, and interacting with databases.

Agent management startup LangChain has raised a $300 million Series C at a $3 billion valuation led by CapitalG, with participation from investors, including Singapore’s GIC, DFJ Growth, IVP, and Sapphire Ventures, the company announced on Friday.

That’s more than double its $1.25 billion valuation when it raised $125 million about a year ago, led by IVP.

LangChain began in 2022 as a popular open source project that handled the kinds of tasks that early-stage LLMs found difficult, like searching the web, calling APIs, and interacting with databases. As the frontier AI labs delivered harnesses that now competently do those tasks, LangChain turned its focus toward managing AI agents. It has apparently found its stride in this highly competitive area with a simple message: letting businesses own their own intelligence.

In a recent development, with its open source roots, the startup says its agent creation and management software, LangSmith, is not trying to lock customers into any particular model, cloud, or ecosystem, unlike the major clouds or frontier AI labs. It also promises that LangSmith will contain agent behavior and is easy to use.

In a recent development, true, there are plenty of other startups pitching similar advantages these days and also doing well (case in point is newcomer Mintive). However, LangChain has had a head start and now claims 7,000 LangSmith customers, including substantial-name startups like Harvey, Rippling, and Clay, and enterprises like Nvidia, Toyota, and Salesforce.

  • Hours later, it was lifted, and federal officials used the incident to highlight the need for more funding to upgrade aging systems.
  • Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy initially blamed a communication problem impacting all Air Route Traffic Control Centers.

According to recent reports, millions of U.S. travelers were suddenly thrown into limbo Friday afternoon after the FAA revealed a nationwide ground stop at all U.S. airports.

Hours later, it was lifted, and federal officials used the incident to highlight the need for more funding to upgrade aging systems.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy initially blamed a communication problem impacting all Air Route Traffic Control Centers.

In a White House press briefing later on Friday night, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin attributed the disruptions to technology upgrades, for “overwhelming” the antiquated equipment.

“It’s going to continue to fail,” he warned.

According to recent reports, despite recent hacking incidents of freezers in Europe and U.S. military bases, he mentioned it “doesn’t appear” that a cyberattack was involved though he admitted that “there’s nothing certain right now.” Earlier, he ruled out a terrorist attack and said “This isn’t another 9/11.”.

Just days before the ground stop, the FAA announced it would deploy an AI tool to help air-traffic controllers.

During the briefing, Duffy also suggested that the problem was related to old equipment being overloaded.

“Our fix gives us a pretty good indication that it was a legacy network problem that went down,” he remarked.

Duffy also called on Congress to provide emergency funding to fix the FAA’s aging systems, saying the Trump administration needs another $30 billion, then putting the price tag at $50 billion.

In a recent development, still, the massive disruption comes as airlines in Europe suffered a wave of phony bomb threats this week. While they all appeared to hoaxes, at least one flight was diverted to a military base in France.

Spanish Foreign Minister Jose Manuel Albares said Friday that Europe appeared to be facing “hybrid aggression and a form of psychological warfare.”.

Meanwhile, consumers are still grappling with the aftermath of a Microsoft outage that shut down email, collaboration and AI functions. The company mentioned Friday it had no indication that the ground stop is related to its global outage.

The National Weather Service also said there has been no disruption to its radar systems Friday, denying talk online that it had caused the FAA communications glitch.

It has been revealed that the FAA last issued a nationwide ground stop in 2023, when files related to an alert system for pilots was unintentionally deleted. It delayed thousands of flights, but they resumed soon after the disruption.

Earlier this year, flights at Newly introduced York airports were halted when a contractor accidentally cut a fiber communications line in New Jersey.

Jason Ma is the weekend editor at Fortune, where he covers markets, the economy, finance, and housing.

Chan Park feels like “an eternal nomad.” He has since age 12, when he moved from Korea to the U.S., where he attended middle school in Minnesota, followed by high school in Latest Jersey, followed by college in New Hampshire. Then he really began to bounce around. Park worked as a trader in New York out of college, embraced the ski-bum life in Utah, then headed to Asia for Uber, where he spent six years, running its expansion team, then managing its entire Southeast Asia business out of Singapore.

More specifically, he was responsible for eight countries across the region, and 350 people, which didn’t give him a lot of time to organize his home. But he wasn’t overwhelmed by the chaos. Instead, he indicates that in Singapore, something unusual happened. “There’s this huge culture of landlords furnishing space to attract expats,” explains Park. “The furnishings aren’t super high-end, but they’re well-designed and well put together, and it enabled me to be basically moved in as soon as I put my clothes in the closet.” Suddenly, coming home was a treat — a new sensation for him. “For the first time, I was proud to host friends for dinners and barbecues and to just open the door and relax.”.

Industry observers note that park knew his U.S. friends could benefit from the same experience, and before long, he was talking with his Dartmouth classmate turned product and industrial designer Christian Talmage about forming their own firm. Enter Oliver Space, which provides a lot of what that Singaporean landlord delivered to Park. It furnishes places for busy professionals, making moving into a new home as easy as hanging up their clothes.

In a recent development, the now year-old service is available in the Bay Area only. And Oliver Space employs just a dozen people so far. But the manufacturer has already gained enough traction to attract $6.8 million in seed funding from an interesting array of investors, including Mayfield, Abstract Ventures, investors Jana Messerschmidt and April Underwood, Opendoor founder Eric Wu, and Kevin and Julia Hartz of Eventbrite, among others.

Now, Oliver Space just has to grow as rapidly, or more so, than other furniture-as-service startups to recently attract funding.

  • Whoop, the consumer technology manufacturer making screenless fitness bands, wants to track more than just your heart rate.

Industry observers note that you're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Bots are barred from this social network.

Whoop, the consumer technology manufacturer making screenless fitness bands, wants to track more than just your heart rate.

The fitness tracker company released a social network this week called Whoop Humans, and claims in a recent press release that the feature is “the most verifiably human social network.”.

“In a world that’s becoming increasingly artificial, we’re building something deeply human,” remarked Will Ahmed, founder and CEO of Whoop, in the press release. “Every account represents a real person with a verified heartbeat. They have real goals, challenges, and achievements. That’s what makes Whoop Humans different, and it’s a big area of investment for us.”.

Industry observers note that here’s how it works: Whoop members can follow friends, family and other Whoop-wearing people on the wearable’s accompanying app. They can share workout, sleep and recovery milestones in posts. Members can write comments and express reactions within the app.

Whoop designed the network to help customers cheer on each other’s progress and check in with each other if the data is concerning.

In a recent development, whoop Humans rolled out earlier this week on the app. It’s all up to the user if they want to participate.

Whoop member Mika Bublitz said that the social network allows members to give their friends a boost.

In a recent development, “Sometimes people don’t tell you when they’re not feeling their best,” Bublitz said in the press release. “If I see a friend’s Recovery is low, I can check in and say, ‘Hey, it’s okay to take it easy today.’ That’s what I like about Whoop Humans. It gives us another way to look out for each other.”.

It has been revealed that whoop’s fitness bands have become popular. According to the company, more than three million members are part of Whoop’s network and own a wearable. The press release adds that members open the Whoop app more than eight times per day, an indicator of the app’s popularity among people who own a Whoop device.

According to recent reports, whoop sells annual memberships ranging from $199 to $359, each bundled with a wrist-worn fitness tracker. The device monitors sleep, heart rate and stress, with the aim of helping users improve their health and athletic performance. Its battery lasts two weeks on a single charge.

Ahmed has been building the tech giant for 14 years.

Sources indicate that whoop faces competition from Google, which released a screenless wearable earlier this year for $100 called the Fitbit Air. Apple is also reportedly developing a similar screenless device.

Whoop, the consumer technology company making screenless fitness bands, wants to track more than just your heart rate.

The fitness tracker company launched a social network this week called Whoop Humans, and claims in a recent press release that the feature is “the most verifiably human social network.”.

Industry observers note that on Thursday, Nov. 12, a widespread Microsoft outage left millions around the world unable to send emails, open Outlook, or use workplace tools like Teams. At first it sounded like a corporate problem: unanswered emails, derailed meetings, employees unable to get work done. Some even welcomed the break. “Thank you Microsoft. Can you do this every Friday?” one X user joked.

Recent findings suggest that but the damage reached far beyond the office. Police departments struggled to receive online crime reports, hospitals fell back on other ways to communicate, and some government services were suspended.

The disruption exposed how deeply governments and essential public services now depend on a single private tech giant’s technology, and how something as ordinary as an email outage can interfere with the systems people rely on for public safety, health care, and justice.

In California, the Los Angeles County Sheriff’s Department reported disruptions to its email and other essential communication platforms. The Los Angeles Police Department and the county district attorney’s office also had email problems.

Law enforcement elsewhere was hit too. In Florida, St. Lucie County confirmed that its sheriff’s office and fire district were affected. Colorado’s Weld County Sheriff’s Office reported email problems and asked residents to call or text instead.

Across the Atlantic, British police forces including Dorset, Cumbria, South Wales, Wiltshire, and Dyfed-Powys had trouble receiving online crime reports, according to The Sun. Some forces said officers and staff could not access Outlook. Emergency phone lines kept working.

It has been revealed that in Maine, the state’s judicial branch warned that requests for protection orders submitted by email after 12:30 p.m. Thursday might never have reached the courts. In Latest York City, evictions scheduled for Friday, Nov. 13, were suspended; the city’s Department of Investigation said the decision followed consultation with the Civil Court.

In Britain, The Guardian reported that a criminal trial in Manchester was suspended for the day, with jurors sent home and court staff searching for a fax machine. Some civil court judgments were pushed to Monday.

In Colorado, the Arapahoe County Sheriff’s Office said its jail could not process online bond payments because staff weren’t receiving confirmation emails. Anyone seeking an inmate’s immediate release had to pay in person.

It has been revealed that the outage also stalled legislative work and city governments. On Capitol Hill, congressional staffers struggled to reach their email and calendars. “There goes a day of legislative work,” one House staffer told Politico.

The cities of Austin, Texas, Jacksonville, Florida, Richmond, Virginia, and Laurel, Maryland, also reported email or other Microsoft-related disruptions and pointed residents to other channels.

According to recent reports, governments across the Asia-Pacific region were hit as well. Australia’s spy agency, the Australian Security Intelligence Organisation, and the Australian Federal Police confirmed they had been affected, according to CNA.

Singapore’s Government Technology Agency reported disruptions to government systems, though emergency services and Singpass stayed up. Japan’s Foreign Ministry said it could not send or receive emails, and the Philippines’ Supreme Court warned of delays in email responses and other transactions.

In Canada, Unity Health Toronto, which runs several hospitals, declared a Code Grey, an alert used for infrastructure failures, after staff had trouble sending and receiving emails. The network stressed that patient and resident care was not affected and its facilities stayed open. Toronto’s Hospital for Sick Children, known as SickKids, also warned that some calls and emails to staff might not go through.

In Britain, the National Health Service was affected. According to The Guardian, health care workers had trouble accessing emails, appointment information, and patient data, and some services turned to backup systems or paper records. The National Pharmacy Association warned of prescription delays as pharmacies struggled to reach doctors and patients through NHS email.

Transportation companies faced a different problem: reaching passengers.

It has been revealed that canada’s VIA Rail warned that travelers might not receive trip emails and pointed them to its train tracker and text alerts. Britain’s National Rail advised passengers who couldn’t open emailed tickets to retrieve them through their ticket retailer’s website or app.

Airlines including India’s IndiGo and Hong Kong’s Cathay Pacific also reported email problems, although flights generally ran as normal.

Microsoft said in January that it had more than 450 million paid Microsoft 365 commercial seats, according to the Associated Press, though how many users were affected Thursday is hard to pin down.

For people who get verification codes or password-reset links by email, losing Outlook could mean getting locked out of other accounts too. That could hold up online banking, payments, document signing, and other everyday transactions, even when those services were working normally.

For small businesses that run much of their day on Microsoft 365, routine tasks like answering customers, scheduling meetings, or sending invoices could grind to a halt.

The outage also gave scammers an opening. The University of Sussex warned students and staff about people posing as Microsoft engineers and asking for passwords or other login details under the pretense of fixing email.

The full economic cost, including lost productivity and missed business, remains unclear.

In 2022, Google, which sells a competing productivity suite, commissioned a survey warning about the risks of an IT “monoculture,” in which governments rely heavily on one tech giant’s technology. Four years later, this outage demonstrated how far that dependence has spread.

In a recent development, the survey, conducted by Public Opinion Strategies, found that 84% of D.C.-area government employees primarily used Microsoft products. A 2021 report by Omdia, co-commissioned by Google and the Computer & Communications Industry Association, cited an earlier estimate that Microsoft held 85% of the U.S. government’s office productivity software market. Microsoft even offers Office 365 Government, a version of its suite built specifically for government agencies.

Jeanette Manfra, then Google Cloud’s head of risk and compliance, wrote that more than half of respondents believed the government’s dependence on Microsoft made it more vulnerable to hacking or cyberattacks.

The appeal of an all-in-one platform is easy to see. Organizations can use one provider for email, calendars, meetings, and document sharing instead of maintaining separate systems.

But according to Google’s survey, the reason governments stick with Microsoft “has more to do with inertia than innovation.” Nationwide, 59% of respondents who used Microsoft at work remarked their employers chose it because it was the most effective tool for their jobs, while 41% said it was because their employers had always used Microsoft and were reluctant to change.

A June 2026 Government Accountability Office report shows why diversifying isn’t simple. Of the 24 federal agencies examined, 11 reported technical challenges in adopting multiple cloud vendors, including interoperability challenges, and 10 cited resource constraints in building the cloud workforce they need.

Microsoft remarked Friday that it was seeing broad recovery after identifying a technical concern introduced during an earlier network capacity upgrade, which surfaced after a more recent network change. The firm said the incident was not related to a cyberattack or AI systems and apologized for the disruption.

Industry observers note that google’s warning four years ago focused on hackers. This week’s outage needed none. A routine network change at one company was enough to send jurors home, stall protection orders, and leave hospitals reaching for paper.

Nectar, an AI-powered operating system for marketing, is launching a fresh AI agent designed to take a lot of the manual work out of influencer marketing, from finding the right creators to contacting them, managing partnerships, and tracking results.

Founded by sisters Misbah and Farah Uraizee, both former Meta employees, Nectar came out of stealth last year and uses AI agents to help brands manage social media, customer conversations, content moderation, creator partnerships, and competitor research.

Industry observers note that declared Thursday, its newly introduced “Creator Agent” can search for creators, check their content and brand partnerships, send personalized messages, coordinate collaborations, and monitor how campaigns perform. Instead of having marketing teams spend weeks scrolling through social media, building spreadsheets, and sending individual DMs, Nectar wants its agent to handle much of that work automatically.

Sources indicate that nectar joins other companies introducing agentic AI assistants designed to automate influencer outreach, including Aspire and GRIN. The launch also comes as more brands turn to creators to reach customers. U.S. spending on creator advertising is expected to reach $44 billion in 2026, according to the Interactive Advertising Bureau. As companies work with hundreds or even thousands of creators, keeping track of relationships and measuring results can get pretty difficult.

Nectar notes its Creator Agent searches more than 300 million creator profiles to find potential partners, including smaller creators who may not yet have a large following but are gaining traction. The system analyzes videos to understand what creators post about, how their content fits a brand, and whether their previous partnerships are appropriate. It also checks brand safety by reviewing content in context rather than simply searching for specific keywords.

Nectar then creates ranked lists of recommendations and adds fresh matches as creators become more popular.

Industry observers note that once it finds a potential match, the agent can draft and send messages in a brand’s voice, create custom landing pages to collect creator information, and help manage contracts, product gifting, and shipping details. It also remembers previous conversations and interactions, so brands can keep track of relationships without relying on spreadsheets.

Recent findings suggest that “Brands can share voice guidelines in any format, and Nectar picks up the rest from their history,” CEO Misbah Uraizee tells TechCrunch. “On top of that sits a set of proprietary guardrails that keep every draft on tone and in context. Nectar understands what is being stated in a video, reads the tone of the conversation, and knows the difference between a quote post on X and a TikTok comment section. A brand should not sound identical in both, and with Nectar it doesn’t.”.

Another feature looks for personal milestones in creators’ lives, such as an engagement, a fresh baby, or completing a marathon. The agent can then suggest a personalized message or gift, helping brands build relationships that feel less like one-off advertising deals.

Creator Agent is available today globally and covers Instagram creators and TikTokers.

The organization plans to make the agent available through its Model Context Protocol (MCP), allowing teams to use it through AI assistants such as Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini, and Copilot, as well as their own custom-built agents.

This past May, Nectar raised a $30 million Series A round led by Menlo Ventures and its Anthology Fund, which is a joint initiative launched with Anthropic.
