#15. How boards investigate a CEO: 10 parts of an internal probe

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 24 min read (4743 words)
Business & Policy

How boards investigate a CEO: 10 parts of an internal probe

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 24 min read | Sumber: https://qz.com/how-boards-investigate-ceo-internal-probes

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Learn how boards investigate a CEO, from special committees and outside counsel to interviews, disclosure rules and the outcomes directors can choose when an internal probe ends.
  • According to recent reports, every firm has one executive whom the board alone hires, pays, evaluates and can remove: the chief executive.
  • According to recent reports, understanding how boards investigate a CEO starts with a familiar sequence.

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Learn how boards investigate a CEO, from special committees and outside counsel to interviews, disclosure rules and the outcomes directors can choose when an internal probe ends.

According to recent reports, every firm has one executive whom the board alone hires, pays, evaluates and can remove: the chief executive. That makes an inquiry into the CEO different from any other internal investigation. The person under review often controls the budget, the legal department and much of the information directors depend on. Corporate governance practice has developed a set of safeguards to work around that conflict.

According to recent reports, understanding how boards investigate a CEO starts with a familiar sequence. Independent directors take charge. They retain outside lawyers who report to them instead of to management. They write down what the inquiry will examine, lock down relevant records, interview witnesses and follow the money. At each stage, they decide what the company owes regulators, investors and the public.

Two Delaware court decisions define the legal stakes. Delaware is the state of incorporation for many large U.S. companies. Its courts expect directors to make a good-faith effort to oversee major risks. The Delaware Court of Chancery set out that oversight duty in its 1996 Caremark decision. In 2019, the Delaware Supreme Court applied it in Marchand v. Barnhill, a case arising from food safety problems at Blue Bell Creameries. Directors who overlook warning signs about a chief executive can face shareholder claims. A poorly run inquiry carries its own costs. It can put attorney-client privilege at risk, cause a organization to miss a filing deadline or invite closer scrutiny from regulators.

Sources indicate that this slideshow breaks the process into 10 parts. The first four cover who leads the probe, which lawyers do the work, how the scope is defined and how evidence is preserved. The next four explain witness interviews, forensic accounting, whistleblower complaints and the disclosure rules that apply to public companies. The final two describe how the CEO is kept out of the board's deliberations and what directors can do once the findings arrive.

The descriptions reflect common U.S. practice and established law. Bylaws, corporate charters and executive employment contracts differ from company to company. Practice varies from one investigation to the next.

It has been revealed that each slide is written to stand on its own. A reader interested only in Upjohn warnings, clawbacks or Form 8-K deadlines can skip directly to that entry.

When allegations reach the chief executive, a board usually assigns the inquiry to a special committee made up only of independent directors. These directors have no business, family or financial ties to the CEO. That lets them weigh the facts without a conflict of interest.

The committee can be created for the occasion or drawn from a body that already exists. The audit committee is a frequent choice when the allegations concern financial reporting. It already oversees the outside auditor and the manufacturer's internal controls. Claims about workplace conduct or personal behavior may instead go to a purpose-built committee. They can also go to the full board, meeting without the CEO.

According to recent reports, independence is judged by actual relationships, not only by a director's formal status. A director whom the CEO recruited may be left off the committee. The same goes for a director who serves alongside the CEO on another tech giant's board, or one with a long personal friendship with the executive. Boards commonly ask counsel to review each prospective member's ties before the work begins.

Delaware case law gives directors reason to take care. Under the oversight duty recognized in In re Caremark International Inc. Derivative Litigation, directors must make a good-faith effort to ensure the company has information and reporting systems. The Delaware Supreme Court applied that duty in Marchand v. Barnhill, a case involving Blue Bell Creameries. The court stressed that boards must make this effort for the risks most central to the business. Shareholders can bring derivative claims against directors who fail to meet that duty.

A committee needs formal authority as well as independent members. A board resolution, often called the committee's charter, gives it the power to hire its own advisers. The same document lets it demand company records and speak with any employee. It also sets the reporting line, which in most cases runs to the full board minus the CEO.

Recent findings suggest that the choice of committee leader carries weight. A lead independent director or a non-executive chair often acts as the main contact for the outside lawyers. That arrangement keeps the CEO and other senior managers out of the chain of communication. It also helps shield the inquiry from accusations of interference by the executive under review.

A special committee investigating a CEO hires its own outside law firm. That firm takes instructions from the committee rather than from the chief executive or anyone in management. The separate reporting line gives regulators, auditors and shareholders a reason to trust what the investigation finds.

Industry observers note that boards generally avoid the firm's regular outside law firm for this work. A firm that earns large fees from routine corporate matters can look like it has a stake in the result. So can a firm whose partners deal with the CEO regularly. Committees tend to pick a firm with no history of advising the executive under review. They also run a conflicts check on the firm's other clients before signing.

The engagement letter names the committee as the party the lawyers answer to. That wording helps support attorney-client privilege. The privilege can shield confidential communications between a lawyer and a client from disclosure in later lawsuits. It belongs to the tech giant itself. In this setting, the committee typically decides on the company's behalf whether to keep it or give it up.

According to recent reports, the protection can be lost. Handing findings to a government agency or another outside party may lead a court to rule that privilege has been waived for that material. Some committees ask for oral briefings instead of a long written report for that reason. Others want a document they can share with regulators and accept the waiver risk that comes with it.

Investigation teams at these firms often include former federal prosecutors. Those lawyers know how the Justice Department and the Securities and Exchange Commission judge whether a company's internal inquiry was independent and thorough. The firm can also bring in specialists, such as e-discovery vendors, and supervise their work.

The organization pays the legal bills. That puts the CEO's own organization in the position of funding an inquiry into its leader. Committees handle the problem by approving the fee terms themselves and having invoices sent straight to them. Management has no role in setting the budget or signing off on the bills.

Recent findings suggest that counsel also guides the committee's process from the first meeting. The lawyers advise on the order of steps, how to document decisions and when to brief the outside auditor or regulators. That record can matter later if a court or agency examines how the board handled the matter.

Industry observers note that before any witness is interviewed, the special committee puts the scope of a CEO investigation in writing. That mandate names the allegations under review, the time period covered, the people and records involved and the authority the investigators hold.

Industry observers note that the document is usually a committee resolution, an engagement letter with outside counsel or both. Its terms need to be precise. An allegation that the CEO misused a organization aircraft calls for different records and witnesses than an allegation of harassment. Pressure on the finance team to hit a quarterly target would call for yet another set.

In a recent development, A defined scope also keeps the inquiry from drifting. A review of expense reports can surface questions about related-party deals or a vendor contract. Each upcoming thread adds cost and time. With a written mandate in hand, the committee can choose to widen the inquiry, keep it narrow or open a separate review with its own terms.

The mandate states who receives the findings. In most cases that is the special committee, which then decides what to pass to the full board. The document can bar the CEO from receiving drafts. Counsel still reviews the executive's employment agreement and the company's bylaws. Either one may grant the CEO a right to information or a chance to respond.

In a recent development, access is another core term. A typical mandate gives the investigators authority to reach any employee, any tech giant system and any document the business holds. It also directs management to cooperate. Corporate codes of conduct and employment contracts often require staff to assist internal inquiries, and the mandate can cite those obligations.

The document also covers unexpected discoveries. Investigators may find signs of a separate problem, such as possible bribery or an accounting error. The mandate can require them to alert the committee at once. The committee then decides whether to bring in other advisers or notify the outside auditor.

A mandate is not fixed. When the facts change, the committee amends the scope in writing. Each expansion or narrowing then appears in the record as a deliberate decision rather than an accident.

In a recent development, that record has a later use. The company may face shareholder litigation or questions from regulators. A written mandate and dated committee minutes show what the committee asked for, when it asked and why.

Locking down evidence is the first concrete step in a CEO investigation. Early in the process, the company sends a legal hold notice telling employees to keep relevant records intact. Its IT team also switches off the routine deletion of email, files and chat history.

Industry observers note that the chief executive's own data comes first. Investigators move early to secure the CEO's company email, calendar, phone, laptop and cloud accounts. A common method is a forensic image, which is a complete copy of a device's contents made in a way that can be verified later. A copy taken at the outset makes it harder for anyone to argue afterward that material was altered or removed.

Personal phones and messaging apps are harder to reach. Executives may conduct business over text messages, WhatsApp or Signal. Some of these apps can be set to erase messages after a period of time. The U.S. Department of Justice addressed this problem in March 2023, when it updated its Evaluation of Corporate Compliance Programs. The revision covers how companies govern personal devices, communication platforms and messaging applications, including those that make messages ephemeral.

Losing data carries legal consequences. Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 37(e) deals with electronically stored information that should have been kept but was lost. If a party failed to take reasonable steps to preserve it, a court can order measures to cure the resulting harm. Where the loss was intended to deprive another party of the information, the court can impose harsher sanctions. Those include instructing a jury that the lost information was unfavorable to the party that lost it, or dismissing the case.

Recent findings suggest that the hold notice goes to a defined group known as custodians — the people likely to hold relevant records. In a CEO probe, that list usually starts with the executive, direct reports and assistants. It then extends to finance staff and others involved in the matters under review. Counsel adds names as interviews and documents point to other people who handled the material.

It has been revealed that records generated by company systems matter as much as messages. Access logs, badge swipes and expense approval trails show who acted and when. Investigators use them to test what witnesses say against what the systems recorded. Some systems overwrite their logs on a rotating schedule. The hold covers them for that reason.

Collection follows preservation. E-discovery vendors process the gathered data into a searchable form. Lawyers then search it using keywords, names and date ranges drawn from the scope of the investigation.

In a recent development, outside counsel typically opens each witness interview in a CEO investigation with an Upjohn warning. The lawyer tells the employee that counsel represents the firm, not the individual, and that the company controls the privilege over the conversation.

The warning is named for Upjohn Co. v. United States, a 1981 U.S. Supreme Court decision. The Court held that attorney-client privilege can protect conversations between a company's lawyers and its employees. The protection applies when those conversations help the lawyers give legal advice to the company. The Court rejected a narrower "control group" test, which had limited the privilege to senior managers. That ruling lets investigators question staff well below the executive suite and still treat the exchanges as privileged.

Recent findings suggest that the warning is sometimes nicknamed a "corporate Miranda," although it is not a constitutional right. Its job is to prevent a misunderstanding. An employee who assumes the firm's lawyer is also a personal lawyer may speak more freely than intended. A later claim that a personal attorney-client relationship existed can cloud the company's control over the interview.

Recent findings suggest that A standard warning covers a handful of points. The lawyer works for the manufacturer. The conversation is confidential. The company can waive the privilege and share the employee's statements with regulators or prosecutors without the employee's consent. Counsel usually confirms that the employee understands before asking about the facts.

An employee who wants personal advice can hire a separate lawyer. Some companies pay for that representation under their bylaws or an indemnification agreement.

According to recent reports, the order of interviews follows a pattern. Counsel generally reviews documents first and then speaks with people on the edges of the events. Witnesses closer to the conduct come next. The CEO is often interviewed near the end. By then, the lawyers can test the executive's account against emails, records and other testimony.

Interviews are usually not recorded or transcribed. Lawyers take notes and write memoranda that reflect their own impressions and analysis. That approach can strengthen work-product protection for the materials. The memoranda summarize rather than quote, and witnesses do not usually sign them.

Sources indicate that counsel often reminds employees that tech giant policy forbids retaliation for taking part. Witnesses are also asked not to discuss the interview with colleagues. That request helps keep later accounts independent. It cannot stop an employee from reporting possible violations to the Securities and Exchange Commission, which bars companies from impeding such communications.

Recent findings suggest that the CEO occupies a different position as the subject of the probe. The executive can bring a personal lawyer and may negotiate the timing and format of the interview. The special committee decides whether to insist on a face-to-face session or accept a written response.

Forensic accountants trace where manufacturer money went in a CEO investigation. They examine expense reports, wire transfers, vendor payments and sign-off records. The goal is to test whether spending followed company policy and whether the required approvals were actually given.

Their work starts with specific questions. Were the chief executive's travel and entertainment claims backed by receipts? Did company money reach vendors connected to the executive or to family members? Were contracts broken into smaller pieces to slip under approval limits? Did anyone override a control, and who was aware of it?

Recent findings suggest that to answer those questions, the accountants line up ledger entries against bank statements, invoices and email. A payment recorded in the books with no matching invoice becomes a lead for the lawyers. So does a spending approval that cannot be traced to the person who was supposed to give it.

Data analytics widens the search. Software can sort through large volumes of transactions to flag duplicate payments, round-number entries, payments made at unusual times and money sent to new vendors. None of those patterns proves misconduct by itself. Each one points investigators toward documents to pull and witnesses to question.

Related-party transactions draw close scrutiny in an inquiry focused on a chief executive. These are deals between the tech giant and an insider, or someone close to an insider. U.S. public companies must disclose some of these arrangements in their securities filings. A deal that was left out or described inaccurately can become a reporting problem separate from the original allegation.

The accounting firm is usually hired by outside counsel rather than by the manufacturer directly. That structure draws on United States v. Kovel, a 1961 decision by the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit. The court recognized that attorney-client privilege can extend to an accountant who helps a lawyer understand financial information in order to give legal advice. Whether the protection holds in a given case depends on how the engagement is set up and used.

The firm's outside auditor plays a different part. The auditor stays independent of the investigation. It may still ask what the board's special committee has found. Alleged executive misconduct can affect the auditor's view of management's integrity and of the financial statements. The committee and its lawyers decide when and how the auditor is briefed.

It has been revealed that the accountants' conclusions flow into the committee's final report. They put a dollar figure on the amounts at concern. They also help directors distinguish a policy breach from an accounting error or an intentional scheme.

Sources indicate that many CEO investigations begin with a tip, such as a hotline report, an employee complaint or a letter sent directly to a director. U.S. law requires listed companies to keep a channel open for these reports, and it protects the people who use it.

The Sarbanes-Oxley Act of 2002 gave that job to the audit committee. Audit committees of listed companies must set procedures for receiving, keeping and handling complaints about accounting, internal controls and auditing. Employees must be able to raise those concerns confidentially and anonymously. Many companies hire an outside vendor to run the hotline.

According to recent reports, section 806 of the same law addresses retaliation. It protects public-company employees who report conduct they reasonably believe is fraud or a securities law violation. A worker who is fired or demoted after reporting can file a complaint with the U.S. Department of Labor's Occupational Safety and Health Administration within 180 days. Boards that receive a complaint typically document how the complainant is treated from the first day.

Recent findings suggest that the Dodd-Frank Act of 2010 opened a second path. Its whistleblower program lets the Securities and Exchange Commission pay tipsters a share of what it recovers. Awards run from 10 percent to 30 percent of money collected in actions with sanctions above $1 million. An employee can go to the agency at the same time as the board, or without telling the board at all.

According to recent reports, the agency's rules reward internal reporting without requiring it. A whistleblower who reports inside the firm and then contacts the agency within 120 days can be treated as having reported on the date of the internal complaint. The agency's Rule 21F-17 bars anyone from taking steps to impede a person from communicating directly with agency staff about a possible securities law violation. That ban covers enforcing or threatening to enforce a confidentiality agreement.

Sources indicate that the practical result is that a board does not fully control the timeline. A committee that receives a credible tip moves quickly and records when the information arrived. It avoids any step that could look like an effort to unmask or silence the source.

Routing is the first decision. A complaint that names the CEO or the general counsel should bypass both and go straight to independent directors, usually starting with the audit committee chair. That director judges whether the allegation, if true, is serious enough to warrant an independent probe. Investigators typically speak with the complainant early. They protect the person's identity as far as the law and the facts permit.

A public tech giant does not have to announce an internal investigation of its CEO when the inquiry begins. Certain outcomes do trigger fast reporting. If the chief executive leaves, the company generally must file a Form 8-K with the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) within four business days.

Form 8-K is the SEC's current report for major corporate events. The governing provision for a CEO exit is Item 5.02. It covers the departure of directors and certain senior officers, including the principal executive officer. The filing must state that the executive resigned, retired or was terminated, along with the date. A reason is not required. If the company chooses to give one, that description has to be accurate and not misleading.

Sources indicate that the same item covers the other side of a leadership change. When the board appoints a fresh principal executive officer, Item 5.02 calls for a filing on that appointment too.

According to recent reports, financial findings carry a deadline of their own. The board or audit committee may conclude that previously issued financial statements should no longer be relied on. Item 4.02 of Form 8-K then requires a filing within four business days. A probe into executive spending or revenue practices can lead to that conclusion.

Industry observers note that staying quiet about an inquiry still carries legal risk. Rule 10b-5, adopted under the Securities Exchange Act of 1934, bars materially false statements. It also bars omitting facts needed to keep other statements from being misleading. A company that praises its leadership while aware of serious allegations can expose itself to liability. Counsel reviews earnings releases, filings and executive remarks with that risk in view.

Sources indicate that executive certifications add pressure. Sections 302 and 906 of the Sarbanes-Oxley Act of 2002 require the CEO and chief financial officer to certify the company's periodic reports. When an investigation casts doubt on those reports, the committee, the outside auditor and disclosure counsel assess whether the earlier statements still hold.

Reporting to authorities is a separate decision from public disclosure. A manufacturer may choose to tell the SEC or the U.S. Department of Justice about possible violations. The Justice Department has published corporate enforcement policies describing credit for voluntary self-disclosure, cooperation and remediation. The board weighs that option with its lawyers.

Stock exchange rules also apply. The New York Stock Exchange and Nasdaq $NDAQ expect listed companies to release material news promptly. A CEO exit or a restatement can meet that standard.

According to recent reports, A small group controls the message. The committee, outside counsel and the corporate secretary agree on what is said to employees and the public. Conflicting accounts can create legal problems of their own.

During an internal investigation, the chief executive is cut out of every decision about the probe. The CEO does not attend special committee meetings, does not see the committee's papers and has no say over the investigating lawyers. In many cases, the executive continues to run the business day to day.

The arrangement is harder to manage when one person is both CEO and board chair. In that case, the lead independent director or another independent director chosen by the board presides over any discussion of the inquiry. The chair's usual control over meeting agendas and board materials does not extend to the investigation.

According to recent reports, listed companies already have a forum for these conversations. New York Stock Exchange rules require non-management directors to meet in regularly scheduled executive sessions without management present. Nasdaq $NDAQ rules require regularly scheduled executive sessions of independent directors. Those meetings give directors a routine place to discuss the probe without the executive in the room.

Recusal covers votes as well as attendance. The chief executive abstains from any board decision about the investigation, including its budget and its conclusions. The general counsel may also have a conflict. That officer usually reports to the CEO. Committees often limit the general counsel's role to logistics, or keep the general counsel out of the inquiry entirely.

Recent findings suggest that directors also decide how the executive will operate while the work continues. One choice is a leave of absence. Another is to remove the CEO's authority over particular areas, such as the finance function or the employees being interviewed. A third is to make no change when the allegations are narrow. The committee weighs the risk of interference against disruption to the manufacturer.

According to recent reports, the executive keeps rights during the process. A CEO under investigation can hire a personal lawyer and is normally given a chance to answer the allegations. Company bylaws, indemnification agreements and employment contracts can determine whether the company covers legal costs as they arise. Section 145 of the Delaware General Corporation Law permits companies to advance those expenses to officers. The officer typically must promise to repay the money if a court later finds the officer is not entitled to indemnification.

In a recent development, succession planning runs on a separate track. Directors identify who could serve as interim CEO and how operations would stay stable if the executive leaves. That discussion is kept apart from the fact-finding. The separation keeps choices about a possible replacement from shaping the investigation's conclusions.

Recent findings suggest that the rest of the board stays informed. The committee briefs the other independent directors at intervals. Those updates let the full board carry out its own oversight duties.

It has been revealed that at the end of a CEO investigation, the special committee presents its findings and the independent directors decide how to respond. The options range from clearing the executive entirely to firing the CEO for cause. Reprimands, pay cuts and compensation recovery fall in between.

The CEO's employment agreement usually sets the boundaries of that decision. Many executive contracts define cause to include conduct such as fraud, willful misconduct or serious breaches of firm policy. A dismissal for cause can cost the executive severance and unvested equity. Directors and counsel therefore test the facts against the contract's exact wording. Labeling a departure as for cause when the evidence does not meet the definition can lead to a dispute with the former executive.

Industry observers note that recovering pay is a separate track. The Securities and Exchange Commission adopted Rule 10D-1 under the Dodd-Frank Act. It requires listed companies to keep policies for clawing back incentive-based compensation that executives received in error because of an accounting restatement. The New York Stock Exchange and Nasdaq $NDAQ put the rule into effect through their listing standards. Companies had to adopt compliant policies by December 2023.

Rule 10D-1 has a narrow trigger. A restatement sets it off, not misconduct in general. Recovery applies whether or not the executive was at fault. It covers current and former executive officers. It reaches incentive pay received during the three completed fiscal years before the restatement was required. A CEO who broke conduct rules without affecting the financial statements falls outside it.

The Sarbanes-Oxley Act of 2002 contains an older recovery provision. Section 304 covers the CEO and the chief financial officer when misconduct leads to a restatement. It reaches bonuses, incentive pay and profits from selling company stock in the 12 months after the misstated filing. The SEC enforces it, not the board.

It has been revealed that company-written clawback clauses can go further. Depending on how they are drafted and what the executive signed, they may reach compensation tied to misconduct. Collecting the money can still require negotiation or a lawsuit.

The committee's conclusions go to the independent directors, who weigh them before voting on any action. Their reasoning belongs in the board minutes. Those minutes become the formal record of how the company handled the allegations.

Remediation follows the decision about the CEO. Committees often order changes to the controls, approval limits or reporting lines that allowed the problem. A documented record of those fixes can matter if regulators later examine how the board responded.

It has been revealed that not every probe ends with a finding against the executive. When the evidence does not support the allegations, the committee says so in its conclusions. The board then records that it has cleared the CEO. That written record reveals directors examined the allegations and acted on what the evidence demonstrated.

Revolution, the investment firm cofounded 14 years ago by entrepreneur-investor Steve Case, has closed its second Rise of the Rest seed fund with $150 million in capital commitments, just like the debut fund it announced two years ago.

Sources indicate that rise of the Rest — which fund startups outside of the biggest U.S. tech hubs in an effort to foster innovation and momentum elsewhere — has rounded up some of the funding from institutional investors, presumably, but also from numerous very wealthy individuals.

According to Forbes, which is currently hosting a summit where Case revealed the new fund, some of the new fund’s backers include Jeff Bezos of Amazon, Sara Blakely of Spanx, hedge fund manager Ray Dalio, Under Armour cofounder Kevin Plank, former Tennessee governor Bill Haslam, and Apollo Global Management cofounder Joshua Harris.

Some of these investors backed the first fund, too, including Bezos and Dalio.

Very notably, Hillbilly Elegy author J.D. Vance, who ran the first fund with Case, has stepped back, and longtime Revolution investor David Hall will manage the second fund instead.

Sources indicate that certainly, that first fund kept its investors busy, with stakes in 125 companies. Barely a week passes without a startup announcing some funding from the Rise of the Rest team.

In a recent development, ACV Auctions, a five-year-old, Buffalo, N.Y.-based online platform for franchise and used-car dealerships to buy and sell wholesale inventory through 20-minute auctions, is reportedly looking to raise $150 million in Series E funding at a post-money valuation north of $1 billion. Reuters has more here.

Industry observers note that weave, a seven-year-old, Lehi, Ut.-based developer of patient communications software focused on the dental and optometry market, has raised $70 million in Series D funding at a post-money valuation of $970 million. Tiger Global Management led the round, with participation from earlier backers Catalyst Investors, Bessemer Venture Partners, Crosslink Capital, Pelion Venture Partners and LeadEdge Capital. TechCrunch has more here.

1906, a two-year-old, Denver-based cannabis brand that makes a wide variety of edibles, has raised $18 million in funding led by Navy Capital. More here.

Recent findings suggest that aviatrix, a five-year-old, Palo Alto, Ca.-developer of software that allows companies to build hybrid clouds, raised $40 million in Series C funding. Earlier backer CRV led the round, joined by fellow insiders Formation 8, Ignition Partners, and Liberty Global Ventures. VentureBeat has more here.

Sources indicate that choco, an 18-month-old, mobile ordering platform for restaurants and their suppliers, has raised $33.5 million in Series A funding by Bessemer Venture Partners. The manufacturer has now raised $41 million to date. Other investors include Atlantic Labs, Target Global, Visionaries Club and Greyhound. TechCrunch has more here.

It has been revealed that duffel, a two-year-old, London-based startup that connects travel agencies with airline reservation systems, has raised $30 million in Series B funding led by Index Ventures, with participation from earlier backers Benchmark and Blossom Capital. TechCrunch has more here.

Sensely, a five-year-old, San Francisco-based chatbot that helps users navigate insurance benefits, has raised $15 million led by Aflac Corporate Ventures, with participation from NMC, Nippon Life Insurance Company, Susquehanna International Group, Sojitz Corporation, Zuelling Pharma and Silicon Valley Bank. MobiHealth News has more here.

ShiraTronics, a 10-month-old, Brooklyn Park, Mn.-based medical device organization working on a migraine treatment, raised $33 million in Series A funding. USVP, Amzak Health and Strategic HealthCare Investment Partners led the round, joined by Aperture Ventures and LivaNova. American Inno has more here.

Twiga Foods, a six-year-old, Nairobi, Kenya-based B2B food distribution tech giant, has raised $23.75 million in Series B funding led by Goldman Sachs, with participation from IFC, TLcom Capital, and Creadev. Goldman also arranged $6.25 million in debt funding. TechCrunch has more here.

Welcome to the Jungle, a five-year-old, Paris-based recruitment startup, has raised $22.3 million in fresh funding led by Gaia Capital Partners, with participation from Bpifance, XAnge, and Jean-Paul Guisset. TechCrunch has more here.

EnsureDR, a five-year-old, San Jose, Ca.-based company that makes disaster recovery readiness software, has raised $2.5 million in Series A funding led by Awz Ventures. More here.

Sources indicate that own Up, a 3.5-year-old, Boston-based startup that invites promises owners a high-touch service if they connect with its team of online mortgage brokers, has raised $8.5 million in Series A funding. Link Ventures led the round. More here.

According to recent reports, young Alfred, a three-year-old, Philadelphia-based home insurance marketplace, has raised $10 million in Series A funding led by Gradient Ventures, with participation from Pear Ventures, ERA, and Newfund Capital. Insurance Business has more here. Zamna, a three-year-old, London-based company that has built a GDPR-compliant identity platform for the aviation industry (it helps airlines verify passengers’ identities before they arrive at an airport), has raised $5 million in seed funding co-led by LocalGlobe and Oxford Capital. TechCrunch has more here.

Industry observers note that byteDance, the seven-year-old,  $75 billion Chinese start-up that owns the short-form video app TikTok, is eyeing an IPO in Hong Kong as soon as the first quarter of next year, according to the Financial Times. As it notes, ByteDance’s valuation hit $75 billion a year ago, when it closed a $3 billion round led by SoftBank that doubled its valuation from a year earlier. An IPO would help the Japanese conglomerate at a time when many of its other investments are cratering in value. More here.

#17. Tech Report: Blue Origin puts its space station plans on hold to concentrate on moon missions instead

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4 min read (730 words)
General

Tech Report: Blue Origin puts its space station plans on hold to concentrate on moon missions instead

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read | Sumber: https://www.geekwire.com/2026/blue-origin-space-station-on-hold-moon/

💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Alan Boyle on Nov 13, 2026 at 2:35 pmNovember 13, 2026 at 2:35 pm.
  • Jeff Bezos’ Blue Origin space venture has decided not to seek further NASA funding for its Orbital Reef space station project in order to tighten its focus on lunar missions.
  • Industry observers note that for the past five years, Blue Origin has played a lead role in Orbital Reef, alongside partners including Sierra Space and Boeing.

by Alan Boyle on Nov 13, 2026 at 2:35 pmNovember 13, 2026 at 2:35 pm.

Jeff Bezos’ Blue Origin space venture has decided not to seek further NASA funding for its Orbital Reef space station project in order to tighten its focus on lunar missions.

Industry observers note that for the past five years, Blue Origin has played a lead role in Orbital Reef, alongside partners including Sierra Space and Boeing. In late 2021, Blue Origin won a $130 million contract from NASA in the first phase of the space agency’s Commercial Low Earth Orbit Destinations program, or CLD.

According to recent reports, now NASA is seeking proposals for the next phase of the program, which will fund the development of orbital outposts to replace International Space Station in the 2030s. Proposals are due on Dec. 8, with contracts expected to be awarded next spring.

Blue Origin indicated that it will not submit a bid.

Recent findings suggest that “Blue Origin’s mission is to build a road to space for the benefit of Earth so that millions of people can live and work in space. Establishing a sustained human presence on the moon is a critical step toward that future,” the organization stated in an emailed statement.

“As our role supporting NASA’s Artemis and Moon Base missions continues to grow, we’re focusing resources on capabilities that directly advance our lunar projects,” Blue Origin said. “By sharpening that focus, we can move faster on the technologies and infrastructure needed to make lunar permanence a reality.”.

Orbital Reef was once touted as a “mixed-use business park” in space — and was even slated to star in a sci-fi thriller titled “Helios.” But much like that delayed film project, the space station is now on the back burner.

Recent findings suggest that orbital Reef isn’t the only initiative Blue Origin has put on hold to prioritize moon missions. In January, the company suspended its suborbital Newly introduced Shepard program for at least two years for similar reasons.

Industry observers note that blue Origin is building landers for delivering cargo and crews to the lunar surface for NASA. An uncrewed Blue Moon Mark 1 lunar lander is scheduled for launch early next year, and a crew-capable Mark 2 version is scheduled for testing in low Earth orbit next year during NASA’s Artemis 3 mission.

According to recent reports, last week, NASA awarded Blue Origin a $94 million base contract, plus a $140 million option, to deliver a nuclear-powered rover to the lunar south pole. Blue Origin also won a spot in NASA’s broader lunar cargo delivery program. In addition, Honeybee Robotics, a Blue Origin subsidiary, will contribute to a lunar power-generating project known as miniCAST.

Blue Origin is pursuing several other moon development initiatives, including a program called Blue Alchemist that aims to use lunar materials to manufacture solar cells and electrical wire.

Sources indicate that several competitors are still working on commercial space stations. Voyager Technologies, Airbus and Northrop Grumman lead the Starlab consortium, which received CLD Phase 1 funding from NASA and is expected to put in a proposal for Phase 2.

Axiom Space and Vast are also developing outposts that could take the place of the ISS. Meanwhile, Marysville, Wash.-based Gravitics is building space station hardware for Axiom and an orbital carrier for the U.S. Space Force.

Customers share what they learned, and select sessions include live Q&A. Livestream registration is free.

#18. Protein Startups Are Selling Lots Of Snacks And Drinks. Our Sample Tasting Found Most Neither Great Nor Horrible

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6 min read (1145 words)
General

Protein Startups Are Selling Lots Of Snacks And Drinks. Our Sample Tasting Found Most Neither Great Nor Horrible

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read | Sumber: https://news.crunchbase.com/agtech-foodtech/protein-startup-snacks-drinks-sample-taste/

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a perfect world, we would all eat meals and snacks that are convenient, taste great and provide optimal nutrition.
  • According to recent reports, in reality, however, there are tradeoffs.
  • In a recent development, fortunately, as we chronicled earlier this week, both startups and established food brands are making it simpler than ever to up protein intake.

In a perfect world, we would all eat meals and snacks that are convenient, taste great and provide optimal nutrition.

According to recent reports, in reality, however, there are tradeoffs. We crave ice cream, chips and candy bars, which make carbs and fat easy to over-consume. Meeting protein goals, meanwhile, can require conscientious effort, particularly for those, like your author, who aren’t keen on eating lots of meat.

In a recent development, fortunately, as we chronicled earlier this week, both startups and established food brands are making it simpler than ever to up protein intake. From sodas to snack bars to ice cream, it’s now possible to get a fix of this coveted macronutrient with foods and drinks more commonly associated with sugar, starch and fat.

The looming question is: Do they taste good? To find out, we hit up a local Target for a selection of protein foods sold by venture-backed startups. I and a 10-year-old then subjected them to a taste test.

It has been revealed that the verdict? Most of this stuff is indeed edible and drinkable, albeit almost never nearly as tasty as the more protein-deficient alternatives, with just one exception.

No. 1: David Vanilla Bean Frozen Dessert: Anyone who buys or consumes this particular ice cream alternative will be doing so for the nutritional content, not the taste. A single pint packs in a whopping 30 grams of protein and has just 210 calories. The texture is also on point, creamy and easy to spoon, with a distinct vanilla flavor.

That stated, you can’t hide the fact that this is not a product made with your typical ice cream ingredients. Those who don’t like artificial sweeteners or the flavor and texture of whey protein will want to pass. For myself and my co-taster, however, it was a reasonably appealing eating experience. Not as good as traditional ice cream, but not bad for a high-protein food.

Made by: Medici Brands (David parent company).

No. 2 SkyPop Protein Soda: The nutritional stats for SkyPop Protein Soda are also remarkable. A 12-ounce can has just 45 calories, with 10 grams of protein and a single gram of carbohydrates. It’s also properly fizzy, and makes a satisfying pop when you open the can.

According to recent reports, but what about flavor? Our local store only had the Ice Pop flavor in stock and it was, in both tasters’ view, not horrible but not something we’d proposal to buy regularly. I could see consuming it when on a clear fluids diet, as is the case before some medical procedures, as it’d be one of the few available sources of protein.

In a recent development, no. 3: Khloud Protein Popcorn: Unlike many of our other featured foods, Khloud Protein Popcorn isn’t a super protein-rich offering. A serving contains 7 grams of protein and 160 calories, most of which come from carbs and fat. Still, its protein count is higher than other packaged popcorn, which typically has maybe 2 protein grams in a comparable serving.

Overall, the tasters’ conclusion, from our trial of White Cheddar Khloud, was that this is a decent snack food. The flavor of milk protein and whey protein concentrate was palpable, but not overwhelming. It’s not exactly a snack food to savor, but for something to casually munch at one’s desk or while watching a show, it served its purpose.

No. 4 Mosh: In the third season of “The White Lotus”, Mosh co-founder Patrick Schwarzenegger plays a fitness and finance bro who makes a daily high-protein shake that other family members find revolting. Perhaps this was inspired by Mosh, the brain-supporting protein bar startup he rolled out with his mother, Maria Shriver.

In a recent development, the Mosh bar, which we purchased in the peanut butter cup flavor, crams 20 grams of protein, 6 grams of fiber, plus brain-supporting ingredients like creatine and lion’s mane, into a compact, shelf-stable bar. It’s an impressive feat. Yet while our brains’ may have appreciated the nutrition and supplement boost the Mosh bar provided, our taste buds decidedly did not.

I’d put Mosh in the functional food category. It’s something that you might eat if you wanted that particular nutrient mix. But it’s not something to consume for pleasure.

It has been revealed that no. 5 Cadootz Crackers: We tried two varieties of Cadootz Crackers — cheddar and sea salt — and walked away neither enthused nor repulsed.

For people interested in a gluten- and seed oil-free small snack cracker with about 5 grams of protein per serving, Cadootz rises to the occasion. It’s got a nice crunch and decent flavor.

Sources indicate that as someone who’s not particularly seeking to avoid gluten and seed oils or to get a modest protein bump from my crackers, I’ll probably pass on follow-on purchases. But for its target audience, Cadootz should serve well.

No. 6 Frozen One: For those who thought the David frozen dessert was a marvel of protein engineering, the folks at Frozen One would like a word. Their protein ice cream has a whopping 40 grams of protein in each pint.

Yes, but how does it taste? Not that bad, according to our two-person tasting team. We tried both the chocolate and apple pie varieties, preferring the former. Like the David offering, Frozen One tastes like a product made with milk protein concentrate and sugar substitutes. You won’t mistake it for Ben and Jerry’s. But if the goal is to consume a steak-like quantity of protein in the form factor of a pint of ice cream, it does its job.

In a recent development, no. 7 Brami Protein Pasta: We saved the best for last. That, unexpectedly, was Brami Protein Pasta, a noodle made from semolina and lupini beans that boasts about 70% more protein than standard pasta and more than double the fiber.

With about 12 grams of protein for a 200 calorie serving, Brami isn’t a dense protein source. But, with the right topping, it’s enough to transform a typically starchy noodle meal into something reasonably protein rich.

According to recent reports, most notably, however, Brami tastes quite good, with no discernable weird aftertaste or texture concerns. I made both standard and Brami noodles to taste the difference. For seconds, I went with the Brami.

#19. Breaking: Agentic AI Governance Doesn’t Have to Be Complicated. Most of It Comes Down to These 4 Questions.

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6 min read (1253 words)
AI & Tech

Breaking: Agentic AI Governance Doesn’t Have to Be Complicated. Most of It Comes Down to These 4 Questions.

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read | Sumber: https://www.entrepreneur.com/business-news/tech/agentic-ai-governance-frameworks-questions

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Agentic AI governance frameworks look complicated, but every one asks your business the same four questions.
  • Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.
  • In a recent development, leaders face a growing stack of agentic AI governance frameworks.

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Agentic AI governance frameworks look complicated, but every one asks your business the same four questions.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

In a recent development, leaders face a growing stack of agentic AI governance frameworks. Underneath the jargon, every one of them asks the same four questions about your AI agents.

When I ask leadership teams which agentic AI governance framework they follow, the answers usually split along geography. Some point to Singapore, some to the European Union (EU) and some to the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) in the U.S. Most assume these frameworks compete, and many conclude governance can wait until the rules settle.

The frameworks do not compete, and governance cannot wait. Underneath the acronyms, every serious framework for AI agents asks the same four questions: what an agent may do, who answers for it, how it can be stopped and how the business proves it. A organization that can answer them has done most of what any framework will ask.

The 2026 AI Index from Stanford’s Institute for Human-Centered AI demonstrates why. AI agents completed 66.3% of tasks on a leading computer-use benchmark in 2025, up from about 5% in 2024, while reported AI incidents reached a record 362, up from 233 the year before.

Industry observers note that my work advising retail and consumer companies across the Americas, Europe, Australasia and Japan gives me a split-screen view of this debate. The vocabulary changes from market to market, but the questions boards and regulators ask about agents are remarkably similar.

The landscape is smaller than it seems. In January, at the World Economic Forum in Davos, Singapore’s Infocomm Media Development Authority (IMDA) released what it describes as the first governance framework built specifically for agentic AI. NIST’s voluntary AI Risk Management Framework organizes the work into four functions, and researchers at the University of California, Berkeley published an agentic AI profile built on that structure in February.

It has been revealed that two other pieces complete the picture. ISO/IEC 42001, from the International Organization for Standardization, is the first global standard for an AI management system, and the law sets a floor in some markets. California’s rules on automated decision-making apply to covered businesses starting January 1, 2027, and the EU’s AI Act requires human oversight of high-risk systems, with most of those obligations now applying from December 2027.

In a recent development, singapore’s framework starts here. It asks organizations to choose suitable use cases first and then limit each agent’s autonomy and its access to tools and data. The World Economic Forum proposed in May that every agent carry an authorization profile recording what it may do, under what conditions and with what oversight.

In practice, that means a written mandate before an agent goes live. It should state what the agent may decide alone, what it may spend or promise and when it must hand a case to a person. A customer service agent might problem goodwill credits up to a fixed amount but hand off any conversation that involves a safety issue or a legal claim.

Industry observers note that the mandate should also name what the agent is measured on. Economists Bengt Holmström and Paul Milgrom indicated in 1991 that when some duties are easy to measure and others are not, strong rewards on the measurable ones pull effort away from the rest. An agent scored only on speed will optimize speed, and the customer relationship quietly becomes the unmeasured duty.

Every framework insists that accountability stays with people. Singapore calls for checkpoints where human approval is required, and NIST places accountability structures inside its “govern” function.

California’s rules offer the most precise standard. Human involvement there means a reviewer who knows how to interpret and use the technology’s output, analyzes it alongside other relevant information and has the authority to make or change the decision. Covered or not, any business can use that as the job description for an agent’s owner.

Sources indicate that one consumer business I advised gave its service agent a generous credit budget and no single owner. Credits crept upward for weeks because each team assumed another was watching. The fix took one meeting: a named owner, a ceiling and a weekly report.

The EU’s Article 14 states this question most clearly. It requires that the people overseeing a high-risk system can monitor it, override its output and intervene or halt it safely, for example with a “stop” button.

It has been revealed that singapore’s framework calls for technical controls across the agent’s life cycle, including baseline testing and restricting access to approved services. NIST launched an initiative this year that focuses in part on identity and authorization for AI agents.

In a recent development, this matters because an agent using an employee’s login leaves no clear record of who acted. The practical version is simple: Give each agent its own credentials, log every action and test the off switch before launch rather than during an incident. A short weekly review of what each agent decided, escalated and reversed will show whether its limits are too tight, too loose or simply unclear.

The final question is the one customers, auditors and boards eventually ask. ISO/IEC 42001 answers it by treating AI governance as a management system, embedded in everyday processes alongside existing quality and information security systems. Singapore’s fourth dimension adds transparency and training for the people who use agents.

Recent findings suggest that boards are already asking. More than 62% of directors in the National Association of Corporate Directors’ 2025 survey said they now set aside agenda time for full-board AI discussions. A one-page register listing every agent, its owner, its limits and its last review gives those discussions something concrete to examine.

The first three steps are simple. Build the agent register this quarter, starting with the agents already handling customers or money. Choose one framework as the spine, NIST for its widely used vocabulary or ISO/IEC 42001 when customers expect certification, and borrow Singapore’s agent-specific controls.

In a recent development, then check the legal floor in each market where the business operates. Agents will keep getting more capable, and the frameworks will keep multiplying. The four questions will not change, and the leaders who can answer them for every agent at work will find that compliance becomes a byproduct of good management rather than a project of its own.

Leaders face a growing stack of agentic AI governance frameworks. Underneath the jargon, every one of them asks the same four questions about your AI agents.

The frameworks do not compete, and governance cannot wait. Underneath the acronyms, every serious framework for AI agents asks the same four questions: what an agent may do, who answers for it, how it can be stopped and how the business proves it. A company that can answer them has done most of what any framework will ask.

#20. Air traffic control, phone systems and emails are all down following China’s AI espionage scandal — is there a common answer?

Air traffic control, phone systems and emails are all down following China’s AI espionage scandal — is there a common answer?

💡 Key Takeaways
  • An old English proverb anchored in superstition from ancient Greek and Roman beliefs is that bad luck always comes in threes, but that does not mean bad luck was always random.
  • In a recent development, the United States has now experienced two debilitating, unprecedented blackouts across critical infrastructure in two days.
  • Industry observers note that could China and other hostile foreign actors be targeting U.S.

An old English proverb anchored in superstition from ancient Greek and Roman beliefs is that bad luck always comes in threes, but that does not mean bad luck was always random.

In a recent development, the United States has now experienced two debilitating, unprecedented blackouts across critical infrastructure in two days. The timing is almost too coincidental to be a coincidence – coming on the heels of the removal of Jensen Huang as Nvidia CEO amidst an affair with a suspected Chinese spy, widespread recriminations about chip exports to China, and demands for tighter export controls and more hawkish policies against China.

Industry observers note that could China and other hostile foreign actors be targeting U.S. infrastructure? It’s too early to know for sure, but the country deserves far more transparent answers than we have received so far.

It has been revealed that at 3:54 p.m. ET on Friday, November 13, the Federal Aviation Administration grounded every departing flight in America, “due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety.” It was only the third nationwide ground stop ever ordered. The first came on Sept. 11, 2001; the second more than 20 years later, on Jan. 11, 2023.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy would say only that “a communication issue” had struck every one of the 22 centers that guide planes across the country, and that technicians were investigating. A subsequent press conference by Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin did little to reassure anyone, with no answers about what happened and little reassurance that it would be fixable anytime soon, with airports sending travelers home and communicating that flight cancellations would persist for many hours at a minimum, if not days.

Recent findings suggest that it was the second time in two days that critical infrastructure the country cannot function without simply stopped, potentially for very nefarious reasons. The day before, Microsoft’s Outlook, Teams and Copilot went dark in 74 countries and stayed down for hours. Both blackouts struck within a day-and-a-half of the most damaging China espionage story in years.

In a recent development, the last nationwide ground stop, in 2023, lasted about 90 minutes and still delayed more than 10,000 flights and canceled 1,300. Friday’s lasted hours with no resolution imminent on the horizon. At the four-hour point of this latest ground stop, 10,243 flights were already delayed and 3,234 cancelled, with flights grounded not only at single regional airports but across the entire nation, suggesting systemic breakdowns rather than localized concerns.

In a recent development, microsoft’s failure began at 11:17 a.m. ET on Thursday and spread across 19 Microsoft 365 services. Within an hour, complaints about Outlook were running at more than 2,000 times their normal level. Microsoft counts more than 450 million paid commercial seats, with many millions of those users locked out entirely from their inboxes and other critical services.

Recent findings suggest that the casualty list reads like a roll call of essential services: the U.S. House of Representatives was substantively incapacitated; a federal appeals court that could not send or receive email; Britain’s Parliament and its National Health Service, where the failure threatened patients’ prescriptions; Australia’s spy agency and federal police were sent offline as well.

When a botched CrowdStrike update crashed 8.5 million machines in 2024, the Fortune 500 alone lost an estimated $5.4 billion. One risk adviser already puts Microsoft’s bill in the billions for Australia alone, not to mention the lost economic value in the U.S. or the rest of the world. This was the first time in history so many people were locked out for so long – with shifting and unsatisfactory explanations. Similarly, this is the first time in global aviation history where there has been a nationwide ground stop with no satisfactory, clear explanation and immediate fix.

Industry observers note that microsoft wrote the playbook for false comfort. For a full day it insisted there was “no indication” of malicious activity while its own bulletins demonstrated it did not know what had broken. If it did not know for sure, then how could they know for sure there was no indication of anything malicious amidst shifting explanations?

First it blamed elevated load, then servers that had unexpectedly dropped out. It found no recent change that lined up with the failure. Hours later, it was rolling back a network change that did. Early Friday, engineers were still trying to “pinpoint the underlying cause of the traffic influx.”.

Only on Friday afternoon did Microsoft name a culprit: a flaw introduced during a network capacity upgrade, “not related to cyber.” That sequence is as nonsensical as it is falsely reassuring. No patient would trust a doctor who swears it is not an infection before he can diagnose the fever. You cannot rule out what you cannot yet explain, and nobody can feel particularly reassured from this disturbing sequence of events and shifting explanations.

Industry observers note that on Thursday morning, Nvidia, whose board failures we dissected in Fortune this week, announced the resignation of Jensen Huang, the chip industry’s loudest advocate for selling to China, after he admitted an affair with a businesswoman U.S. officials suspect of spying for Beijing. Beijing has been vocal in calling it a smear amidst a rapid escalation of U.S.-China tensions. Lawmakers in both parties are demanding testimony and tighter export controls. Within three hours, inboxes went dark from Capitol Hill to Canberra. A day later, planes stopped and were grounded.

Perhaps we are being too conspiratorial, but there is a certain uncanny resemblance to Beijing’s favorite playbook, which is to divert from negative news stories by shutting down internet services and diverting public attention.

Industry observers note that for example, in 2011, a petition to free Ai Weiwei got Change.org knocked offline. In 2012, exposés of the family fortunes of Xi Jinping and Wen Jiabao got Bloomberg and The Newly introduced York Times blocked in China and targeted by hackers. In 2014, as Hong Kong marched for democracy, a newspaper and a voting site were buried under one of the largest attacks the internet had ever seen. In 2015, China’s “Great Cannon” hammered GitHub for days for hosting banned news. In 2019, Telegram and the LIHKG forum were swamped as Hong Kong marched again. In 2022, news of the zero-COVID protests on Twitter drowned in a deluge of spam. Maybe this pattern of untimely hacks was merely a coincidence – or could it have been more than coincidence?

Microsoft knows this adversary better than anyone. Hackers tied to Beijing tore through its customers’ Exchange servers in 2021 and stole some 60,000 State Department emails through its cloud in 2023, a breach a federal review board blamed on a “cascade of security failures” at Microsoft. Just three weeks ago, Microsoft itself said a China-aligned group had turned AI agents loose on more than 2,250 Microsoft 365 customers.

It has been revealed that whatever the cause, the lesson is identical. Some cyber experts are warning about potentially economically destabilizing cyberattacks, with researchers warning that AI-enabled hacking is spreading like a virus: attacks on previously unknown flaws have roughly doubled since capable open-source models arrived.

U.S. agencies say China’s Volt Typhoon hackers have already burrowed into American communications, transportation, energy and water networks, in some cases for five years, positioning themselves to disrupt them. They sat inside one small Massachusetts electric and water utility for more than 300 days. If the inbox and the skies can go dark on consecutive days, why not the grid, or the tap? Is it time for every business and household to buy storage batteries, water tanks, MREs and porta potties?

In a recent development, of course, regardless of whether this was a Chinese or foreign malevolent actor attack, or whether it was merely the coincidental degradation of antiquated and outdated infrastructure systems, all of this takes place against the backdrop of the substantive hollowing out of U.S. government counterintelligence and cyber capabilities, with more than 1,500 special agents having departed the FBI and almost 1,000 staffers—about one-third of the workforce—have left the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) since Trump returned to office. Domestic commentators point out that this comes despite $1 trillion in Pentagon spending; and that the upgrades needed for aviation infrastructure would have cost $40 billion.

Legendary Intel CEO Andy Grove’s renowned book was titled, “Only the paranoid survive”, suggesting paranoia is not entirely unwarranted. The poet Delmore Schwartz remarked in 1966 that “even paranoids have enemies.” And everyone from Joseph Heller to Henry Kissinger to Kurt Cobain has repeated some variation of “just because you’re paranoid, doesn’t mean they’re not out to get you.”.

Industry observers note that sometimes, superstition that seems delusional can connect authentic facts. And sometimes it behooves us to look at “worst case” scenarios in an effort to avoid them.

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 13, 2026 at 12:51 pmNovember 13, 2026 at 4:38 pm.

Araceli Biosciences, a Portland-area biotech tech giant, has secured $4.5 million in funding to help commercialize technology and develop new products that support using human cells instead of animal studies to test new drugs.

Sources indicate that the Tigard, Ore., startup offers instruments and software for creating images of cells and automating analysis. Its technologies fall under the umbrella term “New Approach Methodologies,” which includes human-tissue models, computer simulations and AI-based approaches that reduce or avoid experimentation on animals such as mice, rats and monkeys.

Recent findings suggest that supporters of the methods, known as NAMs, argue that they can yield better outcomes because animals are not a perfect substitute for humans and can generate irrelevant findings. That can lead to costly, time-intensive development of drugs that fail to perform in people. Advocates also promote the alternatives as more humane.

The National Institutes of Health confirmed $84 million in September to build infrastructure for NAMs research at 10 sites nationwide.

“[T]he efforts signal a significant investment into human-based technologies as the future of preclinical science, aiming to make research faster, more predictive, and more directly relevant to human health,” the NIH said in a release.

Araceli said it has raised a total of $22.7 million from investors. The new round was led by William Cortelyou and included Fluke Venture Partners, according to PitchBook. The company disclosed Thursday that businessman and animal welfare advocate Jeff Swickard was also an investor.

Swickard owns 54 auto dealerships across Western states and is a commercial real estate investor with $250 million invested in Portland properties.

Shawn MacDonald, chief financial officer for Araceli, stated Swickard’s “support reflects a belief that we share, which is that better science and more humane science go hand-in-hand.”.

Araceli launched in 2023 as a spinoff from Phoseon Technology, which makes UV LED units for industrial curing and life sciences applications.

In a recent development, the tech giant noted that companies and institutions using Araceli technology include the Max Planck Institute and Evotec in Germany, the Wertheim UF Scripps Institute in Florida, VALID Therapeutics in Boston, and Ginkgo Bioworks, as well as large pharmaceutical companies. It has 30 employees.

#22. Phota Labs uses AI to turn everyday photos into professional-looking shots

Phota Labs uses AI to turn everyday photos into professional-looking shots

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read | Sumber: https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/12/phota-labs-uses-ai-to-turn-everyday-photos-into-professional-looking-shots/

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A new iOS app called Phota Labs gives owners access to a personal AI photo assistant that turns everyday snapshots into images that look like they were taken by a professional photographer, all while preserving the authenticity of the image.
  • Rather than giving consumers yet another photo-editing tool, Phota Labs aims to use advances in AI to automate the editing process so it’s easier for anyone to get access to better photos.
  • The a16z-backed startup was founded by Cecilia Zhang and Zach Xia, who met at Adobe while working on computational photography products, including Project Indigo, Lightroom, and Photoshop.

A new iOS app called Phota Labs gives owners access to a personal AI photo assistant that turns everyday snapshots into images that look like they were taken by a professional photographer, all while preserving the authenticity of the image.

Rather than giving consumers yet another photo-editing tool, Phota Labs aims to use advances in AI to automate the editing process so it’s easier for anyone to get access to better photos.

The a16z-backed startup was founded by Cecilia Zhang and Zach Xia, who met at Adobe while working on computational photography products, including Project Indigo, Lightroom, and Photoshop.

The duo saw a gap in the editing tools on the market and believed that although editing tools can be powerful for enhancing photos, they aren’t very effective at fixing a photo that wasn’t captured well in the first place. Phota Labs changes that by focusing on fixing the shot itself while preserving the natural appearances of those in the image.

“Phota is your personal photo assistant that can make great photos for any moment you want to keep before you even ask, which means that it’s a very proactive experience,” Zhang told TechCrunch in an interview. “Think of it almost like a photographer or virtual photographer who looks over your camera roll and tries to understand what’s happening and how they could have taken that photo for you on the spot for that scene.”.

The idea is to use AI to transform photos, whether that’s turning a wide-angle group photo into a tighter portrait or transforming a selfie into a regular shot.

Users can choose from different photography styles that determine how AI transforms their images, ranging from subtle edits that preserve the original lens and composition to more dramatic transformations that introduce effects like fish-eye lenses, alternative angles, and entirely different perspectives.

While some people turn to ChatGPT and other generative AI tools to enhance or edit images, these tools can often alter a person’s appearance, especially when working with blurry photos because they don’t know what that person actually looks like.

Recent findings suggest that “For Phota, we built our own tech,” Zhang said. ”We built this personalization technology that actually learns about people’s identity and is able to preserve them in any transformation we do to a photo.”.

Images edited with Phota Labs feature invisible watermarks that identify them as altered by AI when shared on social platforms.

According to recent reports, the startup is initially targeting people who take tons of photos and like to share them on social media, but don’t want to deal with the tedious process of editing photos. Over time, the founders envision a broader audience, from retirees looking to create beautiful photos for their grandchildren to parents who want to share polished family albums with friends and relatives.

According to recent reports, “We have this obsession with authenticity,” Xia remarked. “I think there’s so much value in connecting AI with real moments and making sure those photos are not perfect, in a sense. That’s why we spend a lot of research into understanding personal context, into building this identity model because we want to make sure the photos are authentic. They’re just better photos of the same moment, rather than saying, ‘Oh, this is an AI image’.”.

Xia said beta users were excited to see better versions of moments they had actually lived and saw the results as photos of real memories rather than AI-generated images. The founders discovered that users were taking more photos because they knew Phota Labs could enhance them later.

Recent findings suggest that “We’re turning something that’s unusable into something that people want to print,” Zhang stated. “People who just love photos but never really got into editing can now experience professional quality that could never have been possible. So, I think that meant so much to us. There’s so many cherished moments for photos, and we really want them to be actually meaningful and something that you can remember.”.

In terms of funding, the company raised a $5.6 million seed round led by a16z last year.

According to recent reports, phota Labs is launching as a free app to build an initial user base before exploring a freemium model. The startup also plans to launch an Android app in the future.

It has been revealed that before we dive into the newsletter, one more bit of great news about our upcoming event (which we promise we’ll stop talking about soon): Michael Grimes, the star tech banker from Morgan Stanley at the center of Uber’s IPO (and Facebook IPO, and Slack’s and Spotify’s), has been persuaded to come and talk about direct listings, which we’re very excited about. If you’re as confused as we are about whether these make sense for more than a couple of companies each year (current status: we don’t think they do), you won’t want to miss this rare conversation with “Wall Street’s Silicon Valley whisperer.”.

Note that seats are almost gone. Ben Horowitz,  the co-founder of the venture firm Andreessen Horowitz, has a fresh book coming out this coming Monday titled “What You Do is Who You Are,” that takes a look at how to create “culture” at a manufacturer.

Industry observers note that it’s a word that’s thrown around a lot but that’s very hard to grasp, let alone implement in a sustainable way. Horowitz learned firsthand as a CEO how elusive it can be when he took stock of his company, only to discover it was made up of “screamers who intimidated their people,” others who “neglected to give any feedback,” and at least one compulsive liar who excelled at sucking up to Horowitz and also making up stories from whole cloth.

Horowitz claims creating culture was a missing part of his education, and in this new book — a follow-up to his best-selling “The Hard Thing About Hard Things” — he does his best to fill that gap for other CEOs, using his own experience, as well as lessons gleaned from historical figures Toussaint Louverture and Genghis Khan, along with Shaka Senghor, a contemporary who served time for murder and today is a criminal justice reform advocate.

It’s an instructive and novel combination, and we suggest picking up the book, especially if you love history. In the meantime, we sat down recently with Horowitz to talk about its timing and whether some of the biggest cultural blow-ups in the startup industry — Uber and WeWork — could have been avoided. These excerpts have been edited for length and clarity. Note that we’ll have more of the conversation — including Horowitz’s thoughts about dual-class shares —  for readers of Extra Crunch on Monday.

In a recent development, you’ve just written a book about culture that’s coming out just as a lot of questions are being raised about culture because of WeWork. What happened there?

[Cofounder Adam Neumann] had a certain kind of culture there. He had some holes — some great strengths and great holes. And sometimes that happens. When you’re really good at part of it, you can delude yourself into thinking that you’ve got everything you need when you have some massive incompleteness.

Adam is so amazing. Like, the way they got all the money and everything. And the vision was so spectacular. And everybody there believed it, and they recruited some phenomenal talent. But when you’re that optimistic, it does help to have something in the culture that indicates [allows] people to bring you the bad news, like, if the accounting is all over the place or what have you.

In a recent development, as with Uber’s Travis Kalanick, whose culture also came under fire, Neumann operated in very plain sight. He wasn’t hiding who he was or what he was spending.

Right, everybody knew how Travis was running the tech giant. Everyone in Silicon Valley knew, let alone everyone on the board. The culture was published. You can look up Uber’s values [from that period].

Industry observers note that travis designed, I think, a really compelling culture, and believed in it, and published it. And the consequences of what he was missing were also super well-known. It’s only when board members think people are coming after them that [they take an interest in these things].

What are the biggest lessons in these two cases?

It has been revealed that I obviously know more about Uber [as a Lyft investor who follows the space]. In Uber’s case, it’s a very subtle thing. Travis had a really good code. But he had a bug in it.

In a recent development, I think it was reported that, like, Travis encouraged bad behavior. I don’t think he did at all. I just think he didn’t make it clear that legal and ethical [considerations] were more important than competitiveness. As a result, when left to their own devices, in a distributed organization where there was a lot of distributed power, that combination had people doing things that were out of bounds.

Sources indicate that and he was making everybody so much money. And the manufacturer was growing so fast that, for the board members, I suspect they were like, ‘As long as it’s making money, I’m not going to worry about what happens next.’.

Sources indicate that to me, the unfair part is, like, they shouldn’t get any credit at the end. Whatever you’re blaming Travis for [you should blame them, too] because they didn’t see it, either. I think that’s a charitable way of putting it.
