#25. From NDAs to exit interviews: 10 ways companies protect trade secrets

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 22 min read (4426 words)
Business & Policy

From NDAs to exit interviews: 10 ways companies protect trade secrets

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 22 min read | Sumber: https://qz.com/trade-secret-protection-insider-threats

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Trade secret protection against insider threats depends on layered controls, and these 10 measures, from access limits and NDAs to exit interviews, show how companies keep secrets in-house.
  • It has been revealed that in court, the value of a formula or a customer list is only half the test of a trade secret.
  • According to recent reports, insiders are the hardest case for trade secret protection.

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Trade secret protection against insider threats depends on layered controls, and these 10 measures, from access limits and NDAs to exit interviews, show how companies keep secrets in-house.

It has been revealed that in court, the value of a formula or a customer list is only half the test of a trade secret. The other half is whether its owner worked to keep it secret. Under U.S. law, information keeps trade secret status only if its owner takes reasonable measures to protect that secrecy. The Defend Trade Secrets Act of 2016 and the Uniform Trade Secrets Act, adopted in some form by most states, both contain that requirement. Source code or a pricing model left open to anyone can lose that protection.

According to recent reports, insiders are the hardest case for trade secret protection. Employees, contractors and vendors already hold legitimate access to the information a company most wants to keep. They do not need to break into anything. They need only copy a file, forward an email or carry knowledge out the door when they leave.

According to recent reports, A 2018 federal case highlights how that risk can surface. Prosecutors charged former Apple $AAPL engineer Xiaolang Zhang with stealing trade secrets related to the company's self-driving car work. The case involved an employee, not an outside intruder.

No single control closes the gap. Companies tend to layer legal, technical and human measures so that a failure in one can be caught by another. Contracts set expectations and give an employer a route to court. Software limits what a person can reach and records what they do. Training and offboarding practices shape whether people understand the rules and treat them as binding.

Those layers also serve a second purpose. If a dispute reaches court, a record of classification policies, access reviews and signed agreements helps show that the tech giant took reasonable measures. Without that record, the legal claim itself can weaken.

This list covers 10 measures companies commonly use, from the first day of employment to the last and in some cases beyond it. It is a selection, not a complete catalog, and the order is not a ranking. Each slide explains one method, how it works in practice and where its limits lie. Security, legal and human resources teams can use it as a starting framework for an insider threat program. Other readers can use it to understand how organizations approach the risk of someone with a badge and a login walking away with what they know.

Companies start guarding trade secrets by deciding, in writing, which information qualifies. A firm cannot easily show a court that it protected a secret it never identified. It also cannot direct staff or software to protect information that no one has labeled.

The legal definition explains why this step comes first. Under the Defend Trade Secrets Act of 2016, information must draw independent economic value from not being generally known. A written inventory shows which information the company believes meets that test. It also gives the company a dated record to point to if it must show that it took reasonable measures.

An inventory typically begins with the categories that give a business its competitive edge. These can include product formulas, manufacturing processes, source code, algorithms, pricing models, supplier terms and customer lists. People from engineering, sales and research usually take part. They know which details would help a rival most. The inventory records where each item is stored, who is responsible for it and which teams use it.

Recent findings suggest that classification comes next. Many companies use tiered labels, such as public, internal, confidential and restricted. The tier determines how the information is stored, shared and eventually destroyed. A formula for a flagship product might sit in the highest tier. A general employee handbook might sit in the lowest.

Confidentiality markings put those labels into practice. A header or watermark on a document, a banner on a database login screen or a tag in file metadata tells a reader the material is protected. Markings also matter in litigation. A departing employee has a harder time claiming ignorance about a file stamped "confidential.".

The approach has a known weakness. If a company marks nearly everything as confidential, the label stops signaling anything. Employees may learn to ignore it. In a dispute, an opposing lawyer can argue that the company never separated real secrets from routine paperwork.

Sources indicate that inventories also go stale. Newly introduced products, acquisitions and reorganizations change what a organization holds and what it values. For that reason, many firms review their lists on a regular schedule. The goal is a record that matches what the business actually guards.

Least privilege means each employee, contractor or system account gets only the access its job requires, and nothing more. Need-to-know applies the same logic to the information itself: a person sees a specific secret only when their work depends on it.

Sources indicate that the idea has deep roots in computer security. Jerome Saltzer and Michael Schroeder listed least privilege among their design principles in a 1975 paper, "The Protection of Information in Computer Systems." Need-to-know comes from government handling of classified material. In that setting, a security clearance alone does not open every file.

According to recent reports, companies usually put these rules into practice through role-based access control, often shortened to RBAC. Administrators attach permissions to job roles, such as sales engineer or formulation chemist, rather than granting them person by person. A newly introduced hire inherits the rights of the assigned role. Researchers at the U.S. National Institute of Standards and Technology helped formalize the RBAC model in the 1990s.

Segmentation adds a second layer. A manufacturer might keep its process recipes in a repository separate from general engineering files. A software company might split its source code so that most developers can reach only the modules they maintain. An employee who copies everything within reach then leaves with a fragment rather than the whole.

Industry observers note that permissions tend to pile up over time. A worker who moves from research to marketing may keep the old research access unless someone removes it. Security teams call this privilege creep. Periodic access reviews, run on a fixed schedule or triggered by a role change, ask managers to confirm that each permission still matches the person's current duties.

Sources indicate that orphaned accounts create a related gap. Logins left behind by finished projects or reassigned staff give an insider a path that no one is watching.

Sources indicate that the cost is friction. Tight controls can slow collaboration, and engineers locked out of a needed file may look for workarounds. Many firms answer this with a documented request process. Temporary access is granted, logged and set to expire on a fixed date.

A nondisclosure agreement signed at hiring defines what an employee must keep confidential. It also gives the manufacturer a contractual basis to sue if that information leaves.

In a recent development, most employee confidentiality agreements follow a similar structure. They define confidential information, often by category, such as source code, manufacturing processes, pricing data and customer lists. They limit how the employee may use that information, usually to work performed for the employer. They also list exclusions, such as information that is already public or that the employee knew before joining.

Timing matters. Companies typically present the agreement before a new hire receives system credentials or sees sensitive material. A signature collected after months of access leaves a gap in the record for that period.

Sources indicate that duration is a separate drafting choice. Many agreements keep obligations for trade secrets in force for as long as the information stays secret. Less sensitive business information often carries a fixed term instead.

Sources indicate that U.S. federal law adds a specific requirement. The Defend Trade Secrets Act of 2016 grants immunity to employees who disclose trade secrets in confidence to a federal, state or local government official, or to an attorney. That protection applies when the disclosure is made solely to report or investigate a suspected violation of law. It also covers disclosures filed under seal in a lawsuit.

According to recent reports, employers must give notice of that immunity in any agreement governing the use of trade secrets or confidential information. The rule applies to contracts entered into or updated after the law took effect in May 2016. The notice can appear in the agreement itself or through a cross-reference to a manufacturer policy document.

Leaving the notice out has a defined cost. The employer cannot recover exemplary damages or attorney fees from that employee in a later action under the federal statute. The company can still sue, but it gives up part of the available remedy.

According to recent reports, an agreement has limits. A signature does not block a file transfer or a printout. Its value comes after a breach, when it supports a claim for an injunction or damages.

In a recent development, noncompete and nonsolicitation clauses limit what a former employee can do after leaving, not just what they can disclose. Companies use them as a second layer behind confidentiality agreements. Whether a court will enforce them depends heavily on where the employee works.

Sources indicate that A noncompete agreement bars a worker from joining a competitor or starting a rival business for a set period after departure. Its value for trade secret protection is indirect. If an engineer cannot work for a direct competitor for a year, a formula or product roadmap is less likely to travel with them. A nondisclosure agreement works differently. It lets the person work anywhere but forbids sharing protected information.

Enforceability is the central constraint. California voids most employee noncompete agreements under Business and Professions Code section 16600. Employers there cannot rely on them to keep departing staff away from rivals. A handful of other states also restrict them sharply.

Where noncompetes are allowed, courts commonly ask whether the restriction is reasonable. They look at its length, its geographic reach and the type of work it covers. A clause written too broadly risks being narrowed or thrown out entirely.

Rules also differ across borders. A multinational employer may face one standard in Texas, another in Germany and another in the U.K. Legal teams often draft jurisdiction-specific versions rather than relying on a single global template.

Nonsolicitation clauses are narrower. They typically bar a former employee from recruiting ex-colleagues or pursuing the company's clients for a defined period. They do not block someone from taking a new job. For that reason, courts in many jurisdictions treat them more favorably than noncompetes. California courts have limited many of these clauses as well.

Garden leave is another option, common in the U.K. financial sector. The departing employee stays on the payroll during a notice period but stops working and loses access to company systems. Their knowledge of current projects ages while they remain bound by their employment contract.

In a recent development, federal trade secret law draws its own line. The Defend Trade Secrets Act bars courts from issuing an injunction that prevents a person from entering an employment relationship. Any conditions placed on fresh employment must rest on evidence of threatened misappropriation. What the person merely knows is not enough. The law also says such injunctions cannot conflict with state laws that prohibit restraints on a lawful profession, trade or business.

Industry observers note that data loss prevention software, usually called DLP, tracks where sensitive files go and can stop a transfer before the data leaves the firm. It checks email, web uploads, USB drives and print jobs against rules that define what information must stay inside.

DLP tools generally operate in three places. Endpoint agents run on laptops and desktops. There they can see files copied to removable drives, pasted into other apps or sent to a printer. Network tools inspect traffic leaving the corporate network, including outgoing email and web uploads. Cloud tools connect to file-sharing and collaboration services, where much tech giant data is stored.

In a recent development, the software decides what counts as sensitive by inspecting content. Simple rules match fixed patterns, such as the format of a credit card or Social Security number. Trade secrets rarely follow a fixed pattern. Companies therefore rely on other detection methods. Document fingerprinting lets a tool recognize a protected file, or a large excerpt from it, even after someone renames it. Exact data matching compares outgoing content against a registered set of records, such as a customer database.

Classification labels make the job easier. When a file carries a tag such as "confidential" or "restricted," a DLP policy can act on that tag instead of guessing from the text. Microsoft $MSFT Purview, for example, lets companies tie data loss prevention policies to sensitivity labels applied to documents and email.

Sources indicate that policies can respond in several ways. A tool may block a transfer outright. It may warn the user and ask for a business justification. It may encrypt the file or log the event for later review. Companies often start in monitoring mode to learn how data normally moves before they turn on blocking.

DLP has clear limits. Rules that are too broad generate false positives. Those alerts interrupt legitimate work and bury security teams in noise. Rules that are too narrow miss compressed, encrypted or heavily edited files. Inspecting encrypted web traffic requires the firm to decrypt it first, which raises its own technical and privacy questions.

In a recent development, some channels sit outside the software's view entirely. An employee can photograph a screen with a personal phone, copy details by hand or remember a process. DLP cannot stop what a person knows. Companies treat it as one layer that narrows the easiest exit routes, not as a guarantee that nothing leaves.

User and entity behavior analytics, or UEBA, spots insider risk by learning what normal activity looks like for each person and system. It then alerts security teams when behavior departs from that baseline, catching patterns that fixed rules can miss.

The approach starts with data. UEBA platforms take in logs from identity systems, file servers, cloud applications, VPNs and endpoint devices. Over time, they model typical behavior for each individual and for peers in the same role. An engineer who regularly opens design files has a different baseline from a sales manager who works mostly in a customer database.

Alerts come from deviations. One common trigger is a sudden spike in downloads. Others include access to repositories outside a person's usual projects and logins at odd hours or from fresh locations. Bulk activity shortly before a resignation is another pattern security teams watch for.

Industry observers note that many systems combine several weak signals into a single risk score. A late-night login on its own means little. A late-night login followed by a large export to a personal cloud account carries more weight.

It has been revealed that logging and audit trails sit underneath all of this. A record of who opened which file, when and from where serves two purposes. It feeds the analytics as events happen. It also becomes evidence if the tech giant later needs to show what an insider took. Retention policies matter here. Logs deleted after a short window cannot support an investigation that begins months later.

The tools have limits. Baselines take time to form, so latest hires and people changing roles can generate noise. An anomaly is not proof of wrongdoing. A flagged spike may reflect a legitimate deadline or a new assignment. Human analysts still need to review alerts before anyone acts on them.

Industry observers note that law shapes how far monitoring can go, and the rules differ by region. In the EU, the General Data Protection Regulation requires a lawful basis and transparency when employers process employee data. In Germany, works councils have co-determination rights over technical systems capable of monitoring staff. In the U.S., federal law sets fewer limits on workplace monitoring, but some states add their own. New York and Connecticut require employers to notify workers about electronic monitoring.

Companies using UEBA commonly set out their monitoring rules in a written policy that employees receive before the monitoring applies to them. Access to the behavioral data is usually limited to a small group of analysts. Those steps address the transparency duties in Europe and the notice laws in U.S. states such as Latest York and Connecticut.

Sources indicate that employee training turns a manufacturer's secrecy rules into daily habits. Staff who know what counts as confidential, how it is labeled and how to respond to suspicious requests are better placed to avoid leaking information by accident. They also cannot easily claim they never knew the rules.

It has been revealed that programs typically start at onboarding. Upcoming hires learn which categories of information the organization treats as confidential, such as product formulas, manufacturing processes, unreleased designs, source code, pricing models and customer lists. They also learn where that material may be stored and who may see it.

Recurring sessions keep the message from fading after the first week. Companies often pair annual refreshers with shorter reminders tied to specific events. Examples include a product launch, a merger or a move to new collaboration software.

Much of the content is practical. Employees learn what a marking like "Confidential" or "Restricted" requires of them. That can mean not forwarding a document to a personal email account and not saving files to unapproved cloud services. It can also mean not discussing a project in public places such as airport lounges or trade show floors.

Industry observers note that training also covers approaches from outside the manufacturer. Social engineering attempts, including phishing emails and phone calls from people posing as colleagues or IT staff, aim to trick employees into handing over access or documents. Engineers and researchers may also hear from recruiters, consultants or expert network firms seeking details about current work. Training explains how to decline those requests and where to report them.

It has been revealed that another topic is what upcoming employees bring with them. Companies commonly instruct hires not to bring files or confidential information from former employers. That instruction reduces the risk that the new employer gets drawn into another tech giant's trade secret dispute.

According to recent reports, training matters in court as well as in the office. U.S. trade secret law protects information only when its owner takes reasonable measures to keep it secret. Records showing who attended which session, and when, can help a company show a court that it took those measures.

Training has limits. It cannot stop someone who has already decided to take information. It is aimed mainly at preventing careless mistakes and at making clear, in writing, what the rules required.

In a recent development, companies extend trade secret protection beyond their own payroll in two ways. They bind contractors, vendors and partners to written confidentiality terms, and they share only the information each outside party needs. Third parties often hold access similar to what employees have. The controls have to follow the data outside the manufacturer.

It has been revealed that outside parties sit in a gap that internal policies can miss. A software contractor may work inside a company's code repository. A contract manufacturer may hold full production specifications. A marketing agency may receive customer lists or pricing plans. None of these people signed the employee handbook, and many work for firms that also serve competitors.

The legal stakes are direct. Handing confidential material to an outside firm with no confidentiality obligation can undercut a company's claim that it kept the information secret. A nondisclosure agreement, or NDA, signed before any disclosure gives the company evidence that it treated the information as confidential.

In a recent development, vendor contracts often go further than a basic NDA. They can define what counts as confidential information and limit its use to a specific project. They can require the vendor to bind its own staff and subcontractors to the same terms. Many also require the return or destruction of materials when the work ends, with written certification.

Recent findings suggest that audit rights add a check on those promises. A contract can allow the company to inspect how the vendor stores and handles its data, or to request security documentation. Without such a clause, a company may have little visibility into what happens after data leaves its systems.

Sources indicate that technical controls mirror the contract terms. Contractor accounts can be set to expire on the contract's end date. That removes the need for someone to remember to close them. Access can also be confined to a single project folder, a separate environment or a virtual desktop that keeps files off the contractor's own machines.

According to recent reports, joint ventures and research partnerships raise a different problem. Each side wants to collaborate without handing over everything it knows. Partners often disclose information in stages, starting with nonconfidential summaries before sharing detailed specifications. Some set up clean teams — small groups walled off from the rest of the business — to review sensitive material. Clean teams are common in merger due diligence between competitors, where antitrust rules also limit what can be shared.

In a recent development, records carry weight throughout the relationship. A log of what was disclosed, to whom and when lets a company show which secrets a partner actually received. That record can be central to a misappropriation claim if the relationship ends in a dispute.

The weeks around an employee's departure are a high-risk window for trade secret theft. Companies reduce that risk with a structured offboarding process. It covers recent account activity, an exit interview, returned devices, signed acknowledgments and same-day credential cutoff.

The review often starts before the person walks out. Once someone gives notice, security and legal teams may examine that employee's recent account activity. They look for large downloads, files sent to personal email addresses or cloud accounts, and access to projects outside the person's current role. A finding at this stage gives the tech giant time to act before the employee starts a upcoming job.

It has been revealed that the exit interview serves a legal purpose as well as a human resources one. A manager or HR representative reminds the departing worker which categories of information remain confidential after the job ends. The employee is asked to confirm that organization documents, code and customer lists have been returned or deleted from personal devices. Many companies ask for that confirmation in writing. A signed certification restates obligations the employee already accepted. It also creates a record if a dispute follows.

Physical and digital property comes back at the same time. Laptops, phones, security badges, hardware tokens and external drives are collected and logged. Returned devices are often preserved rather than wiped right away. That way, their contents can still be examined if questions arise later.

Access revocation belongs on the last day of employment. In tense departures, it can happen at the moment the person is notified. The cutoff covers network logins, email, VPN connections, cloud applications, shared drives and building entry. Accounts in third-party tools, such as code repositories or customer relationship management systems, are easy to miss. A single forgotten account can leave a door open after the person is gone.

The case of Anthony Levandowski indicates how much scrutiny one departure can draw. Levandowski was a Google $GOOGL engineer who left to found a self-driving truck startup that Uber $UBER acquired. Waymo, Alphabet's self-driving car organization, then sued Uber over trade secrets tied to his departure. The companies settled in February 2018. Levandowski later pleaded guilty to one count of trade secret theft. He received a presidential pardon in January 2021.

An insider threat program gives a tech giant one team and one strategy for spotting, investigating and answering suspected trade secret theft. Pairing it with a prepared legal response lets the company act rapidly once evidence points to a specific person.

These programs commonly bring together three groups. Security staff understand the systems and the logs. Lawyers know what evidence a court will accept and what employment law allows. Human resources sees performance disputes, resignations and complaints that may give context to a technical alert. When these groups work separately, warning signs can sit in three different places without anyone connecting them.

The CERT National Insider Threat Center at Carnegie Mellon University's Software Engineering Institute publishes guidance that companies can use as a reference when building such a program. Its material treats insider risk as an organizational problem, not only a technical one. It addresses governance, policy and coordination between departments.

A written charter usually defines who sits on the team and who can authorize an investigation. It also sets out how employee privacy is protected along the way. An investigation launched without clear authority can expose the manufacturer to claims of its own. It can also weaken the case it was meant to build.

The response initiative covers what happens after a credible alert. The first step is usually evidence preservation. That means securing laptops, phones, email accounts and access logs before anything is wiped or overwritten. Forensic examiners can then reconstruct which files were opened, copied or sent, and when. A documented chain of custody helps that evidence hold up later.

The legal options depend on what the review finds. The Defend Trade Secrets Act of 2016 lets a trade secret owner sue in federal civil court. In extraordinary circumstances, a court can order an ex parte seizure of property to keep a secret from spreading. Ex parte means the order is issued without advance notice to the other side. The law also allows courts to grant injunctions and award damages.

Sources indicate that some cases move beyond civil court. The Economic Espionage Act of 1996 makes trade secret theft a federal crime. Companies can refer matters to federal prosecutors. A referral puts the criminal case in the government's hands. Legal teams weigh that step against the company's own goals, such as speed or confidentiality.

Teams test the blueprint through tabletop exercises, which walk members through a simulated incident step by step. They also keep contact lists current and revise the plan when systems or laws change. Those exercises show whether the team can secure devices and logs fast enough to support a request for emergency court relief.

#27. McKinsey Global Institute: Climate adaptation could need $1.2 trillion a year by 2050. $690 billion of it is stuck

📅 03 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4 min read (796 words)
Business & Policy

McKinsey Global Institute: Climate adaptation could need $1.2 trillion a year by 2050. $690 billion of it is stuck

📅 03 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read | Sumber: https://fortune.com/2026/11/03/climate-adaptation-cop31-mckinsey-global-institute-690-billion-barriers/

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that mekala Krishnan is a partner at the McKinsey Global Institute.
  • Industry observers note that after a sweltering summer on both sides of the Atlantic and a fall marked by storms in the Pacific, climate adaptation will be top of mind for many attending this year’s COP.
  • Sources indicate that the problem is neither a lack of solutions nor economic value.

Industry observers note that mekala Krishnan is a partner at the McKinsey Global Institute. Kanmani Chockalingam is a senior fellow at the McKinsey Global Institute. Sylvain Johansson is a senior partner and a director of the McKinsey Global Institute. The piece draws on the McKinsey Global Institute’s own research.

Industry observers note that after a sweltering summer on both sides of the Atlantic and a fall marked by storms in the Pacific, climate adaptation will be top of mind for many attending this year’s COP. Yet newly introduced research from the McKinsey Global Institute suggests that by 2050, the world could be leaving $690 billion in potential annual adaptation spending on the table.

Sources indicate that the problem is neither a lack of solutions nor economic value. Cooling systems can protect people from heat, irrigation can safeguard crops, and flood defenses can protect homes and businesses. On average, adaptation measures deliver benefits in avoided losses worth three times their cost.

It has been revealed that the question is how to turn that economic value into protection for those who need it. For adaptation to be “deployment ready,” someone must want and be able to implement it, and someone must be willing to finance it. Yet what makes economic sense for society does not always make financial sense for those expected to act.

At 2°C of warming, which current emissions trajectories suggest could be reached by 2050, protecting people and places to developed-economy standards could cost $1.2 trillion annually.

According to recent reports, the good news: About $460 billion, or 40%, is likely to be deployment ready. Much of it would fund cooling, stormwater management, and irrigation in high-income places with greater ability to pay and access to financing.

It has been revealed that that leaves 60% of adaptation needs facing barriers to deployment. We identified three challenges—affordability, willingness and ability to act, and bankability. Different barriers call for different responses. Lower costs cannot solve a coordination problem, just as more financing cannot create demand where incentives are missing.

The biggest barrier is affordability, affecting measures costing about $440 billion annually. In lower-income regions exposed to heat and drought, adaptation competes with food, housing, and other essentials, and lenders may doubt a borrower’s ability to repay. Protecting people to developed-economy standards at 2°C would cost about $130 per person annually on average—roughly half of an average household’s monthly income in Bangladesh.

In India and Sub-Saharan Africa, adaptation could cost 2% to 3% of GDP, with less than 20% of needed investment expected to be deployment ready. In higher-income regions, costs would be just 0.3% to 0.5% of GDP, with more than half deployment ready.

Industry observers note that making adaptation affordable requires lower-cost solutions and financing that can reach underserved households. In Ahmedabad, India, reflective cool roofs offered a relatively inexpensive way to protect low-income households from extreme heat. But individual installations were too small to attract conventional financing, while upfront costs remained out of reach for many residents. By bringing thousands of households together and combining subsidies with credit, the city and the Mahila Housing Trust helped overcome both obstacles.

It has been revealed that A second set of barriers affects measures costing about $210 billion annually, where willingness or ability to act is missing, even when financing may not be constrained. Some landowners or institutions may bear disproportionate costs for measures that benefit entire communities, weakening incentives to cooperate. Wildfire protection can prevent catastrophic losses, but its value may be invisible until disaster strikes. Large-scale projects often require years of coordination across governments, businesses, and communities.

Singapore’s Marina Bay district cooling network illustrates how execution challenges can be overcome. A shared district cooling system promised substantial efficiency gains over separate building-level cooling, but required developers to connect to common infrastructure and rely on a dedicated operator. Singapore integrated cooling pipes into the district’s infrastructure, established connection requirements, and licensed an operator to run the network.

The remaining $40 billion faces financing barriers, even where demand exists. Projects that prevent losses instead of generating income may struggle to attract financing. In England’s Wyre catchment, insurers, utilities, and public agencies agreed to pay for flood protection they expected to receive. Those payments created a revenue stream to support private lending.

For businesses, financiers, insurers, and governments, the implication is clear: adaptation is not one market, but a collection of opportunities at different stages of readiness. Some can be pursued today; others require latest technologies, partnerships, or financing models. Understanding the barriers to deployment is the first step toward turning adaptation needs into viable investments—and protecting lives and livelihoods.

#28. Tech Executives Tell Me What They Tell No One Else, and I Think ‘The Audacity’ Got Silicon Valley Mostly Right.

Tech Executives Tell Me What They Tell No One Else, and I Think ‘The Audacity’ Got Silicon Valley Mostly Right.

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read | Sumber: https://www.entrepreneur.com/business-news/tech-executives-tell-me-what-they-tell-no-one-else-and-i-think-the-audacity-got-silicon-valley-mostly-right

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that you're viewing the US website.
  • An executive coach who hears what tech leaders say behind closed doors weighs in on how “The Audacity” gets Silicon Valley right.
  • Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

It has been revealed that you're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

An executive coach who hears what tech leaders say behind closed doors weighs in on how “The Audacity” gets Silicon Valley right.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

Sources indicate that “More than physical pain, I fear humiliation.” That’s the first line of The Audacity, spoken by tech CEO Duncan Park (Billy Magnussen) to his therapist. I’ve coached tech leaders for more than a decade, including people who reported directly to Mark Zuckerberg, Elon Musk and Steve Huffman, and I can’t recall a client ever saying the word “humiliation” to me. They say “insecure” and “imposter syndrome” instead. The show names a real fear in its opening seconds, using a word I rarely hear.

The series aired on AMC this spring and landed on Netflix in August, where it’s finding a second audience.

According to recent reports, most of the reviews came from TV critics, but I watched it as the person executives say these things to. They tell me things they keep from their boards, their teams and their partners.

With that in mind, I wanted to share what the show gets right about the people leading the tech industry and what was stretched to make good TV.

According to recent reports, in episode seven, Duncan indicates the fear of humiliation is behind every little lie. His therapist, Dr. JoAnne Felder (Sarah Goldberg), puts it another way: Everyone spins, even to themselves. That’s the most accurate line in the series.

Executives spin to me, too. It usually sounds like catastrophizing what a boss might say or fixating on the worst-case scenario of an notable meeting or presentation. When I hear it, I ask them to pause and take a breath. Then we get clear on what they value and what they want. Then they pick one small step forward. It’s simple, and that’s why it works.

Sources indicate that the pause does most of the work. Once a leader slows down, the spin falls apart on its own.

According to recent reports, in the first episode, Duncan screams at his housekeeper for failing to catch a tungsten cube he throws to her. One recap called his outbursts one of the funniest elements of the premiere. I call it reality. I’ve coached executives whose CEOs screamed at them and berated people in executive meetings — at companies that have been voted “best place to work.”.

Sources indicate that the show also gets right the fact that founders and boards tolerate this behavior. When it’s the CEO yelling, the people in the room have few options. A senior executive I coached reported directly to a CEO like this. Our work focused on how to manage themselves long enough to get out and find a healthier environment, which they did. Sometimes the only fix is a fresh employer.

Carl Bardolph (Zach Galifianakis) is the billionaire Duncan wants to become. A teenager in the show describes him as worth a bazillion dollars and the saddest man you’ve ever seen. Everyone in the series has money and wants more of something else, whether it’s legacy, power, impact or control.

Recent findings suggest that I hear this constantly. A client of mine had led teams through back-to-back acquisitions and an exit, and he told me it still didn’t feel like enough. I didn’t tell him he had a problem or suggest he look for happiness outside work. He brought the questions to me, and my job was to help him unpack them. He wanted to know:.

Recent findings suggest that he chose his career goal, C-suite roles and added conditions that had never been on the list, such as remote or hybrid work, time with his school-aged children and partner, real work-life balance and room to travel. Eventually, he landed a role on those terms.

Sources indicate that duncan blackmails his therapist. I’ve never been blackmailed by a client, and I’m confident that’s the norm. The jargon also runs heavier than real life. Silicon Valley loves shorthand, but “quant ben” for quantifiable benefits was fresh to me.

Recent findings suggest that the biggest stretch comes from Ethan Stern (Patrick Gilmore), Orson’s biological father, who is back in Baltimore while his son gets shipped off to Palo Alto. He tells Orson the world there is not the real world, but Silicon Valley is the world for a lot of people. Meta alone reports 3.6 billion people using its apps on an average day. Carl also claims that every billionaire eventually decides whether to save the world or control it, and that “most of us go Dr. Evil.” In my experience, most of the leaders I work with are focused on making a positive difference. The bad ones just get more publicity.

Sources indicate that one line made me laugh out loud, and it turned out to be accurate. In the first episode, Anushka Bhattachera-Phister (Meaghan Rath) refers to Xander, the AI her husband Martin (Simon Helberg) is building, as “a digital child.” I’ve heard a tech executive use that exact phrase. The realtor telling Dr. Felder “$2.5 mil is a steal around here” got me too, as did their portrayal of office space costing $175 an hour. That’s why I coach from my home office over Zoom.

It’s lonely at the top, and the show gets that right in every storyline. Each major character is isolated, and none of them says so out loud. Some leaders I work with run from that conversation with themselves. The ones I’ve watched make progress bring it to someone else instead, whether that’s a coach, mentor or therapist, and speak honestly about their feelings.

The Audacity packs stock fraud, blackmail, ayahuasca, a tungsten cube and a wildfire into eight hour-long episodes, and AMC renewed it for a second season before the first one even aired. I’d give it a thumbs up as a composite portrait of working in tech, two thumbs up for entertainment and a thumbs down for anyone hoping to feel better about the industry afterward. Nobody was watching it for that anyway. Remember, you’ve got this!

#29. How Founders Can Reduce Platform Risk Before It Threatens Growth

📅 12 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4 min read (859 words)

How Founders Can Reduce Platform Risk Before It Threatens Growth

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read | Sumber: https://news.crunchbase.com/ai/startup-founders-reduce-platform-risk-filippenko-intch/

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that one day, I woke up to a notice that our app had been removed from Apple’s App Store.
  • It has been revealed that for years, the App Store’s unwritten contract seemed simple.
  • It has been revealed that in 2025, Apple removed 166,899 apps and reported just 423 restorations after appeals.

Sources indicate that one day, I woke up to a notice that our app had been removed from Apple’s App Store. For the next month or so, we racked our brains trying to find out why. We even reached out to our internal contacts, only for them to tell us that helping us could put their jobs at risk. Nothing seemed to work.

It has been revealed that for years, the App Store’s unwritten contract seemed simple. As long as you followed the guidelines, your storefront would remain available. Then a removal notice arrives, and you wonder whether your business can survive.

It has been revealed that in 2025, Apple removed 166,899 apps and reported just 423 restorations after appeals. As we learned, being caught in it feels like watching your business collapse, with no guarantee of recovery.

It’s not all bad news, though. We survived, and this episode taught me that platform dependency is ultimately infrastructure risk. As founders, we prepare for cloud outages and payment failures, but losing access to the platform that brings us customers deserves the same attention. Fortunately, we were prepared, and this is how you can be, too.

Financially, Apple immediately freezes funds from the previous three months and turns off recurring subscriptions. For a subscription-dependent company, this can send its monthly recurring revenue to zero.

It has been revealed that before spending another cent on acquisition, consider what would happen to those customers if your app disappeared tomorrow. Could they still use your product and continue paying you?

If the answer is no, every new customer makes your business more dependent on a platform decision you cannot control.

According to recent reports, cal AI, reportedly generating $100,000 daily, was pulled without warning and later reappeared. But its reinstatement tells you little about how long your business might wait.

In Intch’s case, the explanation was so generic it told us nothing. We had 30 days to appeal, but the process ended with a canned rejection.

In a recent development, your appeal may succeed, but your business must operate while you wait. Preparing in advance lets you keep going, whatever the outcome.

Our experience was grueling, but fortunately, two years earlier we had decoupled from the App Store by building a web version and making it our primary payment channel.

Recent findings suggest that it also let us ship updates 10 times a day while escaping Apple’s predatory commissions. We weren’t the only ones. Pavel Durov, founder of Telegram, has also promoted web access to bypass store restrictions and potential censorship.

The lesson is straightforward. Customers need a working alternative before access disappears. Building one only after removal leaves the business exposed while the team races to replace its storefront.

Recent findings suggest that we initially feared the user experience would suffer, but that concern proved unfounded. After the removal, every key metric fully recovered.

If you share this concern, test it while your app is still available to see whether customers can use and pay for the web version before they must rely on it.

Most founders see the App Store as a distribution channel, but rarely account for how much control it gives Apple over their business.

It has been revealed that before investing more in growth, examine how much revenue depends on continued access and what would survive a removal. Know how long the tech giant could survive an unanswered appeal.

In a recent development, investors should ask those questions too, because a growing subscription base deserves closer scrutiny when a single platform decision can interrupt its revenue. That exposure belongs in funding and valuation discussions.

Monopolies act in their interests, and if your business falls outside their vision, you may have little say in a decision that could destroy it.

You cannot control it, but you can decide whether it has the power to end your firm. By building an alternative while your app is still available, you’ve made the wisest choice.

According to recent reports, yakov Filippenko is a seasoned entrepreneur with more than 10 years of experience in IT and technologies, as well as scaling businesses internationally. As a product manager at Yandex, he led a team that grew the product’s user base from 500,000 to 1.2 million and secured its entry into the international market. Subsequently, he co-founded SailPlay, which he scaled to 45 countries and eventually exited, after it was acquired by Retail Rocket in 2018. In 2021, Filippenko debuted Intch, an AI-powered platform connecting part-time professionals with flexible roles.

#32. Nine Korean startups vie for a spot in Disrupt 2027’s Startup Battlefield 200 competition

Nine Korean startups vie for a spot in Disrupt 2027’s Startup Battlefield 200 competition

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read | Sumber: https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/12/nine-korean-startups-vie-for-a-spot-in-disrupt-2027s-startup-battlefield-200-competition/

💡 Key Takeaways
  • TechCrunch’s yearly Startup Battlefield 200 competition sees hundreds of companies from across the world trying every year to get a chance to pitch in front of VCs and the international tech community at the TechCrunch Disrupt conference.
  • This week, nine early-stage South Korean startups pitched at DETO 2026, a technology conference in Seoul, to earn a spot in next year’s Startup Battlefield 200.
  • Industry observers note that the startups work across the deep tech sector, including healthcare, fintech, energy, semiconductors, and AI.

TechCrunch’s yearly Startup Battlefield 200 competition sees hundreds of companies from across the world trying every year to get a chance to pitch in front of VCs and the international tech community at the TechCrunch Disrupt conference.

This week, nine early-stage South Korean startups pitched at DETO 2026, a technology conference in Seoul, to earn a spot in next year’s Startup Battlefield 200.

Industry observers note that the startups work across the deep tech sector, including healthcare, fintech, energy, semiconductors, and AI. All nine startups are looking to enter the U.S. market as part of the broader international expansion aims.

Recent findings suggest that voinosis, which develops AI to detect changes in brain health through voice analysis, won the competition. The other eight startups are listed below in alphabetical order.

Voinosis is developing an AI tool that analyzes speech patterns such as pitch, pauses, rhythm, and response times to detect changes linked to brain health. Each voice check takes less than five minutes.

The company says its technology has been tested in Greek, Japanese, and English, and its product doesn’t require separate training for each language. In a clinical study involving 146 participants, the startup claims its tech achieved 88% accuracy in screening for potential cognitive issues.

Voinosis targets hospitals, senior living facilities, insurers, and individual consumers. It also prepares to link voice checks with cognitive training, assessments, and treatment provided by healthcare professionals.

The startup was founded by Grace Shin, who spent more than 25 years as an otologic surgeon. The startup is presently raising a Series A round and has already secured a South Korean pharmaceutical company as a strategic investor.

Awesome Lab, based in Seoul, makes ThermoFlux, a heating system that uses water electrolysis and ionization to generate heat. The system can manage heat production for buildings, water supply, and industrial processes. The company says its technology can reduce energy consumption and carbon emissions.

Sources indicate that for its international expansion, Awesome Lab is taking a different approach in each market. In the U.S., it aims to supply core OEM modules and work with boiler, water heater, and HVAC companies on product development.

Sources indicate that crosshub helps travelers and international visitors verify their identities and set up payment methods abroad. Its platform, IDBlock, combines identity verification and payment services using self-sovereign identity (SSI) and zero-knowledge proof.

According to recent reports, the manufacturer says its platform helps users prove their identity across borders without sharing unnecessary personal information. Crosshub is also integrating this technology with payment systems to improve access to financial services for travelers.

Industry observers note that deepFusion AI has developed a 4D radar-based imaging system with additional sensors for autonomous mobility, robotaxi, maritime surveillance, and defense applications. The system combines RF sensors with radar and lidar to detect objects, movement, or distance without a direct line of sight. All sensors are supposedly packed into a single, customizable unit.

EFLOW develops special motors that can produce more torque, or rotational force, while taking up less space for use in robots, drones, satellites, and other mobility applications. The startup also develops actuators that control how robotic joints move.

Otiton Medical makes two medical devices: One specializes in measuring body temperature, while another can capture ear canal images and analyze the eardrum. The company claims its AI was trained on about 55,000 images of eardrums, and the device has received medical certification in South Korea.

In a recent development, riibotics states it can deploy robots into warehouses within a day. Riibotics wants to reduce deployment costs for warehouses by streamlining setup, which includes infrastructure setup, warehouse mapping, system integration through custom middleware, task programming, and safety checks.

Ternell, a semiconductor startup based in Ulsan, is developing a latest type of memory to help AI chips use less power.

Unlike conventional two-state memory, Ternell’s T-SRAM system adds a third state for more efficient data storage. Founded in 2019 by KyungRok Kim, a former Samsung Electronics engineer, Ternell reports that tests with 28-nanometer chips highlighted a 33% to 102% increase in memory capacity per area, and a 55% to 71% reduction in energy needed to access data, compared with conventional SRAM.

Testbank is a Korean edtech startup developing Solve, an app that converts printed study materials, such as workbooks and test-prep books, into interactive digital versions.

Sources indicate that the startup uses AI to identify question and answer spaces in publishers’ PDF files while preserving the original layout. Solve lets you write answers directly on the page and be graded automatically.

Kate Park is a reporter at TechCrunch, with a focus on technology, startups and venture capital in Asia. She previously was a financial journalist at Mergermarket covering M&A, private equity and venture capital.

#33. What I Learned Spending Thousands on Meta Ads to Launch a Newly introduced Product

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6 min read (1215 words)
AI & Tech

What I Learned Spending Thousands on Meta Ads to Launch a Newly introduced Product

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read | Sumber: https://www.entrepreneur.com/building-a-business/what-i-learned-spending-thousands-on-meta-ads-to-launch-a-new-product

💡 Key Takeaways
  • I used to measure ad spend of tens of millions a month with a large team.
  • Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.
  • Recent findings suggest that about a year ago, I was working for a global fintech headquartered in London.

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

I used to measure ad spend of tens of millions a month with a large team. Now I do most of that work on my own with AI, and here is what it can’t do.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

Recent findings suggest that about a year ago, I was working for a global fintech headquartered in London. We had a budget of tens of millions of dollars per month to spend on marketing, so we worked with a fairly large marketing team. As director for growth, I was responsible for all sorts of technical marketing duties, including measurement, signals engineering, analytics and the measurement of performance in general.

We employed a large team of dozens of developers to do this. Now things have completely changed. I can do a lot of the things that I used to do with a team just on my own with AI. I wrote SQL code for years, but I’ve not written any SQL for over a year now. Most of my analyses are not done in dashboards, but via chatbot.

Industry observers note that having spent most of my career advising other people how to grow their business, I put it to work on my own product, RunInk, an app that turns your running routes into posters, and spent about $1,700 on Meta ads in the first month. Sales so far add up to around $200. I understand that there is a testing budget involved in these things. It’s not going to go immediately well. And in fact, it got more profitable once the ads had more to learn from.

Sources indicate that there was a team of dozens of designers making different creatives, and many of them got released and tested and measured. Whereas now I can get Claude to make a ton of different ideas, and Meta’s AI can just test them.

In a recent development, it’s also not just a question of speed. Yes, AI’s creatives are often visually unappealing. But I’m not a designer. I can’t make nice things. I don’t know how to make nice things. But with the prompting, I can get AI to do it. I can focus on the winners and on getting lots of different variants out that I think might be useful.

According to recent reports, signals engineering was generally the martech job, and it was not an easy job — both for large companies like the one I worked for, which had a relative dearth of signals compared to ecommerce, and for small brands starting out. There can be a significant increase in performance by just doing this well.

In a recent development, ad platforms run on machine learning, which requires lots of signals to be able to learn what type of person is interested in your product. Meta notes an ad set needs about 50 optimization events a week to get out of its learning phase. However, if you’re starting out from zero, you have no one interested in your product. This is also the case if you sell few, but high-ticket items. You have relatively few people coming by, but you need to figure out who they are and somehow advertise something to them.

It has been revealed that so what you start doing is breaking down the funnel into smaller steps. Do they land on my website? Do they create an account? In my case, do they connect their Strava account? Do they create an image? Do they export an image? Do they export various images?

Then you try to add some monetary value to all of these steps and break it down from there. And then you can slowly tune and adjust these values so that you stop paying for page views and for signups and eventually start buying purchases.

Recent findings suggest that AI is a powerful tool, but it still makes mistakes. You need to double check AI, ask questions and validate everything. Not necessarily by manually redoing the numbers yourself, but by asking probing questions the way you would ask an intern.

Back when I managed a team, the way I would ensure numbers were right (or at least vaguely right) was by probing them. I’d tell my team: “Hey, that number seems high; are you sure about it?” or “That number seems off; can you double-check?”.

Also, don’t forget that your AI agent often lacks the context you do. If you know that five of the last 10 purchases made on your site were you testing a new feature, tell it!

Recent findings suggest that it is hard to build a product if you have no customers. Once I had the first 100 or so users on the website, I surveyed the people who made posters.

Recent findings suggest that I saw that there was some sort of demand, some happiness with the product itself. But 11 of the 16 who answered remarked the free digital file was enough for them. And the only way I made money was via printed posters!

It has been revealed that this told me that I should offer a digital product. And it instantly became my best seller! Business success is about finding the right price point and the right product, and to do that, you need to talk to your customers.

If you’re starting out with a brand latest product, be aware that it’s going to cost you a lot more than $1,000. To get this to work, you’re most likely going to have to spend more than that.

According to recent reports, that being remarked, it’s a great way to get people to your product. If you want to find out more, I write about measurement and AI on my site.

About a year ago, I was working for a global fintech headquartered in London. We had a budget of tens of millions of dollars per month to spend on marketing, so we worked with a fairly large marketing team. As director for growth, I was responsible for all sorts of technical marketing duties, including measurement, signals engineering, analytics and the measurement of performance in general.

We employed a large team of dozens of developers to do this. Now things have completely changed. I can do a lot of the things that I used to do with a team just on my own with AI. I wrote SQL code for years, but I’ve not written any SQL for over a year now. Most of my analyses are not done in dashboards, but via chatbot.

Having spent most of my career advising other people how to grow their business, I put it to work on my own product, RunInk, an app that turns your running routes into posters, and spent about $1,700 on Meta ads in the first month. Sales so far add up to around $200. I understand that there is a testing budget involved in these things. It’s not going to go immediately well. And in fact, it got more profitable once the ads had more to learn from.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • That WeWork deal could fall apart yet, suggests a latest Bloomberg report that states SoftBank Group will seek approval of its bailout package with the Committee on Foreign Investment in the U.S., which has stymied SoftBank before.
  • Tesla delivered a strong third-quarter earnings report after the bell today, posting a surprise profit and telling shareholders it’s ahead of schedule with a latest factory in Shanghai.
  • A couple of years ago, the cofounder and CEO of a blood-testing tech giant was publicly taken to task for implying in articles and professional profiles that he has a PhD when in reality, he’d left a prestigious graduate group three years after enrolling, without a degree.

That WeWork deal could fall apart yet, suggests a latest Bloomberg report that states SoftBank Group will seek approval of its bailout package with the Committee on Foreign Investment in the U.S., which has stymied SoftBank before. As the report notes: “SoftBank won approval from the panel to buy Sprint Corp. and U.K. chip designer ARM Holdings. However, the committee put conditions on its ownership of Sprint, and restricted its control of alternative-asset manager Fortress Investment Group. More recently, SoftBank was unable to fill two board seats at one of its portfolio companies, Uber Technologies, because it did not have Cfius approval.”.

Tesla delivered a strong third-quarter earnings report after the bell today, posting a surprise profit and telling shareholders it’s ahead of schedule with a latest factory in Shanghai. Shares rose more than 20 percent after hours. CNBC has more here.

A couple of years ago, the cofounder and CEO of a blood-testing tech giant was publicly taken to task for implying in articles and professional profiles that he has a PhD when in reality, he’d left a prestigious graduate group three years after enrolling, without a degree.

The CEO is hardly alone in intentionally or otherwise sowing confusion around his credentials, however. Over the years, we’ve mistakenly believed that a number of founders have obtained specific college degrees based on their LinkedIn bio, only to learn offline that they enrolled for some period of time in a particular program that they didn’t complete.

According to recent reports, it happened most recently with the cofounder of a startup who one would might surmise based on his LinkedIn profile has a master’s degree from Harvard but does not. We also misunderstood the CEO of a robotics tech giant to have a PhD based on her LinkedIn. It was our fault; it mentioned under the credit that she’d left to start a company. But anyone scanning the site might have come to the same wrong conclusion. (We pointed this out to her team, and mention of the PhD was deleted.).

In a higher-profile case, James Damore, the fired Google engineer who authored that infamous memo about the organization’s diversity practices and whose LinkedIn page cited under “Education” a “PhD, Systems Biology,” removed mention of those doctoral studies after Wired confirmed with Harvard that he was enrolled in the program but didn’t complete the doctorate.

According to recent reports, damore tried to defend his own LinkedIn profile, tweeting at the time, “I never told anyone I have a PhD. LinkedIn can’t distinguish between being in the PhD program and having a PhD (I forgot to update it).”.

In a recent development, fabric, a four-year-old, Latest York-based startup that wants to make automated logistics available to retailers of all sizes, has raised $110 million in Series B funding. Corner Ventures led the round, joined by Aleph, CPPIB, Innovation Endeavors, La Maison, Playground Ventures, and Temasek. TechCrunch has more here.

Disperse, a four-year-old, London-based startup whose computer vision-driven construction software aims to identify problems on a site, has raised $15 million in Series A funding led by Northzone. VentureBeat has more here.

Fairmarkit, a two-year-old, Boston-based procurement platform that tries to find the best vendors for its enterprise customers, has raised $11 million in Series A funding led by Insight Partners. Built in Boston has more here.

Lemon Way, a 12-year-old, Paris-based payment processor for marketplaces and crowdfunding platforms, has raised €25 million from Toscafund Asset Management. Tech.eu has more here.

Literati, a three-year-old, Austin, Tex.-based subscription book service for kids, has raised $12 million in funding led by Shasta Ventures. Crunchbase News has more here.

PeerNova, a six-year-old, San Jose, Ca.-based manufacturer that aims to enables financial institutions to perpetually synchronize their data across multiple internal and external systems, has raised $31 million in funding. Super Micro Computer indicates that Megaspeed, the Singapore company at the center of the spy scandal that brought down Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang, has never been one of its customers.

The assertion by Super Micro, whose cofounder was arrested earlier this year on charges of smuggling Nvidia chips to China, comes as observers look for possible connections between two companies whose business dealings with Nvidia are under scrutiny.

It has been revealed that “Megaspeed is not, and has never been, a Supermicro customer,” a spokesperson told Fortune in a statement. The organization also said it “has been responsive to inquiries and has fully cooperated with U.S. and Taiwanese officials, while also voluntarily providing information and engaging with all requests from Singapore authorities to date.”.

Supermicro’s statement came after Singapore’s Ministry of Home Affairs remarked Thursday that the Singapore Police Force and Customs had opened investigations into Megaspeed and Alice Huang, a former top executive there who had an affair with Nvidia’s Jensen Huang, and who some authorities believe was acting as a spy for China.

Industry observers note that singapore authorities said they had asked Supermicro for information and had received only “limited cooperation.” The ministry said the Supermicro cooperation matter was first raised with U.S. authorities on July 7, 2025 and then repeatedly afterward with the Department of Justice and the FBI.

Alice Huang, who isn’t related to ex-Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, drew intense scrutiny after reports that she and the Nvidia co-founder were having an affair, which came out before his resignation on Wednesday. The U.S. Attorney’s Office in Manhattan is reportedly looking into whether entities linked to her helped smuggle Supermicro hardware with Nvidia GPUs into China. Multiple probes have been initiated into export control breaches related to Alice and her businesses, including Megaspeed. Jensen, Nvidia, and Supermicro have not been charged with wrongdoing.

However, Jensen’s downfall has cast a dark cloud over Supermicro at an intensely complicated moment for the hardware and liquid cooling tech company. One of Supermicro’s three co-founders, Charles Liang, is a longtime friend of Jensen’s and the two both hail from Taiwan. They’ve shared the stage at multiple massive Computex tech events in Taiwan, including in 2024 when Jensen was photographed having drinks with Alice. Both cofounded their companies in 1993 and Supermicro’s close relationship with Nvidia has been a boon for customers hoping to be first in line for the latest generations of high-performing chips Nvidia churns out.

Industry observers note that another Supermicro cofounder, Yih-Shyan “Wally” Liaw, was arrested and charged in March along with two others for allegedly working to route about $2.5 billion in servers with Nvidia’s H200 and B200 GPUs into China through a Southeast Asian front firm. Liaw has pleaded not guilty, and his trial has been pushed to March 2027. A co-defendant, Ting-Wei “Willy” Sun, pleaded guilty in October. Supermicro has noted it was a victim of the scheme and conducted an internal investigation finding no evidence current members of senior management were aware of the alleged conspiracy. Supermicro’s stock fell nearly 4% this week.

In August, prosecutors in Keelung, Taiwan indicted nine people over 130 Supermicro servers with Nvidia B300 chips that were allegedly cleared for shipment using forged data-center inspection records. Some 74 of the servers made it to China and customs intercepted the rest. The defendants include two former Supermicro Taiwan employees and a former Nvidia Taiwan employee, who face breach of trust and document forgery charges. In Taiwan, unauthorized AI chip exports to China aren’t at the moment considered a criminal offense, which is why the charges relate to forgery and breach-of-trust charges. Neither Nvidia nor Supermicro was charged.

The manufacturer noted in a statement that it “maintains a robust compliance program and continues to work closely with authorities and industry partners to combat diversion and help protect American innovation.” The company has disclosed a grand jury subpoena and inquiries from the SEC, the Commerce Department’s Bureau of Industry and Security, and foreign authorities.

Industry observers note that the S&P 500 assigns each company a weight based on its float-adjusted market capitalization. Companies with more tradable market value take bigger slices of the index, and smaller companies take thinner ones.

Industry observers note that market capitalization is a firm's share price multiplied by its shares outstanding. The float adjustment trims that share count to the stock available for public trading. Every constituent's weight is a share of one combined total. All the weights together add up to 100%. When one tech giant gains weight, others must lose some.

Former high-flying plant-based meat startups Beyond (now public) and Impossible Foods have seen their valuations wither. Others have shuttered.

According to recent reports, in response, more recent startup investment has shifted away from meat substitutes and toward stuffing more protein into other packaged foods and drinks. It’s a fad that’s obvious on supermarket shelves, where startups and established brands alike relentlessly tout the added protein in their noodles, pancakes, cereals, energy bars, popcorn and so on.

In startup circles, protein-related investment looks tiny in comparison to the billions bet on AI. Deal flow, however, remains fairly robust, with Crunchbase identifying a few dozen protein-focused startups funded in the past year. Moreover, some of these rounds are quite sizable, like a $250 million September Series B for Medici Brands, maker of David Protein snack bars.

To illustrate, we used Crunchbase data to put together sample sets of recently-funded protein-focused companies across several themes. These include packaged foods, drinks, ingredients and processes, and animal feed.

Snacks and packaged foods look like the largest fundraisers among protein startups, securing hundreds of millions in the past year.

For a sense of who’s raising, we put together a list of seven recently funded brands that are finding their way to store shelves.

Recent findings suggest that the bulk of recent funding went to the aforementioned parent of David Protein. That brand, in addition to churning sweet-flavored bars with a protein content to rival cod, has been expanding into ice cream and milkshakes.

Wilde Brands, which makes crackers from chicken breasts, has also proven popular with investors, pulling in $40 million last month. Among early-stage startups, meanwhile, Frozen One has been off to a brisk start, raising over $8 million for a line of high-protein ice creams now selling at Target.

It has been revealed that startups and investors are also catering to people who want their high-protein diet in drinkable form. To illustrate, we put together six recently funded examples below.

Ripple Foods, which makes a vegan milk using pea protein, is the highest historical funding recipient, raising over $300 million in its 12-year-history, even though it hasn’t officially joined the unicorn club.

Clear protein drinks are also increasingly a thing, with multiple startups including protein soda brand Juuz and sports drink purveyor Protein2o.

According to recent reports, quite a few funded startups are focused more on novel, protein-rich ingredients rather than their own branded retail lineup. In many cases, they’re using precision fermentation to deliver.

The Every Co., which makes animal-free egg white proteins through fermentation, is the biggest funding recipient and one of the older names on our list. It’s raised nearly $300 million in the past 10 years, including a $55 million round a year ago.

Early stage is also seeing some action from startups including Edonia, which makes a high-protein cooking ingredient from spirulina,.

A number of funded protein startups are also focusing on pets and livestock — a target audience that’s not quite so overwhelmed by supermarket options.

To illustrate, we aggregated five such companies that raised funding in recent quarters.

According to recent reports, notably, two of them — InnovaFeed and nextProtein — are bug-focused. InnovaFeed has raised over $500 million to raise insects for feeding livestock, pet food and aquaculture. NextProtein is using fly larvae for feedstock.

Others are focused on pets. Meatly, for instance, secured a Series A round this spring to build what it says will be Europe’s largest cultivated meat facility. It plans to partner with pet food brands and sell its own branded lineup once production scales.

If we were to encapsulate a broad trend across most of the protein-related financings it would be that startups aren’t trying to convince people that vegetables are meat. Rather, they’re focused largely on protein as an in-demand macronutrient that can be increasingly concentrated and stuffed into a bewildering variety of flavors and form factors.

That might not all taste as good as their more sugary, high-fat and carb-laden alternatives, but at least they’ve got protein.
