Massive Microsoft outage disrupts businesses, government agencies worldwide

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read | Sumber: https://siliconangle.com/2026/11/13/massive-microsoft-outage-disrupts-businesses-government-agencies-worldwide/

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A glitch in Microsoft Corp.’s network has disrupted the work of businesses and government agencies in more than 70 countries.
  • Industry observers note that the bug, which reared its head on Thursday about 12:35 p.m.
  • It has been revealed that deployments of Exchange Server, a version of the platform that users run on-premises, are not affected.

A glitch in Microsoft Corp.’s network has disrupted the work of businesses and government agencies in more than 70 countries.

Industry observers note that the bug, which reared its head on Thursday about 12:35 p.m. EST, knocked the company’s popular Exchange Online platform offline. Organizations use the cloud service to store employees’ inboxes and calendars. Microsoft has still not fully restored its infrastructure.

It has been revealed that deployments of Exchange Server, a version of the platform that users run on-premises, are not affected. However, the outage did disrupt a number of Microsoft Teams and Microsoft Copilot 365 features that rely on data from users’ Exchange inboxes. Intune, a tool that administrators use to manage employee devices, is also experiencing technical complications.

Sources indicate that the outage has hit numerous companies worldwide. Workhorse Group Inc., an electric vehicle maker, pushed back its earnings call from today to Monday. Shipping giant Maersk and stock exchange operator Euronext notified customers that they’re experiencing communications issues.

According to recent reports, the public sector is also impacted. Several U.S. municipalities reported technical problems, while a number of court cases had to be delayed. In the U.K., the National Pharmacy Association warned that the Exchange Online outage may slow prescription processing. Hospitals, public transportation agencies and schools are affected as well.

The operator of Downdetector, an outage tracking service, received downtime reports from hundreds of thousands of users.

Sources indicate that parts of Microsoft’s infrastructure started recovering early this morning. In an update published at 2:30 a.m., the company stated that it was seeing “positive results” after patching an “upstream authentication/routing configuration” module. About three hours later, Microsoft’s systems in the Asia Pacific region began regaining service access. North America and Europe followed suit shortly there.

Microsoft shared its first explanation of what went wrong around noon today. “The incident was introduced by an matter during an earlier network capacity upgrade that surfaced following a recent network change,” the company explained. “We have addressed the underlying issue and continue to restore service to remaining customers and regions.”.

Microsoft added that the outage wasn’t caused by a cyberattack or artificial intelligence agents.

The firm’s status page indicates that infrastructure restoration work is still ongoing. As a result, some users may have trouble accessing Exchange Online and certain Microsoft products that interact with it. The company is monitoring the backlog of emails that piled up while the service was offline to ensure no data loss occurs.

Microsoft plans to release a detailed technical report about the outage once all its services are fully restored.

Anthropic is seeking to secure up to $88.5 billion in its planned IPO and a concurrent private placement, potentially making it the largest-ever fundraise tied to a public market debut.

On Tuesday, the AI giant submitted an updated S-1 filing for its upcoming public offering, unveiling latest details including a proposed share price range offering size. The offering could set a fully diluted valuation of up to $1.4 trillion for the San Francisco manufacturer.

Anthropic’s expected valuation comes in below earlier projections, with many investors reportedly forecasting something closer to $2 trillion. That said, even at $1.4 trillion, Anthropic would still be going public at the second-highest valuation in history, topped only by SpaceX’s June debut.

Recent findings suggest that for the IPO portion of its fundraise, Anthropic prepares to sell just over 800 million shares 1 at $70 to $78 each. At the high end, that would bring in around $62.5 billion — the largest ever IPO fundraise after SpaceX’s $75 billion offering.

Anthropic also expects to pull in another $26 billion from a private placement slated to close immediately following the IPO. Investors in this include AMD, Broadcom, Google, Micron Technology, Microsoft, Nvidia and TSMC.

Put together, it’s a record-setting capital haul for a company making its market debut, which Anthropic is expected to do later this month on Nasdaq under the ticker symbol ANT.

Anthropic also recently updated its financial disclosures, showing results through September of this year.

For the first nine months of the year, the company had $33.2 billion in revenue, up from $2.5 billion in the same period a year ago. It’s an astounding growth rate, albeit Anthropic is already known for this.

In a recent development, the firm claims it has the fastest enterprise adoption of any technology in history, growing revenue from zero at commercial launch in the first quarter of 2023 to $17 billion for the three months ended Sept. 30, 2026.

As of yet, however, it’s not profitable. Anthropic posted an operating loss of $1.3 billion for the first nine months of the year, down from $5.2 billion a year earlier. Its net loss widened to $104 billion, up from $25.1 billion a year ago.

The total offering is for 825 million shares, of which 23.6 million will be from selling shareholders.↩.

  • In a recent development, despite years of U.S.
  • Kai-Fu Lee, an AI entrepreneur and former president of Google China, remarked in a Fortune Daily interview that U.S.
  • In response to these limits, which American companies don’t face, Chinese AI developers have built open-weight models that Lee estimates are now just six to 12 months behind those created by some of the biggest American AI companies, including OpenAI as well as Anthropic—which is reportedly preparing to go public as early as next week.

In a recent development, despite years of U.S. efforts to gain an edge over China in the AI race by restricting its access to the most advanced chips, one AI pioneer says America’s efforts have instead helped create a newly introduced generation of Chinese AI models that are quickly catching up to their American counterparts.

Kai-Fu Lee, an AI entrepreneur and former president of Google China, remarked in a Fortune Daily interview that U.S. export restrictions on the most powerful American chips have shaped Chinese companies’ strategy of building competitive AI models with fewer resources.

In response to these limits, which American companies don’t face, Chinese AI developers have built open-weight models that Lee estimates are now just six to 12 months behind those created by some of the biggest American AI companies, including OpenAI as well as Anthropic—which is reportedly preparing to go public as early as next week.

Yet when Americans think about China and the motivations of Chinese companies, they’re often getting some key things wrong, Lee said. In an interview with Fortune Daily published this week, he detailed three of the biggest misconceptions about China’s AI industry that he says have taken hold in America.

One of the biggest misconceptions about Chinese companies is that they are more focused on winning the AI race and becoming the first to develop artificial general intelligence (AGI)—widely considered the ultimate goal of AI development—than on building profitable businesses. That assumption is incorrect, Lee said.

“Chinese companies are born to make money. That’s the primary purpose,” Lee mentioned. “It’s not so much to win AGI or win the race.”.

He compared questions about the profitability of the current wave of Chinese AI developers like DeepSeek with those surrounding other Chinese tech companies like Pinduoduo, Meituan, and ByteDance. These tech giants’ business models were also initially questioned before they became some of China’s biggest companies.

It has been revealed that “You may reasonably doubt China’s ability to do a breakthrough, which is valid. [The] U.S. is way ahead on that, but never doubt Chinese ability to find a way to make money,” he said.

A second misconception, Lee noted, is that China’s embrace of open-weight models and open-source technology is part of an organized government effort to compete with America.

Instead, Lee remarked, market competition has driven the shift. He pointed especially to DeepSeek, a Chinese startup that stunned American AI companies in early 2025 by releasing a highly capable AI model by the same name that it claimed was trained using significantly less computing power than its American competitors.

“Chinese companies are venture funded just like the American companies,” Lee said. “They just want to serve their investors.”.

Industry observers note that beijing has played a significant role in shaping the country’s AI industry. Investors with ties to the government participated in more than 140 Chinese AI deals in 2025, Fortune reported earlier this year, citing a Pitchbook analyst note.

Sources indicate that china’s president, Xi Jinping, has also encouraged AI development in China. In 2025, Xi called for the country to develop “an independent, controllable, and collaborative artificial intelligence basic software and hardware system.”.

Lee stated in the interview that American companies have good reasons to spend more, including attracting the world’s best researchers and giving them enough computing power to experiment.

The third misconception, Lee argued, is that U.S. export controls are the main reason Chinese companies have shifted toward models that require less computing power, while American companies pour billions into data centers.

He argued that Chinese companies are naturally more frugal because they have different priorities than their American counterparts.

“The Chinese companies are naturally parsimonious; not just the startups,” he stated, adding that “prudence and survival instinct” are more key to them than the pursuit of AGI.

According to recent reports, that contrasts with the American approach, which emphasizes spending heavily on computing power to attract top researchers and accelerate AI development. Because of their resourcefulness, Chinese companies can develop and operate models for as little as one-tenth the cost of their American competitors, making their products attractive to businesses that don’t want to pay premium prices for AI services.

Despite the growing competitiveness of Chinese AI developers, American companies still produce more top-tier models and higher-impact patents, according to a Stanford University study. OpenAI and Anthropic are also the world’s most valuable AI companies.

Recent findings suggest that openAI was valued at $1.25 trillion in a November funding round and is eyeing a potential IPO in 2027. Anthropic, meanwhile, is preparing to go public as early as next week in what could be one of the largest IPOs in history, seeking a valuation of up to $1.4 trillion.

Still, when DeepSeek indicated it could compete with America’s leading AI developers, it helped boost the hopes of Chinese AI developers. Before DeepSeek, these developers believed their country was years behind the U.S. After DeepSeek showed off its model in 2025, sentiment shifted, he said.

According to recent reports, “It’s a national pride thing, so people say, ‘Okay, we thought we were never going to catch up. Now we have a shot.’ So, it was quite a special moment,” he mentioned.

Nick Huzar co-founded Juicer Energy in 2023 to make electric vehicle charging more widespread and reliable. Now the Seattle-area startup is pursuing a broader goal: helping buildings manage rising electricity demand and costs.

Juicer installs and operates EV charging systems at apartment buildings, hotels and other properties. It is also developing battery systems to store electricity on-site and help manage the power needed for charging and other building uses.

In a recent development, the push comes as data centers and the growing use of electricity for transportation, heating and other needs put more pressure on the grid. Batteries can help balance supply and demand by storing energy when electricity is plentiful and releasing it when demand peaks. In some cases, they can reduce the need for costly grid upgrades or newly introduced power plants built to meet peak demand.

Sources indicate that “We think there’s a massive opportunity there,” Huzar mentioned. He spoke at an event this week hosted by GeekWire and Bank of America at the Bellevue showroom of Ferrari of Seattle.

Other companies are similarly pairing EV charging with battery storage. Fellow Seattle startup Electric Era has deployed battery-backed fast chargers at retailers including Costco and convenience stores. ADS-TEC Energy and XCharge also sell fast-charging systems with integrated batteries.

Recent findings suggest that huzar, OfferUp’s co-founder and former CEO, sees an opportunity to make buildings more self-sufficient by combining hardware and energy-management software. He remarked Juicer has a project scheduled to come online in 2027 with 70 chargers in one building.

His longer-term vision also includes tapping the energy stored in vehicles connected to those buildings.

Recent findings suggest that “Imagine you’re an apartment owner and you have 20 EVs, 40 EVs plugged in,” Huzar noted. “That is a huge amount of power. Like you’re a mini power plant at that point.”.

He described feeding excess electricity back to the grid as a possibility that remains years away. He also predicted that most businesses, apartments and homes would have on-site batteries within the next decade, in part because battery costs continue to fall.

Juicer started with EV charging, Huzar remarked, “but the more we’ve gotten into this, the more we realize that we actually can build an asset for buildings versus relying on the grid.”.

#58. How MLB free agency works: 10 rules from opt-outs to compensation picks

How MLB free agency works: 10 rules from opt-outs to compensation picks

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 23 min read | Sumber: https://qz.com/mlb-free-agency-rules-explained

💡 Key Takeaways
  • MLB free agency runs on service time, qualifying offers, opt-outs and draft pick rules, and these 10 explainers show how each piece shapes where players sign.
  • According to recent reports, free agency in Major League Baseball is rarely a simple auction.
  • Nearly all of those procedures come from the collective bargaining agreement between Major League Baseball and the MLB Players Association.

Free daily briefing on global business news.

MLB free agency runs on service time, qualifying offers, opt-outs and draft pick rules, and these 10 explainers show how each piece shapes where players sign.

According to recent reports, free agency in Major League Baseball is rarely a simple auction. Before a player signs with the highest bidder, a set of calendars, salary formulas and draft penalties comes into play. Those rules decide when he can talk to other clubs and what his signing will cost. They can change what a player is paid and which teams bid on him. They also help explain why one star signs in November while another is still unsigned when spring training camps open in February.

Nearly all of those procedures come from the collective bargaining agreement between Major League Baseball and the MLB Players Association. The current agreement was reached in March 2022, ending a 99-day lockout. It is scheduled to expire on Dec. 1, 2026. That date matters for anyone reading about the rules. The next round of bargaining could rewrite parts of the system described here.

The system follows a clear sequence. A player first has to earn enough service time to qualify. His club then gets a short head start to negotiate with him. After that, league rules and contract terms shape the bidding. A qualifying offer can attach a draft-pick cost to a player. A non-tender can push a younger player onto the market early. The competitive balance tax can lead a payroll-conscious club to walk away. An opt-out clause can return a star to the market before his contract was due to end.

This slideshow covers 10 of those mechanisms. It is a selection of key pieces, not a complete catalog of every provision in the agreement. Each slide explains one rule on its own terms, from the six-year service-time threshold to the compensation picks a club collects when a top player leaves. The final slide covers the posting system, which lets Japanese clubs make players available to major league teams before they reach free agency at home.

It has been revealed that taken together, the slides offer a working guide to MLB free agency rules for fans who follow the offseason closely and for readers who are newly introduced to it. Terms such as qualifying offer, non-tender, club option and competitive balance tax appear in transaction reports every winter. Each has a specific meaning. Each can also change where a player ends up and how much he earns.

It has been revealed that A major league player becomes eligible for free agency once he has six full years of service time and his contract has expired. One year of service equals 172 days on the active roster or the injured list.

Sources indicate that the regular season lasts longer than 172 days. A player can therefore earn a full year of service without spending every day in the majors. He cannot bank more than one year of service in a single season, however long the schedule runs.

In a recent development, clubs and agents write service time as years and days. A player listed at 5.171 has five years and 171 days. One more day would give him six years. Without it, he stays under his club's control for another season.

Industry observers note that the path to six years has three stages. Early in his career, a player's salary is set by his club at or near the league minimum. He then becomes eligible for salary arbitration, which covers the seasons before he reaches six years. Free agency comes last, when all 30 clubs can bid for him.

Industry observers note that the six-year standard grew out of a long fight over the reserve clause. That clause once bound a player to his club from one year to the next. After the 1969 season, outfielder Curt Flood refused a trade from the St. Louis Cardinals to the Philadelphia Phillies. He sued to challenge the clause. The U.S. Supreme Court ruled against him in 1972 in Flood v. Kuhn.

The clause gave way through arbitration rather than the courts. In December 1975, arbitrator Peter Seitz ruled that pitchers Andy Messersmith and Dave McNally were free to negotiate with other clubs. Owners and the players union then wrote free agency into their 1976 labor agreement.

Service time also shapes when clubs promote their best prospects. Keeping a top young player in the minors for the first weeks of a season can delay his free agency by a full year. The 2022 collective bargaining agreement addressed that practice in part with the Prospect Promotion Incentive. Under it, a club can earn an extra draft pick when an eligible top prospect accrues a full year of rookie service. The player must then win Rookie of the Year or finish in the top three of MVP or Cy Young voting before he reaches arbitration.

For five days after the World Series ends, a team holds exclusive negotiating rights with its own free agents. Once that window closes, all 30 clubs can make offers. The open market then runs through the Winter Meetings in December and often well beyond them.

Recent findings suggest that inside the window, a player can re-sign with his current club before anyone else bids. His club must also decide by the end of those five days whether to extend him a qualifying offer. Rival clubs may not discuss contract terms with him during this stretch.

According to recent reports, MLB's anti-tampering rules bar a team from negotiating with another club's player before the market opens. The league can discipline clubs that break those rules.

After the window closes, agents collect offers and clubs compare their options. A reported agreement is not final until the player passes a physical exam and the club introduces the deal.

Sources indicate that shortstop Carlos Correa's winter of 2022-23 indicates how much rides on that last step. In December 2022, he agreed to a 13-year, $350 million deal with the San Francisco Giants. The Giants raised concerns during his medical review, which focused on a lower right leg injury dating to 2014. The deal fell apart. He then agreed to a 12-year, $315 million deal with the Latest York Mets. That agreement also stalled over the medical review. In January 2023, he signed a six-year, $200 million contract with the Minnesota Twins.

It has been revealed that the offseason calendar has other fixed dates. In November, clubs set their 40-man rosters. That roster decides which minor leaguers are protected from the Rule 5 draft. Clubs also face a November deadline to tender contracts to players still under team control. Players who are not tendered contracts become free agents.

In a recent development, the Rule 5 draft takes place at the Winter Meetings. Clubs also use those meetings for much of their face-to-face business with agents.

The market does not shut down after December. Manny Machado agreed to a 10-year, $300 million deal with the San Diego Padres in February 2019. Bryce Harper's 13-year, $330 million agreement with the Philadelphia Phillies came at the end of that same month. A player's timing tends to reflect what clubs want to spend, what rival bidders can offer and whether a draft-pick penalty is attached to his name.

The rules set the order of events, but they set no signing deadline. A free agent can stay unsigned past Opening Day while he waits for a better offer.

A qualifying offer is a one-year contract that a club can extend to its own departing free agent. The salary equals the average of the 125 highest player salaries in the majors. It was $20.325 million for the 2023 offseason and $21.05 million for both the 2024 and 2025 offseasons.

The figure is recalculated every year because it follows the top of the salary market. Every player who receives an offer that winter is offered the same amount. A club cannot adjust it for age, position or performance. The same salary can sit well above one player's market value and well below another's.

The timing is fixed. A club must extend the offer within five days after the World Series ends. The player then has 10 days to accept or reject it. If he accepts, he returns for one season at that salary. If he rejects it, he enters the open market with draft compensation attached to his name.

Sources indicate that eligibility has limits. The player must have spent the entire season with the club that makes the offer. A player traded at the deadline therefore cannot receive one from his new team. A player can also receive a qualifying offer only once in his career. Any later trip through free agency comes without the tag.

The system dates to the 2012 collective bargaining agreement. It replaced the older Type A and Type B rankings, which used statistical formulas to sort free agents and set compensation. Under the current rule, the club chooses which players to tag.

Sources indicate that clubs weigh two risks. If the player accepts, the club owes a large one-year salary. That commitment can strain a tight payroll. If the club does not make the offer, it gives up any claim to compensation when the player leaves. Teams with room to spend often tag players they expect to depart. Teams with thin budgets tend to hold back when an acceptance looks plausible.

Players face the reverse calculation. Accepting guarantees a high salary for one season. It also returns him to free agency the next winter, when no tag is possible. Rejecting opens the door to multiyear offers. It also adds a draft-pick cost that any signing club must absorb.

Most players who receive the offer decline it. No player accepted until November 2015, when Matt Wieters, Colby Rasmus and Brett Anderson each took that winter's $15.8 million offer. Players who accept have tended to be those facing questions about their age, injury history or demand on the open market.

It has been revealed that A club that loses a free agent after making him a qualifying offer receives an extra pick in the next amateur draft if he signs with another team. The new club pays nothing to the old one directly. The reward comes only as a draft selection.

Recent findings suggest that compensation applies only when the player rejects that offer, the one-year contract his club can extend after the season. Two outcomes produce no pick at all. If the player re-signs with his former club, nothing is owed. If he accepts the offer, he stays under contract, and again there is no compensation.

In a recent development, two factors decide where the extra pick lands. One is the size of the player's new contract. The other is the financial status of the club that lost him. The $50 million dividing line arrived with the 2016 collective bargaining agreement, and it remained in place under the 2022 agreement.

Under that framework, a club that receives revenue sharing gets a pick right after the first round if the departing player signs for $50 million or more. If he signs for less, its pick comes after Competitive Balance Round B. A club that paid the competitive balance tax in the previous season receives a pick only after the fourth round. Clubs in neither group receive a pick after Competitive Balance Round B.

It has been revealed that the placement matters because of how the draft pays out. The draft now runs 20 rounds. Every selection in the first 10 rounds carries an assigned slot value. Those values add up to a club's bonus pool, the total it can spend to sign its picks. An earlier pick means a larger slot value, a bigger pool and an earlier choice among the available prospects.

The 2022 agreement added a lottery that sets the first six selections among clubs that missed the playoffs. Compensation picks sit outside that lottery. They are slotted into fixed positions after the rounds described above.

It has been revealed that the system has changed shape before. When the qualifying offer began under the 2012 agreement, compensation picks were placed after the first round, with no payroll-based tiers. The tiered structure that followed ties a club's reward partly to its finances. Revenue-sharing recipients receive the most valuable placements. Tax-paying clubs receive the least valuable ones.

The compensation pick is a newly created selection. It is not taken from the team that signs the player. That club faces its own separate penalty. The two sides of the transaction run on different rules.

It has been revealed that compensation picks also cannot be traded. Only Competitive Balance Round picks can change hands in MLB. A club that earns compensation keeps the pick and makes the selection itself.

Recent findings suggest that A club that signs a free agent who turned down a qualifying offer gives up draft picks and, in most cases, international bonus pool money. The size of that cost depends on the signing club's payroll status. Clubs that pay the competitive balance tax lose the most.

The tiered penalty dates to the 2016 collective bargaining agreement, which took effect for the 2016-17 offseason. The 2022 agreement largely kept it in place. A club that receives revenue sharing forfeits its third-highest pick in the next draft. A club that neither receives revenue sharing nor pays the tax forfeits its second-highest pick. It also loses $500,000 of international bonus pool money. A club that paid the tax in the prior season forfeits its second- and fifth-highest picks, along with $1 million of pool money.

It has been revealed that the earlier rules worked differently. Under the 2012 agreement, which governed the 2012-13 through 2015-16 offseasons, a club that signed a tagged free agent generally lost its first-round pick. If that pick fell in the top 10, the club lost its second-round pick instead. That approach put a club's highest available selection at stake, regardless of its payroll.

The tiered system did not remove friction from the market. A club may value a tagged player less once it counts the lost selection. Pitcher Dallas Keuchel and closer Craig Kimbrel both rejected qualifying offers after the 2018 season. Neither signed during the winter or spring. Both agreed to deals on June 7, 2019, after that year's draft had begun. By then, a signing club no longer had to surrender picks for them. Keuchel joined the Atlanta Braves, and Kimbrel joined the Chicago Cubs.

The international bonus pool is the second half of the cost. Each club receives a pool of money for signing amateur players who are not subject to the draft. Those players come from outside the U.S., Canada and Puerto Rico. Losing part of that pool narrows a club's options in the next international signing period.

According to recent reports, clubs can offset the loss only in limited ways. Most draft picks cannot be traded under MLB rules. Picks in the Competitive Balance Rounds are the exception. International bonus pool space can also change hands in trades. A club that forfeited pool money can acquire more from another team to restore its spending room.

Sources indicate that an opt-out clause lets a player walk away from the remaining years of his contract after a set season and return to free agency. The player alone makes the choice, typically shortly after the World Series ends.

Each clause is negotiated deal by deal. Some large contracts include one, and others do not. A player who declines to use it keeps playing under the original terms.

For a player, the clause offers a second shot at the market. He may outperform his salary, or prices around the league may climb after he signs. In either case he can leave guaranteed money behind in search of a larger deal. If he gets hurt or struggles, he stays and collects what he was promised.

That imbalance makes the clause a cost for the club. The team carries the risk of a declining player. It also risks losing one who plays well. A club may agree to the clause in exchange for a lower total commitment or other concessions in the deal.

Carlos Correa's contract with the Minnesota Twins demonstrates the clause at work in a short deal. In March 2022 he signed for three years and $105.3 million, with opt-outs after the first and second seasons. He exercised the first one after the 2022 season and returned to the market.

Sources indicate that alex Rodriguez used one on a much larger contract. His 10-year, $252 million deal, first signed with the Texas Rangers, allowed him to opt out after the 2007 season. He did, and then re-signed with the New York Yankees for 10 years and $275 million.

A player who opts out enters free agency on the same footing as other players. If he meets the eligibility conditions, his former club can extend a qualifying offer and attach draft compensation to his signing.

Industry observers note that clubs can act before the deadline arrives. A team can offer extra years or more money to persuade a player to give up the clause. It can also proposal its payroll around his likely departure.

Industry observers note that the clause changes how a contract's length should be read. A five-year deal with an opt-out after the third season may work like a three-year deal if the player performs well. Contracts and transaction reports sometimes describe a similar right as a player option, and the two labels overlap in practice. The key details are who holds the decision and which years it covers.

In a recent development, an option is an extra contract year that one side, or both, can choose to keep or decline. The player holds a player option, the team holds a club option, and a mutual option requires agreement from both. Club and mutual options usually carry a buyout that is paid if the year is declined.

These decisions come shortly after the World Series, in the same early-offseason stretch when clubs handle the rest of their roster business. A declined option, from either side, sends the player into the market without a contract.

It has been revealed that A player option puts the choice in the player's hands. If he believes he can earn more on the open market, he declines it and becomes a free agent. If he would rather keep the guaranteed salary, he exercises it and stays. A player coming off an injury or a weak season has a clear financial reason to keep the money.

A club option reverses that control. The team can pick up the year at the stated salary, or it can decline the year and pay the buyout. Clubs often decline when the salary is higher than the value they expect from the player. Picking up the option does not commit the team to keeping him. Clubs sometimes exercise an option and then trade the player. Club options also appear often in early-career extensions. There, they give a team control over what would have been a player's first free agent seasons.

In a recent development, A mutual option requires both sides to want the same thing at the same time. A player who has performed well tends to prefer the market. A club whose player has struggled tends to prefer the buyout. As a result, these options are rarely exercised, and the buyout often becomes the payment that matters.

The buyout is a fixed sum written into the contract. It counts as guaranteed money, so a club that declines an option still pays something. It also counts toward the contract's guaranteed value.

Sources indicate that vesting options add a performance trigger. The extra year becomes guaranteed automatically if the player reaches a target in the prior season, such as a set number of innings pitched or plate appearances. That structure shields a club from paying for an injured player's final year while still paying a healthy one.

Options also affect how headline figures read. A deal reported as seven years may include a club option on the final season, which means only six are guaranteed. The contract terms show how many years a team actually owes.

The competitive balance tax charges clubs whose payrolls pass a set threshold. Under the 2022 collective bargaining agreement, that threshold was $230 million for 2022 and $241 million for 2025. Clubs pay tax on every dollar above it.

The rate climbs with repetition. A club over the threshold for the first time pays 20 percent on the excess. A second consecutive year raises the rate to 30 percent. A third or later year raises it to 50 percent. Clubs that exceed the threshold by wider margins also pay surcharges on top of those base rates.

According to recent reports, the higher rates do not last forever. A club that finishes a season under the threshold returns to the first-time rate the next time it goes over. The Newly introduced York Yankees stayed under the 2018 threshold, which reset their rate after years as a repeat payer.

Recent findings suggest that the tax payroll is built from average annual value, not the cash a player receives in a given season. A club takes the total guaranteed money in a contract, including any signing bonus, and divides it by the number of years. That figure counts against the threshold in every season of the deal. A front office can calculate a signing's tax effect before it agrees to terms.

Industry observers note that deferred money changes that calculation. In December 2023, Shohei Ohtani agreed to a 10-year, $700 million contract with the Los Angeles Dodgers. He is scheduled to receive $2 million a year during the contract. The remaining $680 million is deferred and paid from 2034 through 2043. Deferred dollars are discounted to present value for tax purposes. The deal counts about $46 million a year against the Dodgers' tax payroll.

The penalties reach beyond cash. A club whose payroll sits $40 million or more above the first threshold has its highest draft pick moved back 10 places in the next amateur draft. If that pick falls among the first six selections, the club's second-highest pick moves back instead.

The threshold also shapes the market below the stars. A club just under it may pass on a mid-tier free agent whose salary would push its payroll over. A club with room beneath the line can absorb the same contract without a tax bill.

Salary arbitration sets pay for players with three to six years of major league service time. A non-tender sends a player to free agency before he reaches the six-year mark. Both processes shape which players are available each winter.

According to recent reports, A player in the arbitration window cannot sign with any club he chooses. His team still controls his rights. He can, however, ask a neutral panel to set his salary when he and the club disagree.

In a recent development, the format is known as final-offer arbitration. The player and the club each submit one salary figure, typically in January. If they do not settle, a panel of three arbitrators chooses one of the two numbers at a hearing. The panel cannot split the difference or pick a figure in between.

It has been revealed that that all-or-nothing design raises the cost of an unrealistic filing. A club that files too low risks losing the hearing outright. A player who files too high faces the same risk. Most cases settle before anyone enters a hearing room. Hearings that do go forward are held in February. The panel weighs factors such as the player's performance and the salaries of comparable players.

Some players reach arbitration a year early under a rule known as Super Two. The group includes players with at least two years of service but fewer than three. To qualify, a player must rank in the top 22 percent of that group in service time. He must also have accrued at least 86 days of service in the previous season. A Super Two player gets four arbitration years instead of three. His salary begins to climb a year sooner as a result.

Industry observers note that the tender deadline in November is where arbitration and free agency meet. By that date, a club must offer a contract to every arbitration-eligible or otherwise reserved player it wants to keep. A player who does not receive one is non-tendered. He becomes a free agent immediately, with no qualifying offer or draft compensation attached.

Clubs non-tender players for practical reasons. A projected arbitration salary may exceed what the club thinks the player is worth. A player may be recovering from an injury. A club may need to clear a spot on its 40-man roster. A non-tendered player can sign with any team, including the one that let him go.

According to recent reports, the non-tender list adds a group of established major leaguers to the market weeks before the Winter Meetings. Unlike veterans who reached six years of service, many of these players are still in their arbitration years when they hit the open market.

Recent findings suggest that A separate group arrives through minor league free agency. These players have spent a set number of seasons in the minors without being added to a 40-man roster. Most sign minor league contracts with newly introduced organizations. Some of those deals include invitations to major league spring training.

Recent findings suggest that the posting system lets a Nippon Professional Baseball club make one of its players available to MLB teams before he reaches international free agency. If a major league team signs him, that team pays a release fee to his Japanese club.

The decision to post belongs to the NPB club, not the player. Once a player is posted, he has a 45-day window to negotiate with major league teams. Every MLB club can make an offer. If no deal is reached before the window closes, he returns to his Japanese team for the coming season.

The release fee is tied to the size of the contract and rises on a sliding scale. It equals 20 percent of the first $25 million, 17.5 percent of the next $25 million and 15 percent of any amount above $50 million. The signing team pays the fee on top of the contract. It does not come out of the player's salary.

Posting offers an earlier route than waiting out a career in Japan. NPB players can become international free agents on their own after a set number of years of service with their clubs. A Japanese club that expects to lose a star may post him a year or two early. That way it collects a fee instead of watching him leave without one.

In a recent development, pitcher Yoshinobu Yamamoto took this route. The Orix Buffaloes posted him, and he agreed to a 12-year, $325 million contract with the Los Angeles Dodgers in December 2023. The fee went to Orix and was not part of the contract total.

Age and experience change the rules. A foreign professional must be at least 25 and have six seasons in a recognized foreign league to sign a standard free agent deal. A younger or less experienced player counts as an international amateur. His signing bonus is limited by each club's international bonus pool.

Industry observers note that the Hokkaido Nippon-Ham Fighters posted Shohei Ohtani in 2017. He was younger than 25, so he came to the majors under those amateur limits when he signed with the Los Angeles Angels. He then completed six years of major league service. After the 2023 season, he entered free agency as an established player with no bonus pool restrictions.

#59. PSI is trying to make a business out of AI-driven scientific discovery

📅 10 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5 min read (1020 words)
AI & Tech

PSI is trying to make a business out of AI-driven scientific discovery

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read | Sumber: https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/10/psi-is-trying-to-make-a-business-out-of-ai-driven-scientific-discovery/

💡 Key Takeaways
  • David Turturean, a recent MIT graduate and a member of the technical staff at the startup lab Physical Superintelligence (PSI), used early access to Anthropic’s Fable 5.2 model to solve an 18-year-old problem about quantum computing.
  • “I’m totally accepting the idea that this might be the last paper I ever put out,” Turturean, who deferred plans to pursue a master’s at MIT’s prestigious computer science and AI lab to join PSI, told TechCrunch.
  • The problem in question, the Aaronson-Ambainis conjecture, concerns the ability of quantum computers to solve problems faster than classical ones.

David Turturean, a recent MIT graduate and a member of the technical staff at the startup lab Physical Superintelligence (PSI), used early access to Anthropic’s Fable 5.2 model to solve an 18-year-old problem about quantum computing.

“I’m totally accepting the idea that this might be the last paper I ever put out,” Turturean, who deferred plans to pursue a master’s at MIT’s prestigious computer science and AI lab to join PSI, told TechCrunch. “In a few months, like, why would you even put out a paper?”.

The problem in question, the Aaronson-Ambainis conjecture, concerns the ability of quantum computers to solve problems faster than classical ones. Scott Aaronson, one of the two researchers who posed the problem, writes that he doesn’t quite understand the proof but that he believes it’s correct because it was autoformalized in Lean, a coding language for math, and explained by a team of top researchers with whom PSI shared the solution.

The solution appears to close the door on one avenue quantum computers could follow to solve certain difficult problems at high speed, but not all of them. “It’s a negative result that allows people to know, okay, we’re no longer looking there,” Turturean remarked.

More broadly, it reflects the upheaval in the scientific world caused by AI problem-solving.

Sources indicate that “A proof of full [Aaronson-Ambainis conjecture] was one of the last remaining open problems in quantum query complexity that everyone seemed to agree was centrally key,” Aaronson, who described himself feeling satisfied, awestruck, disappointed, and fatigued by the news, wrote. “I was surprised, honestly, to see it missing from OpenAI’s Mathocalypse dump a few weeks ago. Surely they tried it, so was it really so much harder than all the problems that were solved?”.

That’s a point in favor of PSI’s model, which is to solve scientific problems with specialized model harnesses and scaffolding.

In a recent development, “An effective kind of research system should have lots of things related to harnesses, lots related to tools, memory systems, simulation infrastructure,” PSI CEO Matt Pines told TechCrunch. “You want to be able to really go after a problem at breadth and depth, and be able to consider a wide range of potential alternatives.”.

For now, the tech giant’s revenue comes from using its tools to optimize data centers, simulating the variables of heat, power, water, sound — “where the performance of that site as well as its impact on the community are a direct function of its physics.” The long play, however, is converting theoretical physics breakthroughs into actual technologies.

Sources indicate that “Six to nine months ago, when I was talking to investors, like I had to sort of stretch to validate that conditional, right? Like, ‘no, no, no, trust me, pretty soon, theoretical physics is going to be mostly the domain of machines,’” Pines stated. “And it’s not there yet, but it’s on its way.”.

Industry observers note that still, while AI has claimed important solutions in fields like mathematics and computer science where it’s possible to express them in validated code, doing so in less abstracted disciplines like the life sciences or physics has proven more difficult. Last week, the startup Discovered Materials released a $1 million grand challenge for researchers using AI to understand problems like superconductivity and heat dissipation.

Recent findings suggest that “At the end of the day, physics is different than math because it’s the real world … nature gets a vote in your models of reality,” Pines said. He said the startup is focused on understanding how to take computational results and validate them with experiments in the most efficient way possible.

Industry observers note that “If it’s a true fact of nature, that’s a trick that you can exploit,” Pines said. “You could build a device out of it, right? The AI suggests an idea; it allows you to do something in the world you weren’t able to do before … and so each of those are kind of loops that PSI is building.”.

As “neolabs for science” become a pathway for potentially groundbreaking science, the participants are still figuring out what the standards are for this fresh world. Because PSI had to hold its result until Anthropic’s model was nearly ready for release, they were able to share it with relevant researchers to better understand it.

Industry observers note that “As an academic, we wanted to play our role in doing things the right way,” Jim Halverson, a professor at Northeastern University who advises PSI, mentioned. He’ll be attending a summit at MIT next week where leading physicists will try to hash out a response to the new pace of science. “Best practices are still emerging … We figured that transparency is a good way to go, and contacting experts is a good way to go.”.

In a recent development, “We had some time to sit on it … and it was the first time that I actually took one of my AI-elicited solutions on print, and I read through it, and I was like, okay, how can I make this … be presented more naturally for a human?” Turturean, who noted the academic community will expect him to be able to explain the result, told TechCrunch. “And I think it also made me realize, oh my God, the weight of what AI can do.”.

#60. Breaking: 15 Years Ago, a Family Celebration Helped Two Sisters Notice a Gap in the Beauty Industry. Here’s How the Moment Sparked a 7-Figure Business.

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 10 min read (1958 words)
General

Breaking: 15 Years Ago, a Family Celebration Helped Two Sisters Notice a Gap in the Beauty Industry. Here’s How the Moment Sparked a 7-Figure Business.

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read | Sumber: https://www.entrepreneur.com/buying-a-franchise/two-sisters-discovered-a-gap-in-the-beauty-industry-leading-to-a-7-figure-beauty-franchise

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Blushington co-CEOs Stephi and Nicki Cohen reveal how they turned a standalone store into a growing franchise.
  • Sources indicate that fifteen years ago, Stephi Cohen and Nicki Maron encountered a common problem.
  • “We started to think, well, you can go to Drybar and get your hair done,” Cohen says in a upcoming interview with Entrepreneur.

Blushington co-CEOs Stephi and Nicki Cohen reveal how they turned a standalone store into a growing franchise.

Sources indicate that fifteen years ago, Stephi Cohen and Nicki Maron encountered a common problem. The two sisters were getting ready for a special event, their younger sister’s bat mitzvah, and their family had all come over. Their house was packed, and they couldn’t afford to have a makeup artist and hair stylist cater to everyone.

“We started to think, well, you can go to Drybar and get your hair done,” Cohen says in a upcoming interview with Entrepreneur. “But where can we go to get our makeup done?”.

That’s where their “aha” moment happened. They thought that there should be a makeup place similar to Drybar but expanded, where customers could go to get their hair, makeup and skincare done, without having to pay the high price of a professional makeup artist coming to their homes.

According to recent reports, cohen called the business Blushington. She was just 21 years old at the time. Maron, her older sister, was 23 years old at the time and helped behind the scenes while pursuing a television career. She eventually joined the business full-time.

Today, the sisters are co-CEOs of Blushington, a company they report has a seven-figure run rate. Getting there meant rebuilding around a franchise model after temporarily closing their doors due to the pandemic.

This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity and concision.

Stephi, what were you doing before you started Blushington?

According to recent reports, stephi Cohen: I went to the University of Arizona and studied a combination of communications and retail. I studied abroad in London and graduated early because I was ready to start my career. I always loved beauty and fashion — I have three sisters, and I was the one who was especially interested in that world. So, I worked in retail, but when I graduated, I wasn’t sure exactly what I wanted to do. I knew I wanted to be my own boss.

According to recent reports, nicki Maron: I was working in television marketing as Bill Lawrence’s assistant on Cougar Town. Working for him taught me about the power of grassroots marketing. While Stephi was developing the idea, I was helping her behind the scenes. Eventually, I realized I was probably spending more time working with her than working for Bill, and that wasn’t right. I needed to make the jump.

Also, I was thinking about how we could introduce the business to people who regularly needed their makeup done, including actresses like Courteney Cox. I was entrepreneurial, and I saw the same need Stephi saw: People didn’t have access to quality makeup applications at an affordable price.

What did you want customers to feel when they walked in?

Maron: We watched Pretty Woman as kids, and that scene where she’s treated badly in the store stayed with us. We wanted Blushington to be the opposite of that. There wasn’t a place where different generations of women could get their makeup done and feel that the artists were really listening to them. That was a significant part of what we wanted to create.

According to recent reports, cohen: Nicki was there from the beginning, even when she had another job. She helped with everything. Having someone I trusted so much made a huge difference.

Where did the name Blushington come from?

According to recent reports, cohen: I had just come back from studying abroad in London. I liked names like Lexington and Kensington, but other names I considered were already trademarked. I wanted something that felt international, even though it was really two girls in Los Angeles. We combined “blush” with that kind of ending and came up with Blushington. Nobody had the name, so we could trademark it. Almost everybody in the family disliked it at first.

Industry observers note that maron: Myself included. I didn’t understand it. I give Stephi a lot of credit for trusting her instincts. If it had been up to me, we probably wouldn’t have gone with Blushington, and that would have been a mistake.

How did you find out whether other people shared your frustration?

Maron: We listened to friends and family. It wasn’t just us. It was our cousins, aunts, grandmothers and friends coming into town. There wasn’t a place that put service first in the way we wanted. The stores were modeled after our mom’s vanity. We wanted them to feel like a home away from home. We say that walking into Blushington should feel like a warm hug.

It has been revealed that stephi also believed makeup didn’t have to be reserved for weddings, prom or other special occasions. We debuted services like Eyes Only for people who didn’t want a full face of makeup but still wanted to look and feel good.

What were the first concrete steps you took to get the business started?

Cohen: First, I asked people what they thought of the concept and tried to get their buy-in. Then I worked on a business plan. After that, we started looking for a location. I was driving down Sunset, near Drybar, and saw a “For Lease” sign. I thought, “This is a sign — I have to call.”.

Sources indicate that the space was a little bigger than we originally wanted, but it worked out well. From there, we needed architects and had to figure out the buildout. You learn as you go, and you surround yourself with people who have more experience than you do. For me, creating the space was the most exciting part. Then came finding the brands and sticking to our approach to product selection.

Cohen: We weren’t going to buy an entire product line just to carry a brand, and we still don’t. At the time, bigger brands often required you to meet a minimum or bring in the full line. We pushed back. We wanted to choose the products that made sense for our artists and customers.

Cohen: We brought together a board and a few investors who helped fund the buildout and the start of the business.

It has been revealed that the pitch was that nobody was doing what we wanted to do. Investors could see the demand for blowout bars, and we were showing them a similar opportunity for makeup applications. Our product selection, artistry, pricing and overall model helped make the case.

Maron: You call everyone you know. You say, “This is what I’m doing. I need to find the right people to help me, and let’s do it together.”.

It has been revealed that cohen: We talked to friends and family and kept getting the word out. Eventually, publicity helped bring people to us, rather than us always having to look for them. But in the beginning, we pounded the pavement.

How did you get your first paying customers?

Cohen: When we opened in 2011, Drybar was right next door. We had a great relationship, and people getting their hair done would come to us afterward for makeup. That helped introduce the business. We still believe in getting out into the community. Sometimes that means literally standing on the street and handing out cards. Nicki will do that herself.

According to recent reports, location matters, too. We want to be near complementary businesses — fitness, wellness and other places our customers already visit. Someone might finish a workout and come to us for a blowout.

Who did you imagine your typical customer would be?

According to recent reports, maron: The women who were in the room for our sister’s bat mitzvah. Someone like me who didn’t know much about makeup, someone like Stephi, who knew a lot, our mom and our grandmother.

I was a college soccer player. I didn’t wear makeup. Stephi would do my makeup, and our younger sister would do our hair.

That customer hasn’t really changed. She’s multigenerational. A mom comes in, and then her daughter comes in.

Cohen: We wanted to change the idea that getting your makeup done was only for a special occasion.

In a recent development, I had very bad acne in high school, and I understood what makeup could do for my confidence. I wanted to bring that experience to our customers.

It could be for a date, or it could simply be because you want to feel good about yourself. Keeping services affordable makes it easier for customers to come in more often, rather than only for a major event.

Sources indicate that maron: That remains part of our approach. You can get hair and makeup done under one roof for less than $200.

Sources indicate that maron: We signed a flagship space in Newly introduced York City on March 11. On March 13, we closed our doors. It was one of the worst days of our lives. We had spent years building this family business, putting our hearts into it. We had to close all our locations and let our team go. Then we had to ask ourselves whether we should keep going at all.

Industry observers note that cohen: Not being able to provide income for our employees was one of the hardest parts. Before we could even figure out what we were going to do, we were worrying about them. We had to decide: Do we close the business, or can we come out of this stronger? Ultimately, we felt the franchise model was the best model for us.

Maron: During the pandemic, we created an online Blushington Academy. We certified artists across more than 40 states, and we have more than 250 artists in our portal. We wanted to support artists when people weren’t getting their hair and makeup done and we also saw more people wanting to become their own bosses. Franchising made sense because Stephi and I live in Los Angeles. Someone who lives in another city knows that community better than we do.

Maron: We have one corporate location in Newly introduced York City and two open franchise locations in Boca Raton and Houston. Both franchisees were customers first. Karen, our first franchisee, had visited our Dallas and New York locations. Courtney, our Houston franchisee, had been emailing us about franchising since 2015.

Why would someone choose a Blushington franchise instead of starting an independent business?

Recent findings suggest that maron: Running a business on your own is difficult. In a franchise system, you have support. Our franchisees have Stephi, me and our team. We can help with real estate selection, marketing and operations because we’ve spent years learning how those things work. We also believe in the combination of blowouts, makeup and skincare in one appointment. Customers save time, and franchisees are working with an established concept and brand.

What affects the cost of opening a location?

In a recent development, cohen: The investment includes the buildout, inventory and the products we select. We offer incentives for veterans and multi-unit owners. Our lounges also aren’t just service spaces. We host private parties and rent out the space, so that influences how we design and build them.

What did you need to demonstrate before asking someone to invest in a franchise?

Industry observers note that maron: We needed to show that customers wanted multiple services under one roof. We’re seeing close to two services per appointment. Someone comes in for a blowout and adds makeup or lashes. People don’t want appointments in different locations, long waits, inconsistent quality or an overwhelming product selection. Our business is built around making that easier.

#62. Exclusive: Onyx Security brings AI agent governance to Glean’s enterprise AI platform

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4 min read (713 words)
AI & Tech

Exclusive: Onyx Security brings AI agent governance to Glean’s enterprise AI platform

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read | Sumber: https://siliconangle.com/2026/11/13/exclusive-onyx-security-brings-ai-agent-governance-to-gleans-enterprise-ai-platform/

💡 Key Takeaways
  • AI agent security startup Onyx Security Inc.
  • Onyx and Glean are pitching the integration at companies that are moving rapidly to roll out autonomous, connected agents across their departments.
  • According to Onyx, security teams now need to keep continuous track of agent access, actions and policy compliance.

AI agent security startup Onyx Security Inc. today confirmed an integration with enterprise artificial intelligence platform organization Glean Technologies Inc. to help enterprises govern the AI agents they build and run on Glean.

Onyx and Glean are pitching the integration at companies that are moving rapidly to roll out autonomous, connected agents across their departments. Onyx claims, however, that most of them are not yet prepared to manage the risks that agents bring.

According to Onyx, security teams now need to keep continuous track of agent access, actions and policy compliance. Under the partnership, Glean provides the platform to build, deploy and operate the agents, while the Onyx secure AI control plane is used to extend governance and security across the AI environment.

It has been revealed that at the core of the integration is discovery, with Onyx able to inventory every Glean agent and the access and capabilities it holds. Ownership, business purpose and a risk classification can then be assigned to each agent, according to the companies.

Industry observers note that enterprise AI governance and compliance policies can also be applied through the integration, after which Onyx continuously assesses changes to the permissions, tools and data access granted to each agent. Intent-aware runtime controls, which Onyx applies to prompts, responses and agent actions, provide protection while the agents are running.

In a recent development, unsafe requests can be blocked outright under the controls. In other cases, the controls are stated to steer unintended agent actions back in line with firm policy. Centralized audit evidence is also maintained across AI environments. From deployment through ongoing operation and expansion, the companies say, agents fall under a single governance model.

Industry observers note that “As agents gain greater access and autonomy, security teams need visibility and control over what they can do,” said Gil Elbaz, co-founder and chief AI officer at Onyx, who previously worked under Nvidia Corp.’s chief technology officer. “By combining Glean’s enterprise context with Onyx’s security control plane, customers can govern agent activity consistently and confidently across their AI environment.”.

Glean regards context and governance as “foundational to making enterprise AI both useful and trustworthy,” according to Zubin Irani, the manufacturer’s vice president of partnerships. The Onyx integration is said to build on that foundation as organizations deploy agents across their business.

Recent findings suggest that coming into the partnership, Onyx has raised $153 million to date, including a $113 million Series B round led by Bessemer Venture Partners in July. The organization launched in March with $40 million in seed and Series A funding.

Glean, for its part, last raised $150 million in a Series F round at a valuation of $7.2 billion in June 2025.

Irani spoke with theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio, in June about how Glean’s AI platform leverages enterprise data to power models and agents:.

#63. Industry News: The Crunchbase Unicorn Board Tops 1,900 Companies In October, With 34 Companies Joining — Half Under 4 Years Old

Industry News: The Crunchbase Unicorn Board Tops 1,900 Companies In October, With 34 Companies Joining — Half Under 4 Years Old

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read | Sumber: https://news.crunchbase.com/venture/october-2026-unicorn-board-gains-34-tops-1900-ai-defense/

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A total of 34 companies joined The Crunchbase Unicorn Board in October, adding more than $96 billion in value and $14.8 billion in total funding to the board.
  • Last month’s new unicorn cohort also highlighted how quickly this AI cycle is awarding some companies with billion-dollar-plus valuations: Half of October’s new unicorns are less than 4 years old, and nine companies that joined the board during the month did so via seed or Series A raises.
  • Sources indicate that leading industries for unicorn formation last month were frontier labs, agentic AI, aerospace and semiconductors.

A total of 34 companies joined The Crunchbase Unicorn Board in October, adding more than $96 billion in value and $14.8 billion in total funding to the board. The board also reached a new record of 1,900 private companies last month, including an all-time high of more than 1,000 such startups based in the U.S.

Last month’s new unicorn cohort also highlighted how quickly this AI cycle is awarding some companies with billion-dollar-plus valuations: Half of October’s new unicorns are less than 4 years old, and nine companies that joined the board during the month did so via seed or Series A raises.

Sources indicate that leading industries for unicorn formation last month were frontier labs, agentic AI, aerospace and semiconductors. The U.S. accounts for 23 of the companies, while China and Korea each added three. Estonia added two, a record for the nation in a single month. Singapore, Germany and Japan each added one newly introduced unicorn.

The most valuable of the newly minted unicorns were electrical infrastructure tech giant Axiom Solutions International, TypeSafe AI  a model developer of Jev, and agentic AI assistant company Manus AI.

It has been revealed that familiar names topped the list of investors backing the latest cohort. Andreessen Horowitz has led rounds across seven portfolio companies over time, Sequoia Capital and General Catalyst in four companies and Eclipse three companies from this batch.

Here are October’s latest unicorn companies by industry segment.

According to recent reports, the Crunchbase Unicorn Board is a curated list that includes private unicorn companies with post-money valuations of $1 billion or more and is based on Crunchbase data. Latest companies are added to the Unicorn Board as they reach the $1 billion valuation mark as part of a funding round.

Sources indicate that the unicorn board does not reflect internal company valuations — such as those set via a 409a process for employee stock options — as these differ from, and are more likely to be lower than, a priced funding round. We also do not adjust valuations based on investor writedowns, which change quarterly, as different investors will not value the same company consistently within the same quarter.

Funding to unicorn companies includes all private financings to companies that are tagged as unicorns, as well as those that have since graduated to The Exited Unicorn Board.

Exits analyzed here only include the first time a firm exits.

Industry observers note that please note that all funding values are given in U.S. dollars unless otherwise noted. Crunchbase converts foreign currencies to U.S. dollars at the prevailing spot rate from the date funding rounds, acquisitions, IPOs and other financial events are reported. Even if those events were added to Crunchbase long after the event was announced, foreign currency transactions are converted at the historic spot price.

#64. Exclusive: OpenAI disbands its stand-alone robotics team as its general models start running robots

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6 min read (1183 words)
AI & Tech

Exclusive: OpenAI disbands its stand-alone robotics team as its general models start running robots

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read | Sumber: https://fortune.com/2026/11/13/openai-disbands-robotics-team-as-its-general-models-start-running-robots/

💡 Key Takeaways
  • OpenAI has disbanded its stand-alone robotics team, moving its researchers onto other teams.The organization confirmed the reorganization when asked about it by Fortune.
  • Recent findings suggest that openAI had a robotics team in its early days but wound it down in 2020, with cofounder Wojciech Zaremba later citing limited robot data and a more efficient path toward artificial general intelligence (AGI)—the human-like AI that has been OpenAI’s goal since its founding—through other methods.
  • This line of thinking—that general AI models can be applied directly to controlling robots without the need to create specialized models with “spatial intelligence”—would seem to challenge the assumptions underpinning many of today’s robotics startups, which have raised billions on the premise that robots need brains of their own.

OpenAI has disbanded its stand-alone robotics team, moving its researchers onto other teams.The organization confirmed the reorganization when asked about it by Fortune. A company spokesperson noted that robotics remains a core part of OpenAI’s long-term vision and portrayed the reorganization as a sign of the company’s commitment to robotics, rather than a retreat from it.OpenAI said it has reassigned its robotics research team to the company’s main research team, reporting to Chief Research Officer Mark Chen, while the applied robotics and hardware teams have been reassigned to the company’s larger Applied organization, which reports to OpenAI President Greg Brockman.The change came recently enough that OpenAI had already registered a booth at CoRL, a top academic robotics conference in Austin, this week. Though the conference app and floor plan marked OpenAI’s spot, when Fortune visited booth #208, it sat empty with OpenAI’s logo nowhere to be seen.

Recent findings suggest that openAI had a robotics team in its early days but wound it down in 2020, with cofounder Wojciech Zaremba later citing limited robot data and a more efficient path toward artificial general intelligence (AGI)—the human-like AI that has been OpenAI’s goal since its founding—through other methods. In particular, OpenAI became increasingly devoted to training ultra-large language models on vast datasets of human-written text. This is the approach that eventually yielded the company’s breakthrough product ChatGPT in late 2022.OpenAI rebuilt a stand alone robotics team in 2024, announcing a partnership with the startup Figure to develop AI models for humanoid robots. That partnership ended in February 2025, when Figure noted it would develop its own robot AI. OpenAI has said it is currently developing its own humanoid robot, with CEO Sam Altman targeting a first public demonstration in 2027. The company spokesperson said that despite the reorganization, OpenAI remains committed to bringing general-purpose robots into the world.The reorganization reflects a bet that is gaining traction across the AI industry: that general-purpose models built for language, code, and vision can also be used for “embodied AI”—where AI models control devices that can act in the physical world, such as robots, driverless cars, or drones. This would obviate the need to have separate robotics teams building specialized AI models just to be the digital “brains” for robots.Researchers have seen surprising performance when connecting GPT-6 Astra to robots, directly using the general-purpose AI model to perform some robotic tasks.Guanya Shi, an assistant professor at Carnegie Mellon University’s Robotics Institute, reacted to the change at OpenAI, telling Fortune that he would interpret the move as a signal that OpenAI sees robotics as “no longer a special problem.” Instead, he said, they likely see robotics as a challenge that can be addressed as a downstream application of general intelligence—similar to the way the same underlying frontier AI models now power specialized coding tools, or tools for legal or financial work.OpenAI seemed to confirm this view in its response to Fortune. It said that at the start of the year, the company’s researchers assumed the best way to make progress on robotics was to build on its work on AI models such as Sora, a video generation model that, in order to create realistic videos, had to have some implicit understanding of how the physical world works.But since then, the company spokesperson said, the company’s general-purpose frontier models, including GPT-6 Astra, have shown that can be directly applied to robotics. This discovery is what motivated OpenAI to disband the stand alone robotics team and move the affiliated researchers onto teams working on more general AI models.The reorganization also comes at a time when OpenAI is under pressure to rein in its costs and show that it is more focused on a few, core products. Last year, Altman told the company that it needed to abandon “side quests,” and the company has jettisoned some efforts—including Sora—in order to reallocate computing resources to more core and potentially-profitable endeavors. The company is under pressure to stanch its heavy operating losses—which reportedly totaled $10.9 billion in the most recent quarter—as it seeks to close a fresh funding round and prepares for a possible IPO in early 2027.

This line of thinking—that general AI models can be applied directly to controlling robots without the need to create specialized models with “spatial intelligence”—would seem to challenge the assumptions underpinning many of today’s robotics startups, which have raised billions on the premise that robots need brains of their own.

But Russ Tedrake, an MIT professor and cofounder and CEO of Walden Robotics, noted robotics companies still have an advantage the AI labs don’t: Their robots are already gaining work experience in real places, such as on factory floors. Such “deployment” experience—and the data these robots gather—helps robots adapt to specific workplaces and tasks. Better foundational models make that site-specific data more valuable because robots can learn from it faster, Tedrake said.

Recent experiments have tested how much work a general-purpose model can do without specialized training on robotic data. Researchers gave Astra camera images, robot information and a control interface that allowed the model to command the robot to take certain actions. In an Nvidia study, an Astra-powered agent achieved a 74.8% success rate on a simulated manipulation benchmark—where the model commands a simulated robot in a digital simulation, as opposed to a real robot—compared with 51.0% reported by the best specialized robotic models on this leaderboard.

Shi said advances in general models’ spatial and reasoning capabilities already let them handle tasks that previously required dedicated training. They can cope when a bottle is in a different position or the lighting changes, and reason about the sequence of a task or which step went wrong, he said.

Meanwhile, large language models are powerful but slow and need to be hosted in the cloud, meaning the robot or device needs a constant network connection. Shi still sees a need for smaller, specialized models that can run on a robot’s onboard computer without needing a constant internet connection.

“There may be different starting points for how to grow intelligence,” Pete Florence, cofounder of Generalist, a startup training general-purpose AI models for robots, told Fortune. He said it was unclear that any existing model would be the one that dominates robotics in the long-run.For its part, OpenAI said it was reassigning its robotics researchers to other teams because it now believes this is the best way to accelerate progress towards building general-purpose robots.

Back at booth #208 at CoRL, a few former members of the once-unified, stand-alone OpenAI robotics team milled about. They still drew a crowd, despite having no display or demo. After all, one of the conference’s hottest questions was how much robotics expertise would remain valuable as general-purpose models grew more capable—and the experience of those former OpenAI robotics researchers, now dispatched to other teams, offered one answer. #66. Breaking: After challenging Google’s Android with Cyanogen, its co-founder takes aim at Windows for AI era

📅 10 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5 min read (1075 words)
