Breaking: After challenging Google’s Android with Cyanogen, its co-founder takes aim at Windows for AI era

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read | Sumber: https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/10/after-challenging-googles-android-with-cyanogen-its-co-founder-takes-aim-at-windows-for-ai-era/

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Almost a decade after Cyanogen shut down its Android operating-system business following a years-long, unsuccessful effort to loosen Google’s dominance, its co-founder, Kirt McMaster, is now targeting Microsoft’s Windows with a latest operating system designed for people who rely heavily on artificial intelligence in their everyday work.
  • According to recent reports, mcMaster’s company, Kora Systems, on Tuesday unveiled a Linux-based desktop operating system that integrates AI models and autonomous agents directly into the computing experience, allowing them to work across applications, access files, and retain context between tasks.
  • Kora is developing the eponymous operating system with a team of about 50 engineers, relying on AI coding tools, including OpenAI’s Codex and Anthropic’s Claude.

Almost a decade after Cyanogen shut down its Android operating-system business following a years-long, unsuccessful effort to loosen Google’s dominance, its co-founder, Kirt McMaster, is now targeting Microsoft’s Windows with a latest operating system designed for people who rely heavily on artificial intelligence in their everyday work.

According to recent reports, mcMaster’s company, Kora Systems, on Tuesday unveiled a Linux-based desktop operating system that integrates AI models and autonomous agents directly into the computing experience, allowing them to work across applications, access files, and retain context between tasks. The software is expected to launch in 2027 as a free-to-use desktop operating system, with support for existing Intel- and AMD-powered PCs as well as machines running Qualcomm’s Snapdragon chips.

Kora is developing the eponymous operating system with a team of about 50 engineers, relying on AI coding tools, including OpenAI’s Codex and Anthropic’s Claude. McMaster told TechCrunch that these tools have accelerated development by at least fivefold, with most of the gains coming over the past six months.

Microsoft has long dominated the PC operating-system market, making it hard for newer players to establish a foothold. Windows held about 77% of the worldwide desktop operating-system market in October, compared with nearly 10% for Apple’s OS X, according to Statcounter’s web traffic data.

However, McMaster believes Kora does not need to compete for Windows’ entire user base. Rather, he is targeting people who use AI extensively and are willing to pay for access to powerful models and services.

“Microsoft can keep its billion consumers,” McMaster noted, estimating that 45 million to 50 million people at the moment account for much of AI usage and revenue. He expects that market to exceed 200 million users by 2033.

McMaster told TechCrunch that his experience at Cyanogen, where he spent over five years, taught him the dangers of relying on the very company he was trying to challenge. Cyanogen remained heavily dependent on Google Mobile Services despite offering features beyond Google’s version of Android. That ultimately restricted its ability to build an independent ecosystem.

“If you are trying to compete with an incumbent but are still reliant on them, you have no chance,” he mentioned.

Kora, McMaster said, builds on an idea he pursued toward the end of his time at Cyanogen, when he began exploring ways to integrate third-party services directly into the operating system. With Kora, he wants AI models and agents to work across applications and access files without being confined to individual apps.

Sources indicate that previously known as Playtron, a gaming operating-system manufacturer led by McMaster, the Palo Alto-based company rebranded as Kora in July 2025 as it shifted its focus to AI. The decision came as early companies, including Perplexity and OpenAI, were moving into AI-powered web browsers, McMaster noted. He believed browsers would not give AI agents enough access to a computer to carry out more complex tasks, making an operating system a better starting point.

The shift also allowed Kora to build on nearly three years of work developing Playtron’s Linux-based gaming operating system, called GameOS, instead of starting from scratch.

It has been revealed that kora is designed to let owners work with different AI models and agents across applications, while keeping track of conversations, documents, and other information. It also allows AI agents to operate in separate workspaces with restricted access to files and other resources.

While McMaster has drawn on his experience at Cyanogen, none of Kora’s engineers worked there. Instead, the company recruited heavily from the Linux gaming community, he told TechCrunch.

It has been revealed that kora’s software is built on Linux and uses Nix. It replaces the Fedora Silverblue foundation of Playtron’s earlier GameOS.

While Linux and Nix are open source, McMaster stated Kora’s own technology, including its Cortex AI engine and desktop interface, remains proprietary. The company, he said, intends to support AI models and services from different providers, although it has not committed to making its own software open source.

Gaming also remains part of Kora’s intends. McMaster said the firm intends to introduce AI-powered tools that would allow developers to create, publish, and play games directly within the operating system. He added that support for Android apps is also on its roadmap.

McMaster told TechCrunch that Kora’s team has worked closely with Qualcomm’s engineers for nearly a year to optimize the operating system specifically for Snapdragon-powered PCs. The collaboration includes support for Qualcomm’s Snapdragon X2 Elite chips.

In a recent development, alongside Qualcomm, Kora is working with Saudi Arabia’s AI company Humain on an enterprise version of the operating system, called Humain OS, which is expected to run on Snapdragon-powered laptops in 2027. Kora also aims to announce partnerships with PC manufacturers at a later date, though McMaster did not identify any companies or provide a specific timeline.

It has been revealed that kora plans to generate revenue through subscriptions that bundle access to AI models and agentic services. Moreover, its Cortex engine is designed to run AI tasks locally when possible and use cloud-based models for work requiring more computing power.

Recent findings suggest that kora’s investors include Samsung Next, Square Enix, Alumni Ventures, Polychain, VanEck, and Circle, all of which previously backed Playtron. The manufacturer, McMaster stated, has raised additional funding since shifting its focus to AI. However, he declined to disclose the total amount raised or its valuation. Kora has enough funding to operate for several years, he said.

Millennials wrote off tax accounting. Now Gen Z has a reason to give it a second look, as six-figure earnings and a talent shortage have resulted in a spike in salaries for tax experts.

Industry observers note that tax work has earned two spots on Monster’s seasonal jobs list. The firm’s 2026 Seasonal Hiring Index names tax associates and tax experts among 13 titles that saw significant seasonal posting activity in 2025. The primary busy season for tax accountants runs from late January through April 15, spurred by individual and corporate tax deadlines.

“Seasonal work is more than a short-term paycheck; it’s often the start of a longer career journey,” the Monster report said. It added that many companies use seasonal roles as a testing ground for permanent ones.

Industry observers note that according to ZipRecruiter, the average salary for U.S. tax associates is $33.40 an hour. The same site states that tax experts make $45.67 an hour in the U.S.

Industry observers note that tax jobs face a significant talent shortage, which is creating an opening for newcomers. The U.S. faced a shortage of 340,000 tax accountants in 2024, according to the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, and employers are still struggling to recruit.

Companies surveyed by Personiv, a global finance and accounting outsourcing organization, reported an average of 17 unfilled accounting and finance positions in 2026, compared with five a year earlier.

In a recent development, for job seekers, a seasonal tax role could lead to more opportunities than a temporary paycheck. It could be the first move toward a full-time career with six-figure earning potential, Fortune reports.

The catch with tax accounting is that the seasonal hiring rush may already be passing.

Anyone waiting until the holidays to start applying for seasonal tax roles risks missing the prime recruiting window.

Monster’s analysis found that seasonal job postings rose 44% between August and September last year, and peaked in October. By November, posting activity fell 24% from October. That indicates that the prime hiring time for these roles may have already passed.

Recent findings suggest that also, the bigger paychecks in accounting come with a higher bar to entry. Tax accountants typically need at least a bachelor’s degree. Meanwhile, earning a certified public accountant (CPA) license can open the door to better-paid roles, but requires an extensive investment of time and money. CPAs provide a range of services, including tax preparation and financial planning.

Investopedia reported total compensation of up to $200,000 for CPAs with four years of experience under their belt.

For young people looking for work, even a temporary position could offer a paycheck and experience. According to the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, only 53.8% of young people (ages 16 to 24) were employed in July. The youth unemployment rate was 9.1% that month.

Industry observers note that additionally, the transition from college to the workforce has become more difficult. A survey from career services site Kickresume found that just 12% of recent graduates secured full-time jobs before graduation this year, compared with nearly 40% of earlier graduates.

Industry observers note that AI is adding to that uncertainty. Goodwill CEO Steve Preston mentioned in an interview with Fortune last year that automation is reducing entry-level opportunities, which are the jobs where young workers traditionally gain experience.

Seasonal openings aren’t always labeled that way.

Industry observers note that in 2025, fewer than 3% of seasonal job postings included “seasonal,” “holiday,” or “temporary” in the title, per Monster. Searching for a specific role, such as “tax associate,” could uncover opportunities that a search for “holiday jobs” misses.

Monster also recommends widening the search across roles and industries.

“A seasonal opening can be hiding among jobs that, by title alone, look like ordinary year-round positions,” the report indicated.

Additional capabilities for electronics are also being added to the center's current capabilities in the near future.

"Events like ManuTech LIVE help people see the career possibilities in front of them and understand the role apprenticeship training can play in building a strong manufacturing workforce.".

ManuTech LIVE is designed for manufacturers, technology companies, students, educators, community leaders and anyone interested in the technologies and training shaping the region's manufacturing future.

#69. Startup Founders Are Using AI To File Patents. Here’s Where DIY Becomes A Liability.

📅 10 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4 min read (856 words)

Startup Founders Are Using AI To File Patents. Here’s Where DIY Becomes A Liability.

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read | Sumber: https://news.crunchbase.com/ai/startup-founder-diy-patents-legal-liabiity-drapkin-mutter-landfall/

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, patents can help startups establish competitive advantage, attract investors and protect innovations.
  • Recent findings suggest that AI is changing that equation.
  • It has been revealed that but AI’s capabilities are jagged.

According to recent reports, patents can help startups establish competitive advantage, attract investors and protect innovations. But the traditional patent process is expensive, slow and difficult to navigate, particularly for companies with limited resources.

Recent findings suggest that AI is changing that equation. General-purpose tools can research existing patents, document inventions and generate drafts that look like patent applications in minutes. Handling the process themselves can seem like an easy way for founders to save money.

It has been revealed that but AI’s capabilities are jagged. AI can perform some tasks remarkably well while missing legal and strategic issues that determine a patent’s commercial value. An application can look sophisticated while providing little meaningful protection.

For example, a patent’s claims define its legal boundaries and what you can stop competitors from doing. Mistakes involving claim scope may remain hidden until an investor, acquirer or competitor scrutinizes the tech giant’s intellectual property.

According to recent reports, the question isn’t whether startups should use AI. It’s how much founders can safely do themselves and when legal expertise becomes essential.

Recent findings suggest that founders can use AI to organize technical documentation, summarize existing patents and identify potentially relevant prior art. Turning engineering notes into an organized invention disclosure, for example, can reduce preparation costs and help counsel focus on strategy.

Recent findings suggest that but the opportunity extends beyond DIY. The right counsel can orchestrate AI across the workflow, coordinating invention discovery, drafting, drawings and quality checks. AI can help counsel explore alternative implementations with the inventors, identify disclosure gaps and check support for claims. Attorneys can direct that work, evaluate the results and connect each step to best protect business needs.

Industry observers note that that combination can produce more comprehensive applications with substantially greater efficiency. It is fundamentally different from generating an application with a chatbot and asking a lawyer to review it afterward.

The cheapest filing option is not necessarily the most economical. A poorly prepared application can create false confidence while leaving valuable innovations exposed.

Counsel can help decide what to patent versus maintain as a trade secret, prioritize filings within the tech giant’s budget and assess deadlines before disclosure or filing limits the available options. An internal process that competitors cannot observe or reverse engineer, for example, may be better kept as a trade secret.

Claim scope requires particular judgment. A fraud detection claim tied to one algorithm may leave competitors free to deliver the same functionality using another. Overly broad claims may overlap with existing technology. Valuable claims target what competitors must do to compete. Ideally, a single identifiable competitor can infringe them, and that infringement can be detected and proven.

Sources indicate that the specification must describe alternatives and variations that support broader claims later without unnecessarily limiting their scope. AI can assist, but strategic judgment must guide the work.

Industry observers note that filing volume says little about commercial value. Investors and acquirers will look beyond the number of pending applications to ask:.

AI’s greatest value is not simply generating more applications at lower costs. It is making meaningful protection more accessible without sacrificing legal judgment.

Recent findings suggest that founders should ask how a firm coordinates its AI tools and legal expertise, not simply whether it uses AI. The answer should explain how that process improves both efficiency and substance.

Ultimately, the most expensive patent mistake may be discovering too late that a DIY application never adequately protected the innovation on which the business was built.

He previously founded one of the largest electronics and computer patent prosecution practices in the U.S. at an Am Law 100 firm and was named U.S. Patent Practitioner of the Year by Managing IP in 2022.

Mutter pioneered the creation of automation systems and tools that enhance efficiency across all aspects of legal services. His clients include both startups and large public companies.

#70. The NFL injury report explained: what questionable, doubtful and out mean

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 19 min read (3877 words)

The NFL injury report explained: what questionable, doubtful and out mean

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 19 min read | Sumber: https://qz.com/nfl-injury-report-questionable-doubtful-out

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The NFL injury report explained, from questionable, doubtful and out designations to practice participation, the Friday report and game-day inactives, and why the labels matter.
  • Recent findings suggest that the NFL injury report is a league-mandated public disclosure.
  • Sources indicate that opposing coaches read it while preparing for a game.

Free daily briefing on global business news.

The NFL injury report explained, from questionable, doubtful and out designations to practice participation, the Friday report and game-day inactives, and why the labels matter.

Recent findings suggest that the NFL injury report is a league-mandated public disclosure. Every team must file one for each regular-season game. The result is that everyone sees the same official information at the same time. It shows which players are hurt, what is wrong with them and whether they are expected to take the field.

Sources indicate that opposing coaches read it while preparing for a game. Fantasy football managers read it to set lineups. Bettors read it before placing wagers. Reporters read it to explain why a starter is missing. Each group works from the identical official list.

The report has a simple structure. Each entry names a player, the body part or illness involved and how much he took part in practice that day. Teams submit the report to the league, and the league makes it public. Later in the week, the report adds a game status for players whose availability is in question.

The game statuses each carry a specific meaning, and they are not interchangeable. Questionable signals uncertainty. Doubtful signals that a player is unlikely to play. Out means the player will not play in that game. A fourth label, probable, once sat at the top of the scale, but the league dropped it starting with the 2016 season.

The labels do not tell the whole story on their own. Practice participation — full, limited or did not participate — adds context that a game status alone does not provide. Timing matters too. For a typical Sunday game, teams release reports on Wednesday, Thursday and Friday. Only the Friday report carries game designations. The final answer arrives on game day, when teams submit their inactive lists about 90 minutes before kickoff.

Recent findings suggest that injured reserve sits outside this weekly system. It is a roster move, not a game status, and it works under its own set of rules.

The 10 slides below walk through each piece of the system. They cover who files the report, what each label means and how the weekly schedule unfolds. They also explain where injured reserve fits and why the league requires accurate information. Read together, they explain how a single injury listing moves from a Wednesday practice note to a game-day decision.

Recent findings suggest that the NFL injury report is a required public disclosure that every team must file for each of its regular-season games. It names the players who are hurt or ill, identifies the body part or illness involved and records how much each player took part in practice.

The requirement covers every club in the league. No team is exempt. The obligation attaches to each game on the regular-season schedule rather than to the season as a whole. A team therefore produces a newly introduced report for every matchup it plays.

Both clubs in a game carry the same duty. Each matchup therefore produces two reports, one from each side, covering the players on each roster who are dealing with a problem that week.

Each entry links a named player to a specific problem. An injury is listed by the part of the body affected, such as a knee, an ankle or a hamstring. A player who is sick rather than hurt is listed with an illness instead.

In a recent development, listing by body part keeps each entry brief. It also means an entry does not reveal a diagnosis or its severity. A knee listing alone does not show whether the problem is minor or serious.

Recent findings suggest that the second core element is practice participation. Alongside the injury itself, the report shows how fully each listed player practiced. That pairing gives readers two separate pieces of information about a player's condition in the same entry.

Recent findings suggest that teams do not publish the report through their own channels. Each club submits it to the league, and the league then makes it public. The information reaches fans, media and opposing teams through a single official route.

The report is a statement about players, not about the whole roster. A player who is healthy and practicing normally does not need to appear on it at all. Appearing on the report does not mean a player will miss time.

Practice participation is the part of the NFL injury report that records how much work each listed player did on a given day. Teams describe it with one of three labels: full participation, limited participation or did not participate.

Industry observers note that these labels describe what happened at practice. They do not say whether a player will suit up for the game. Game-status designations sit in a separate part of the report and serve a different purpose.

Full participation means the player took full part in practice. It is the strongest signal of health this section offers. A player can still appear on the report with a full listing because the injury itself remains on file.

Limited participation means the player practiced, but not fully. The label covers a wide range of workloads. It does not show which drills a player sat out or how much of the session he missed. Two players with the same limited listing may have done very different amounts of work.

Recent findings suggest that did not participate means the player stayed out of practice that day. The label on its own does not explain why. The body part or illness listed beside the player's name usually supplies that context.

Industry observers note that some absences have nothing to do with health. Teams can mark an entry as not injury related. A rest day or a personal matter falls into this group. A did-not-participate entry marked this way says little about a player's physical condition.

According to recent reports, teams do not always hold a real practice. When no real practice takes place, the report lists estimated participation instead. In that case, the team reports the level of work it expects each player would have managed in a normal session.

An estimate is a judgment, not a record of work done. A limited listing on an estimated report reflects the team's assessment rather than a session that actually happened. That distinction matters when a reader compares one day's entry with another's.

Industry observers note that questionable is the NFL injury report's label for a player whose availability for the upcoming game is uncertain. It does not predict that the player will sit or play. It signals only that the team has not ruled him in or out when the report is filed.

Older versions of the report attached a percentage to each game-status label. The league no longer does that. Questionable now carries no official numerical chance of playing. Any figure attached to it today is an outside estimate, not league policy.

It has been revealed that without a number, questionable covers a wide range of situations. A player managing a minor problem and a player facing a real chance of missing the game can carry the same label. The designation itself does not distinguish between them.

Industry observers note that players working through the league's concussion protocol can carry the questionable tag late in the week. A player in the protocol cannot return until both the team physician and an independent neurological consultant clear him. That clearance can come after the team files its final weekly report.

It has been revealed that practice participation helps narrow the picture. A questionable player who closed the week with full participation presents a different case from one who did not practice on any day. A player who moved from did not participate to limited also shows a different trend from one who stayed limited all week.

According to recent reports, the designation reflects the team's view when the last report of the week is filed. A player's condition can still change before kickoff. Teams can downgrade a questionable player to out after that report. A downgrade means he will not play.

The inactive list settles the matter on game day. A questionable player left off that list is available to suit up. One who appears on it will not play, whatever the earlier report stated.

For fantasy managers and bettors, questionable marks an open question rather than a final verdict. The practice record, any late downgrade and the inactive list together carry more information than the label alone.

Doubtful means a player is unlikely to play in the upcoming game. On the NFL's game-status scale, it sits between questionable, which signals genuine uncertainty, and out, which means the player will not suit up.

According to recent reports, the label reveals which way a team is leaning. A questionable player could go either way. A doubtful player carries a clear lean toward missing the game, but the team has not ruled him out.

Doubtful is not a final decision. The team keeps the option of playing him. He stays on the roster and can still be named active on game day. The definitive answer comes with the inactive list the team submits shortly before kickoff.

It has been revealed that A team can also settle the question earlier. If it decides before game day that the player will not play, it can downgrade him from doubtful to out. That change tells everyone the absence is confirmed.

According to recent reports, doubtful appears only on the week's final injury report, the one that carries game designations. Earlier reports in the week list a player's injury and practice work but no game status. A player can therefore be on the report all week and pick up the doubtful tag only at the end.

Doubtful is a game-status designation, not a practice label. Reading it next to the player's practice entries gives a fuller picture. A doubtful player who sat out every session that week presents a different case from one who was limited late in the week. A late-week limited session indicates the player was back on the field in some capacity.

Recent findings suggest that the designation applies to one specific game. A player listed as doubtful this week starts fresh on the next week's report, where he may carry a different label or none at all.

Like the other game designations, doubtful can be attached to an illness as well as an injury.

For anyone planning around the game, the label works as an early signal of a likely absence. A doubtful listing is the team's public notice that it does not expect the player on the field.

An out designation means the player will not play in that game. It is the most definitive game-status label on the NFL injury report. It leaves no room for a late decision.

According to recent reports, questionable and doubtful both describe a degree of uncertainty. Out removes it. Once a team lists a player as out, his availability for that game is settled.

The label covers one game at a time. On its own, it does not say how serious an injury is or how long recovery will take. A player can be ruled out with a minor strain one week and practice fully the next. Another player can carry the same label for several straight games while a longer injury heals.

Each new game brings a new report. The status does not carry over automatically. A player listed out this week has his availability assessed again for the next game.

According to recent reports, the entry also highlights why the player is out. The report names the body part or illness involved, such as a knee, a hamstring or a concussion. Readers see the status and its cause on the same line.

Industry observers note that practice participation sits alongside the designation. The report records whether a player practiced fully, in a limited way or not at all during the week. Those entries describe how the week went. The out designation records the outcome for the game.

Sources indicate that out does not change a player's roster status. He stays on the team's roster even though he will not play. That separates the label from roster transactions, which move a player into a different category altogether.

Recent findings suggest that the certainty matters on both sidelines. A team that rules a player out can build its game blueprint around his absence before kickoff. The league publishes the report. The opponent therefore works from the same information.

In a recent development, the label is read closely outside the stadium as well. An NFL player who does not appear in a game earns no fantasy points. Fantasy managers treat an out designation as a signal to change their lineups. Bettors read it the same way — as a confirmed absence rather than a possibility.

According to recent reports, the NFL stopped using the probable designation starting with the 2016 season. Probable had told readers that a player was likely to play. Its removal left the injury report with three game-status labels instead of four.

It has been revealed that before the change, the report used a four-step scale. Probable sat at the top, followed by questionable, doubtful and out. Each label signaled a different level of confidence that a player would be available on game day.

With probable gone, the scale has three steps: questionable, doubtful and out. Questionable is now the least severe label a team can assign.

Players who once would have carried a probable tag did not disappear from the report. A player who is expected to play but still has an injury is usually listed with his practice status and no game designation. His name, the injury and his participation level still appear. The game-status column next to him stays blank.

In a recent development, that blank space carries meaning. A player on the report without a designation is generally someone the team expects to have available. A player with questionable next to his name is someone whose availability is still uncertain.

The change shifts more of the reading work onto the practice entries. Under the old system, one word summed up the team's outlook for a lightly injured player. Now readers build that outlook from the participation notes logged across the practice week.

Recent findings suggest that older news coverage, archived reports and past fantasy football advice can still mention probable players. Those references describe a system that ended before the 2016 season began. They do not reflect how current injury reports are written.

Anyone comparing injury reports across seasons should keep the switch in mind. A probable listing in 2015 and an entry with no game designation in 2017 could point to the same expectation that a player would suit up. The two entries record it under different reporting rules.

For a typical Sunday game, NFL teams file three injury reports during the week: one on Wednesday, one on Thursday and one on Friday. The Friday report is the one that carries game-status designations such as questionable, doubtful and out.

The Wednesday and Thursday reports serve a different purpose. They record which players are hurt or ill, the body part or illness involved, and how much each player took part in that day's practice. They do not assign a game status. A player listed on Wednesday is not being ruled in or out for Sunday at that point. Teams submit each of these daily reports to the league, which then makes it public.

In a recent development, each report captures a single day. Read together, the three releases form a sequence. A player whose practice participation rises from Wednesday to Friday highlights a different trend from one whose participation stays flat or drops. A name that appears on Thursday but not on Wednesday points to an injury or illness that surfaced midweek.

Friday changes the nature of the document. Alongside the practice information, teams attach a game designation to players whose availability is in doubt. That makes the Friday release the main public statement of a team's expectations before the weekend.

Sources indicate that the Friday report is still not the last word. Game status can shift between Friday and kickoff. A team can still update a player's status after the Friday release, such as downgrading him to out. The final list of players who will not suit up comes later, on game day itself.

It has been revealed that not every game falls on a Sunday. Teams that play on a Monday, a Thursday or another day follow a shifted version of the same cycle. The specific release days move with the date of the game. The Wednesday-to-Friday pattern does not carry over unchanged.

For a non-Sunday matchup, the timing of that week's reports differs from the standard Sunday pattern.

In a recent development, every NFL team must submit its list of inactive players about 90 minutes before kickoff. That list is the final, official word on who will not suit up. It can also differ from the game designations a team gave on its Friday report.

According to recent reports, the inactive list answers a narrower question than the weekly injury report. The injury report describes health and practice work across a week. The inactive list simply names the players on the active roster who will not dress for that specific game.

Industry observers note that those two documents do not always line up. A player listed as questionable on Friday has no settled status until inactives arrive. He either appears on the list or he does not. That ends the uncertainty for that game.

Sources indicate that change can run in either direction. A player who seemed likely to play can suffer a setback over the weekend or in pregame warmups and end up inactive. A player carrying a game designation can also be cleared and take the field.

Not every inactive player is hurt. Teams cannot dress their entire active roster, so some healthy players sit out each week. Coaches decide who stays in uniform based on depth at each position and the needs of that matchup. A name on the inactive list does not, by itself, signal an injury.

The timing matters to anyone tracking player availability. Fantasy football managers and sports bettors watch for the list closely. It is the last official upgrade before the game begins. For a player listed as questionable, it is often the first definitive one.

It has been revealed that A player's status can remain open until that deadline. As a result, a Friday questionable tag can leave fans waiting into game day for an answer. The requirement applies to every game, whether it kicks off on a Sunday afternoon, a weeknight or in prime time.

The inactive list is also separate from roster transactions. A player on it remains on the team's active roster. He can be available the following week without the team making any move. That distinction separates a one-game inactive from longer-term absences handled through formal roster changes.

Injured reserve is a roster transaction, not a game-status label. A player marked out on the weekly injury report is ruled out of one game. A player placed on injured reserve must sit out a minimum number of games before he is eligible to return.

The two terms describe different things. Out is a designation tied to a single upcoming game. It tells the public that the player will not take the field that week. It notes nothing about the weeks after that. The following week, the player goes through the reporting cycle again, and his status is set fresh.

It has been revealed that injured reserve runs on a different timeline. Moving a player there changes his roster status rather than his availability for one game. Once the move is made, the player cannot come back simply because he has healed. He has to wait out the required minimum first.

That minimum has not stayed the same. The NFL has changed the number of games an injured reserve player must miss over the years. To work out how long a specific player will be sidelined, check the rule in force for that season.

The two terms also surface in different places. Out appears on the weekly injury report, next to the player's practice participation. A move to injured reserve is announced as a roster transaction. A player on injured reserve is already ineligible to play. He does not need a weekly game designation to confirm it.

Sources indicate that the terms carry different expectations as well. An out designation leaves open a quick return, sometimes as soon as the next game. Injured reserve signals that the team expects the player to be unavailable for at least the minimum stretch. A team can also list a player as out for several straight weeks without ever moving him to injured reserve.

Recent findings suggest that for anyone following a team, each term answers its own question. Out answers whether a player will appear this weekend. Injured reserve answers a longer question: the earliest point at which he is allowed to return to the field.

The NFL requires teams to report player injuries accurately, and the league can discipline a club that fails to do so. That requirement turns the weekly injury report from a courtesy into an obligation.

Sources indicate that accuracy applies to every element a club files. A game status has to reflect the team's honest read of a player's availability. A practice entry has to reflect the work the player actually did, not a softer or harsher version of it. The obligation holds for each report a team releases during the week, not only the one that carries game designations.

According to recent reports, misreporting can run in either direction. A club might hide an injury to keep an opponent guessing about a key starter. It might also list a healthy player with an injury to create doubt that does not exist. Both versions mislead the opposing staff and anyone else relying on the report.

Industry observers note that competitive fairness is the main reason the rule matters. Both teams in a game prepare with the same official information about each other. A club that shades its report gains an edge its opponent cannot see or correct before kickoff.

Recent findings suggest that public trust is the second reason. The report reaches a far wider audience than the two coaching staffs. For readers outside the building, the report is the league's official record of who is hurt. Their confidence in the report depends on the league holding clubs to it.

Sources indicate that the rules also give teams an honest outlet for absences that have nothing to do with injury. A player can be listed as not injury related. A club therefore has no reason to invent an ailment to explain a missed practice.

Enforcement rests with the league itself. The NFL receives each club's report, publishes it and can act when a filing falls short. Penalties can include fines against the club.

Secretary of Commerce Howard Lutnick is now facing public pressure from his fellow Cabinet members over his decision to not blacklist Megaspeed, the cloud computing company at the center of Nvidia ex-CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with a suspected Chinese spy.

The Treasury Department, among other federal agencies, were in favor of placing trade restrictions on Megaspeed, but the decision ultimately lay with Lutnick, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told CNBC on Friday.

“There was coordination. Treasury, War, USTR, and State were in favor of putting Megaspeed on the entity list for months,” he mentioned. “But Commerce has the pen….You will have to ask them about their internal processes.”.

Megaspeed is under investigation by the Justice Department over the suspected violation of U.S. export controls, which prohibit certain U.S.-made chips from being sold and shipped to China. Helmed by Alice Huang, the alleged spy, Megaspeed and its Malaysian subsidiary Speedmatric shipped at least $7.5 billion in Nvidia chips to China over two years, The Information reported.

Sources indicate that lutnick is facing intensifying scrutiny over reports he took action to protect Nvidia from the Trump administration’s export controls of U.S. AI hardware to China. The commerce secretary reportedly spent months “undoing” efforts to hold Megaspeed accountable for potential export control violations, Axios reported. Bessent confronted Lutnick in the Situation Room following the midterm elections over not placing Megaspeed on the entity list, according to the outlet.

Bessent told CNBC, “We don’t repeat conversations in the Situation Room.”.

Sources indicate that according to the Fresh York Times, when Trump officials approached Oracle about cancelling a $7 billion deal to lease chips to Chinese tech conglomerate Tencent, Lutnick’s top deputy Jeff Kessler spoke up and mentioned Lutnick had complications with a cancellation, as it would halt the shipment of 100,000 advanced Nvidia AI chips. Lutnick reportedly said he didn’t understand the rush to scrap the deal.

The Commerce Department and Nvidia did not immediately respond to Fortune’s request for comment.

Both Republican and Democratic lawmakers want to hold Lutnick accountable for not placing Megaspeed on the blacklist.

“The obvious question is why did he choose to sell advanced chips?” Republican Louisiana Sen. John Kennedy told Politico. “Secretary Lutnick needs to answer that in front of God and country.”.

It has been revealed that lutnick agreed to testify alongside Huang before the Senate Banking Committee to address national security concerns on Dec. 10.

Sources indicate that meanwhile, senior White House officials are now weighing whether to oust the commerce secretary from his position, Reuters reported. Even before news of Huang’s affair broke, Lutnick’s decision not to add 100 companies, including China’s DeekSeek, to the entity list put him in hot water.

Industry observers note that lutnick argued with senior White House officials that export regulations against China would stoke the trade war with China and he insisted on having conversations with Trump about China’s restricted access to U.S. chips, the Times reported.

The commerce secretary also had a friendly relationship and financial ties with Nvidia, bolstering concerns about favoritism toward the tech tech giant.

“Howard is the person I talk to most in the administration—he’s on top of the technology and learning the industry promptly,” Huang stated in September 2025.

Before Lutnick became commerce secretary, he was the CEO and chairman of investment bank Cantor Fitzgerald, which held about $1.2 billion in Nvidia stock prior to President Donald Trump’s second term.

by Todd Bishop on Nov 12, 2026 at 12:15 pmNovember 12, 2026 at 12:16 pm.

Docugami, the Seattle-area startup led by XML co-creator Jean Paoli, has been acquired by Inveniam, a Detroit-area organization that uses blockchain to help investors verify the data behind assets such as commercial real estate and private loans.

The deal follows a partnership this summer in which the companies released DGML, Docugami’s open-source format for turning business documents into data that AI agents can use and check.

In a recent development, financial terms of the acquisition weren’t disclosed. All of Docugami’s employees are joining Inveniam, a Docugami spokesperson remarked. The team numbers about 50 including contractors. Paoli becomes Inveniam’s chief product and technology officer, and Docugami will keep operating from Kirkland, according to the announcement.

Paoli co-founded Docugami in 2018 after more than 20 years at Microsoft, where he helped create XML and the Office file formats.

It has been revealed that the startup, based in Kirkland, Wash., raised a $10 million seed round in 2020 led by SignalFire, with backing from Bob Muglia, the former Microsoft executive and Snowflake CEO. Grammarly, the writing-assistant organization now known as Superhuman, later disclosed that it had taken part in the round, its first investment in another company.

Industry observers note that prior to the acquisition, Docugami ranked No. 155 on the GeekWire 200, our list of the Pacific Northwest’s top independent, privately held startups.

DGML labels each piece of a document by what it is — a base rent, a loan payment, a liability cap — so a single figure can be traced back to the page it came from. Inveniam records a digital fingerprint of each of those data points on its blockchain, called NVNM Chain, so any later change reveals up.

Inveniam executives said Thursday morning on a livestream with Paoli that DGML solves a problem they’ve had in bringing on new clients: every client’s documents are different, which required templates and standard formats before the data could be used.

“One promise I want to make personally: DGML stays open and its openness is strategic to Inveniam,” Paoli wrote in a LinkedIn post.

Inveniam, led by CEO Patrick O’Meara, also acquired Mantra, a crypto company that provided the original technology for NVNM Chain, earlier this year. Mantra co-founder John Patrick Mullin remarked on the livestream that NVNM Chain will move to its own independent blockchain, with the main network expected to launch in the next few weeks.

Fees on that network will help fund buybacks of an NVNM cryptocurrency token, Mullin stated. O’Meara proposed a separate session on when that token will launch.

Chief Technology Officer Harsh Mehta, in turn, spent his time at Google DeepMind and Anthropic working on pretraining projects. Pretraining is a term for the initial phase of the AI development workflow.

It has been revealed that mirendil’s first product, Lor, is a platform that automates many of the tasks involved in model training runs. The company notes that the software does so by splitting work among hundreds of AI agents.

Sources indicate that large language model development involves a significant amount of trial and error. Researchers create multiple versions of an algorithm that differ from one another in small ways and compare them to find the most performant variant. According to Mirendil, Lor can automate that workflow. If an error crops up during the evaluation, the platform fixes it automatically.

Earlier this year, Mirendil asked one of its researchers to build a coding model that can compete with leading open-source LLMs. Usually, such projects are carried out by teams of specialists. Mirendil indicates that its automation technology enabled the researcher to build the model without any help from colleagues. The project cost $10 million and took about 3.5 months to complete.

The company’s agents wrote more than 99% of the code that powers the model, which is called Mirendil-Base. They set up infrastructure, found a suitable training algorithm and collected training data from the web. The agents then refined both the training dataset and Mirendil-Base’s architecture to boost output quality.

It has been revealed that the LLM is the foundation of a specialized coding model called Fern that the company unveiled last month. According to Mirendil, it’s designed to automate programming challenges commonly encountered by AI labs. Fern can process 10 million input tokens per prompt, or 10 times more than Claude Opus 5.5. That’s the equivalent of about a half-million lines of code.

In a recent development, fern is based on a version of Mirendil-Base with 100 billion to 500 billion parameters. Late last month, the company previewed two upgraded versions of the latter model with between 500 billion and 10 trillion parameters. Mirendil plans to use those algorithms to develop more capable LLMs.

With more than 50 million patient consents under management, Gaine is extending its proven capabilities to address the growing need among health intends and healthcare providers to manage consent, communication preferences, and data-sharing permissions across increasingly complex and fragmented technology environments.

As healthcare organizations accelerate interoperability, digital engagement, and AI initiatives, the ability to consistently identify individuals, understand their preferences, and honor consent decisions across systems has become increasingly critical.

"Healthcare organizations have invested heavily in capturing consent, but the real challenge is ensuring those decisions follow the individual across systems, programs, and interactions," said Martin Dunn, CEO of Gaine Technology. Moving Beyond Traditional Consent Management.

Unlike standalone consent applications, Gaine does not require organizations to replace existing systems. Instead, HDMP serves as an enterprise data management and orchestration layer, helping ensure individual choices are consistently understood and applied across the organization.

Expanding a Proven Healthcare Data Foundation.

Gaine's expansion brings established life sciences capabilities into the payer and provider markets, addressing use cases spanning member engagement, care management, patient communications, data sharing, and enterprise governance.

With a healthcare-specific ontology refined over more than 15 years, Gaine provides the identity, context, and relationships needed to transform fragmented consent records into trusted, actionable information.

#77. Series A In 2026: Capital Is Flowing Faster, But Fewer Startups Are Making The Cut

📅 09 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5 min read (1047 words)
General

Series A In 2026: Capital Is Flowing Faster, But Fewer Startups Are Making The Cut

📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read | Sumber: https://news.crunchbase.com/venture/series-a-2026-startup-capital-up-deals-steady/

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that more money is pouring into Series A rounds, but it isn’t opening the door to more startups.
  • Sources indicate that the numbers point to an increasingly divided early-stage market.
  • It has been revealed that investors are responding by moving in opposite directions: Some are writing much larger checks at seed to get ahead of the competition, while others are waiting until Series B or beyond for clearer evidence that a business is taking off.

Recent findings suggest that more money is pouring into Series A rounds, but it isn’t opening the door to more startups. U.S. companies have raised $42 billion at that stage this year through October, up roughly 60% year over year, while deal counts remain on pace with the past few years, Crunchbase data highlights.

Sources indicate that the numbers point to an increasingly divided early-stage market. AI is fueling demand for capital and helping some startups grow at unprecedented speeds, while others struggle to turn their first customers into repeatable sales.

It has been revealed that investors are responding by moving in opposite directions: Some are writing much larger checks at seed to get ahead of the competition, while others are waiting until Series B or beyond for clearer evidence that a business is taking off. (At Series B, too, we’re seeing a similar trend of fewer but larger deals.).

That leaves companies still proving their growth potential navigating a Series A funding crunch even as capital floods into the fastest-growing businesses.

Recent findings suggest that the low point for Series A funding in the past five years was 2023, with $23 billion invested in U.S.-based startups. Series A investment totals each year since have grown, doubling this year compared to 2023.

In a recent development, at the same time, round counts have settled, averaging 1,200 companies funded at Series A at $1 million or more in 2023 through 2025. This year, the trend is holding, with round counts in that range, give or take 100 deals.

“On the application side, it’s a bit harder, and that’s where I think there’s more of a Series A crunch,” according to Siddharth Ramakrishnan, a partner at Scale Venture Partners, which primarily leads Series A and B rounds.

This dynamic — steady deal count despite much more money flowing — is also impacting how early-stage VCs invest.

Recent findings suggest that among investors, there’s more competition, especially at the early stage. In turn, VCs are increasingly pursuing one of two opposing strategies: either writing much larger checks much earlier, or holding back until later rounds, Ramakrishnan said.

Recent findings suggest that with the first strategy, check sizes are getting much bigger, he noted, with $10 million to $20 million seed deals not uncommon. “Instead of waiting till the Series A, where they have $4 million in revenue and growing, you’re going to do it when they have $500,000 in revenue, they have a pilot, the team is smart,” he mentioned.

Sources indicate that other investors are waiting to invest later. “ ‘I’m not getting any new information by the time they’re at $2 million in revenue from $500,000, so I’m just going to wait until they actually take off,’ and then you’re seeing a gap,” Ramakrishnan mentioned, explaining the thinking behind this investment approach. “People are putting in a lot of money at the Series B, Series C onwards, because that’s when you get the signal that things are really working.”.

Sources indicate that scale expects there to be a bit more variance in this current fund. Its preference is to stay at Series A and B risk profile, by “potentially pulling a little bit earlier and a little bit later and recreating it in the aggregate,” he remarked.

The firm’s most recent fund 8 is its largest to date at $900 million, up from its prior $600 million fund.

“We still think that Series A is a great place to be if you can make it happen, because it’s at that point where you ideally have enough information to make an informed bet, but not enough that there’s still some of the growth investors that are scared to come in,” Ramakrishnan stated, “and so you get great companies at great prices.”.

At each quartile, U.S. Series A rounds have trended up in size this year, Crunchbase data shows. So far in 2026, 10% of Series A rounds are $75 million and over, up from $50 million in 2025.

Industry observers note that those much-larger checks are translating into hypergrowth for some companies. “Instead of going zero to $7 million, which in the old world would have been amazing numbers, now there’s people going zero to $20 million, or zero to $30 million,” Ramakrishnan stated.

Recent findings suggest that for founders, securing those larger checks often hinges on turning a handful of early customers into a repeatable sales process. Many startups get stuck in that transition, even as investors compete to back those that break through.

“If you have the ambition to build a world-class tech giant, then you also need to raise a substantial Series A to expand and go abroad, take on different types of markets,” according to European seed investor Anke Huiskes of NP-Hard Ventures, whom I interviewed on-stage at the HumanX Amsterdam conference on AI earlier this year.

“I think the whole messy phase is in this go-to-market phase where you don’t really know who your ideal customer profile is,” stated Huiskes, who invests at the seed stage in product-focused founders.

She’s seen startups get stuck when they have a few customers but aren’t growing fast enough. “A lot of the companies hang out here,” she said.

But for the companies who build that repetitive sales cycle, VCs are eagerly reaching out, she said: “And then I get a text, ‘Can you please give me an intro?’ And all of a sudden, I have 10 term sheets. So it’s really black and white.”.

#78. ‘The easiest way to penetrate a billion-dollar firm’: Ex-FBI operative on how spies target CEOs

Business & Policy

‘The easiest way to penetrate a billion-dollar firm’: Ex-FBI operative on how spies target CEOs

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read | Sumber: https://fortune.com/2026/11/13/jensen-huang-ceo-security-spies-fbi-cia-training/

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Jensen Huang’s exit from Nvidia has put a rarely discussed risk in plain view: for a CEO, a fresh business contact or a budding romance may come from someone more interested in the company’s secrets.
  • “Sometimes the easiest way to penetrate a billion-dollar tech giant is to get close to the person running it,” Eric O’Neill, a former FBI counterintelligence operative, told Fortune.
  • For O’Neill, protecting executives should include teaching them to recognize manipulation—and giving others a way to intervene when the boss won’t listen.

Jensen Huang’s exit from Nvidia has put a rarely discussed risk in plain view: for a CEO, a fresh business contact or a budding romance may come from someone more interested in the company’s secrets.

“Sometimes the easiest way to penetrate a billion-dollar tech giant is to get close to the person running it,” Eric O’Neill, a former FBI counterintelligence operative, told Fortune.

For O’Neill, protecting executives should include teaching them to recognize manipulation—and giving others a way to intervene when the boss won’t listen.

Huang stepped down Thursday as president, CEO, and a board member of Nvidia, No. 16 on the 2026 Fortune 500, amid scrutiny of his relationship with a woman suspected of spying for China. The company named chief financial officer Colette Kress interim CEO while its board searches for a permanent successor.

According to recent reports, in a message to employees Sunday, Huang acknowledged being unfaithful to his wife and noted he would cooperate with the board’s investigation. The New York Times reported that U.S. intelligence officials believed Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed, had been recruited by China’s intelligence service. The Chinese government has denied the allegations.

Nvidia’s board mentioned Sunday that it had no reason to believe manufacturer secrets or national security had been compromised, but that its independent investigation, led by a committee of independent directors, would examine all available information. The company has lost about $450 billion in market value since Huang’s admission.

Recent findings suggest that O’Neill, whose undercover work helped catch FBI spy Robert Hanssen, founded NeXasure AI and wrote Spies, Lies, and Cybercrime. He mentioned an intelligence-gathering attempt often looks, at first, like an ordinary relationship.

He stated an approach rarely begins with someone asking an executive to hand over tech giant secrets. It may start at a conference, through a business introduction, over drinks, or even on a dating app. The operative finds common ground, builds trust, and makes the executive feel key.

Recent findings suggest that romance can speed things up. Using romantic or sexual interest to gain information, access, or leverage is known as “honey trapping,” a tactic far older than dating apps.

It has been revealed that the warning signs can be subtle, O’Neill said: a relationship that moves unusually swiftly, persistent questions about sensitive business matters, requests to meet influential colleagues, or encouragement to keep secrets. The goal may be information, influence over a business decision, or compromising material that could later be used for blackmail.

Those signs are harder to recognize when the person under scrutiny is someone the executive trusts.

“By the time a security professional raises concerns, the executive may already be emotionally invested and unwilling to listen,” O’Neill mentioned.

It has been revealed that CEOs have access to information others want, from intellectual property and strategic plans to government relationships. O’Neill argues their security training should teach them how someone might use a personal relationship to get closer to those assets.

According to recent reports, peter Warmka, a former CIA senior intelligence officer who now trains executives through his Counterintelligence Institute, told Fortune his sessions cover who might target a firm, what they want, and how they approach employees and contractors. Senior executives are prime targets because of their access, he said, but their attitudes toward security can also leave them exposed.

“Unfortunately, they are also perceived as more vulnerable because many believe not all security measures imposed on lower-level employees also apply to them,” Warmka noted.

Much of his training focuses on overseas travel, including the risks of electronic eavesdropping in hotel rooms and on the way to meetings, intelligence collection targeting their devices, and interpreters who may work for intelligence services.

Even with that preparation, recognizing an attempt to extract information can be difficult. “Well-trained operatives know how to elicit information without raising suspicion,” Warmka remarked.

When a CEO dismisses a warning, someone else needs a way to act.

It has been revealed that chief security officers, general counsel, and chief information security officers should have a confidential route to independent directors, O’Neill noted. If the CEO will not cooperate, the board can bring in outside counsel and investigators to assess a credible threat and recommend protective measures. Where warranted, the company should involve federal authorities.

A romantic relationship alone does not prove espionage, O’Neill emphasized. Any investigation should be objective and discreet, balancing the executive’s privacy with the manufacturer’s security. That requires someone outside the relationship to assess the risk.

“No executive, regardless of wealth, reputation, or brilliance, should be the final authority on investigating a threat in which that executive may be personally compromised,” O’Neill said.

Tatiana Sataua is a News Fellow at Fortune covering business, technology, AI, and consumer culture.

#79. How the UEFA Nations League works: promotion, relegation and Euro routes

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 18 min read (3501 words)
